World.title: Tepoztlán: A pulque drinker’s ‘paradise’
World.content:
Arriving in Tepoztlán — the mountainous Pueblo Mágico about 90 minutes south of the heart of Mexico City’s Coyoacán neighborhood — evokes a surrealistic reverence for Mexico’s natural splendor.

Cradled in the Sacred Valley of Tepoztlán, after crossing into the state of Morelos, you’ll make a sweeping, winding descent into the forest-encircled town. A natural amphitheater is formed by the surrounding Sierra de Tepoztlán and Chichinautzin mountain range, while Tepoztlán’s cobblestoned roads and lazy plazas underscore the small town’s relaxing rhythms.

A spiritualist getaway

The pueblo is largely known for attracting hikers from around the globe, conveniently located at the edge of El Tepozteco National Park, which includes a 1.8-mile round-trip trek up a steep hill that culminates with the 500-year-old Pyramid of Tepoztecatl and panoramic views at the summit. In addition, the town provides a modernized mix of high-end dining options (such as Nixte, an upscale smokehouse serving indigenous Mexican food from a wood-fired kitchen), minimalistic elegance (Casa Ayehualco once belonged to the Mexican architects Diego Villaseñor and Ana María Maldonado) and contemporary Mexican art (Dilao, a surrealist sculpture garden, was inaugurated by the artist Eduardo Olbés in 2019).

Above all, Tepoztlán is heralded as a spiritualist getaway, with an abundance of health-forward, organic and old-world experiences focused on rejuvenating the body, mind and spirit. Massages, temazcales and psychedelic-induced retreats abound in the pueblo of just over 14,000.

And yet, one of its greatest features, which perhaps gets overlooked among Tepoztlán’s surplus of attractions and temptations, can be literally traced back to Mexico’s Indigenous roots with pulque.

Tepoztlán, a town of pulque worship

Pulque — the fermented sap of agave plants, known as aguamiel — is believed to be over 2,000 years old. A viscous, milky powerhouse, it’s one of Indigenous Mexico’s most defining libations.

What exactly does Tepoztlán have to do with pulque? Mexicas believed the region to be the site of Tepoztécatl — the god of fermentation and drunkenness. If that’s not convincing enough, Tepoztécatl’s mother, Mayahuel, is celebrated as the goddess of agave, fertility and — you guessed it — pulque.

Both Tepoztécatl and Mayahuel are intimately linked to Tepoztlán’s pre-Hispanic mythology, where Tepoztécatl, in particular, is believed to have founded the community. The nearby pyramid is recognized as an important ceremonial site dedicated to Tepoztécatl, built between 1150 and 1350.

It makes sense, then, that Tepoztlán has become a pilgrimage-worthy center for pulque worship, with more than two millennia’s worth of pulque cultivation and consumption. To date, tlachiqueros — a term derived from the Nahuatl word tlachiqui, or “one who scrapes,” to denote agricultural workers who tend agave sap — can be found throughout the region, gathering the aguamiel that eventually alchemizes into pulque. This fresh supply can be found at various pulquerias in town today, where there is never a shortage of the Mesoamerican “nectar of the gods.”

Pulque consumption in Mexico

And yet, Tepoztlán is not a mass producer of pulque, either. Instead, it’s hyper-local, artisanal and family-operated. Rural areas in Puebla, Hidalgo and Tlaxcala boast the largest pulque production. But Tepoztlán, despite its relatively diminutive size, is still viewed as a pulque drinker’s paradise for its quality and range of pulquerias.

Though deeply steeped in ancient customs, pulque is very much a part of the present-day Mexican lifestyle. According to Scielo, the consumption of pulque has risen in the last few years “due to a greater appreciation of national identity and its organic nature free of conservatives.” The love of pulque is ostensibly trending upward, as has been documented by Mexico News Daily. Tepoztlán, therefore, is in a prime position to showcase its best properties.

Gardens, wellness and pulque

When it comes to the artistry of organic, slow consumption, it doesn’t get more earthy than a glass of pulque. The beverage is a great fit for Tepoztlán’s gastronomic ethos, known for its array of healthy foods and traditional kitchens that serve regional dishes like itacates — a simple, corn-based dish often stuffed with natural ingredients like flor de calabaza.

In a modern-day context, this combination of wellness and indigenous foods translates deliciously for travelers and locals alike, who can taste a range of pulque styles and flavors to go along with it all.

Pulquimia — a botanical garden and pulqueria rolled into one — is a leading example of how the next generation of pulquerias are able to offer an elevated experience that remains grounded in pulque traditions. Flavors include inventive, health-forward combinations like cacao with amaranth, cinnamon and rose petals, or peanut with manzanilla and orange. The elixirs are said to help with one’s digestive and immune systems and overall health. Here, pulque isn’t something of the past to be consumed as a novelty. It’s a daily lifestyle anchored in holistic health practices. The pulqueria includes a covered outdoor patio with views of a lush garden and the abutting mountain peaks. In all, the experience is refreshing and calming, if not medicinal, in a way that would be hard to find in a larger city environment.

A guide to Tepoztlán pulquerias

Of course, there are also classic pulquerias that supply old-school dive-bar vibes rather than that of a glamorous resort getaway. One such joint is Pulques El Nectar Tepozteco, located on one of the pueblo’s main streets — which closes to vehicles on weekends and becomes swarmed by passersby and vendors on foot. The pulqueria is easy to find: it has a giant mural of a rabbit holding up a clay cup that is overflowing with pulque froth. Symbolically, the rabbit is a sign of fertility and intoxication in Mexica cosmology, and it is believed that the goddess of pulque gave birth to 400 rabbits. There is even a codex of drunkenness associated with various rabbits from Mexica times, demarcating one’s various levels of intoxication (loss of control, happiness, etc.).

Reveling in the spirit of pulque

El Nectar embodies this spirit. When I entered upon my first of a few visits, a man was passed out in a chair, drunkenly asleep, while others reveled joyously nearby. The menu is extensive, with no less than 10 options listed behind the counter at any time. I went with a mazapan and later a guayaba — both rich in texture, and one of which included the ground remains of natural ingredients that were at some point broken down to make the base of the beverage.

The pulque is thick, unmistakably fresh and made in-house, poured from ladles into various cup sizes, depending on your level of thirst and appetite. I asked to speak with an owner to get a sense of the place’s history, but I was told he’s only available on weekends, and alas, I was there during the week. But even without a private history lesson, the pulque at El Nectar was truly among the best I’ve ever encountered in my search for the finest “Champagne of the gods.”

Sipping all the way

I was also informed that the creatively named Pulques Tepoztlán, located further up the village roads, was a worthwhile stop on my pulque tour. Unfortunately, I was never able to make it due to ongoing storming conditions during my visit and constant power outages.

Before I left town, I did, however, swing by another purveyor of pulque: Pulque Coyote. Surreptitiously found inside a corner store that otherwise functions as a de facto Oxxo, you can ask the cashier about their pulque. It’s made locally, of course, and is bottled in an old, unmarked plastic jug, which certainly did not have pulque in it before. It’s a bit of a moonshine variety, without much explanation or frills. The place was only on my radar because I asked the concierge at my hotel where he recommends trying pulque. At Coyote, you can ask for your desired amount and take it to go, as there are no seats or places to lounge inside the small corner shop.

Wherever you load up, you will encounter a variety of pulquerias with their own spin on pulque, to be sure, all around town. Go forth, and drink responsibly.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World Cup 2026 Spain are champions of the world

Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time at MetLife Stadium to win the 2026 World Cup. Ferran Torres scored the only goal of a gripping final.

It is Spain’s second world title and their first since they lifted the trophy in 2010. A new generation has now matched the achievement of that side.

Argentina, the defending champions, fell just short of retaining the crown. Their long tournament ended in heartbreak.

A cagey, goalless 90 minutes

The final was tight and tense throughout normal time. Neither side could find a breakthrough across the opening 90 minutes.

Spain saw plenty of the ball but found Argentina well organised. The champions defended with the discipline that had carried them this far.

Chances were scarce as both teams guarded against a costly mistake. The occasion demanded caution and both sides obliged.

Lamine Yamal probed for openings down the right without a decisive breakthrough. Argentina crowded the space and forced Spain into wider areas.

As the game wore on, the prospect of penalties began to loom. Both benches prepared for a night that might run the full distance.

Ferran Torres decides it

The decisive moment came less than a minute into the second period of extra time. Nico Williams headed the ball back across the box and Ferran Torres finished past Emiliano Martínez.

The goal, in the 106th minute, broke Argentine resistance at last. Spain finally had the opening they had been searching for.

From there Spain defended their lead with composure. Argentina pushed forward but could not find a reply.

The remaining minutes were fraught as Argentina threw bodies forward. Spain held their shape and saw out the biggest night in their recent history.

Heartbreak for Argentina

Argentina had built their run on late drama and remarkable resilience. This time there was no comeback to be found.

Lionel Messi ended the tournament with eight goals to his name. His side could not deliver the fairytale ending they had chased.

Retaining a World Cup remains one of football’s rarest feats. Argentina came within 15 minutes of forcing a shootout.

Their run to the final had featured comebacks against Egypt and England. On the biggest night of all, the magic finally deserted them.

The numbers behind the title

According to FIFA’s official match centre, the final was settled by a single goal after 120 minutes of football. It was the 104th and last match of an expanded tournament.

By The Rio Times’ reading, this was a meeting of the reigning European and South American champions, a pairing the World Cup final had not seen in some 60 years. Spain now hold both the continental and world crowns.

Kylian Mbappé finished as the tournament’s top scorer with 10 goals, claiming a second consecutive Golden Boot. He also became the World Cup’s all-time leading scorer.

A new golden generation

Spain’s success was built on a strikingly young and fearless squad. Their control of matches was a feature of the entire tournament.

They knocked out Portugal, Belgium and France on the way to the final. Beating three heavyweight opponents in succession underlines the quality of this run.

Winning the final without their most fluent performance says much about their maturity. Champions find a way even on difficult nights.

Why it matters

The first 48-team World Cup ends with a worthy and compelling champion. Spain were among the most consistent sides across the whole competition.

For Latin America, Argentina’s defeat closes a tournament that promised a second straight title. The region still leaves with pride after a strong knockout showing.

Five Latin American nations reached the last 16 in an encouraging collective showing. Argentina carried those hopes furthest before falling at the final hurdle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who won the World Cup 2026 final?

Spain won, beating Argentina 1-0 after extra time. Ferran Torres scored the only goal.

When did Ferran Torres score?

He scored in the 106th minute, early in the second period of extra time. Nico Williams provided the assist.

How many World Cups have Spain won?

Two. This is their second title after winning the tournament in 2010.

Who won the Golden Boot?

Kylian Mbappé finished as top scorer with 10 goals. Lionel Messi ended the tournament on eight.

Where was the final played?

The final was held at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. It was the last of the tournament’s 104 matches.

World.title: Spain’s Cuenca Eclipse 2026: Book Now Before Prices Jump
World.content:
Spain · Travel & Culture

Key Facts —Premier Event More than 120 events in over 60 municipalities will celebrate the total solar eclipse on August 12, 2026, turning the province of Cuenca into a massive cultural destination. —Total Solar Eclipse On August 12, 2026, Cuenca will fall inside the band of totality for a rare solar eclipse lasting roughly 1 hour and 32 minutes, with peak darkness around 8:44 p.m. local time. —Early July Programming The official ‘Cuenca Eclipse 2026’ program kicks off in the historic capital with guided astronomy visits, tastings, and theatrical routes from July 10 to 12. —International Bookings Local tourism associations report a surge in hotel reservations from foreign visitors, particularly Americans and Europeans, driving demand for premium accommodation. —Premium Experience Design The city council has contracted a firm to design exclusive luxury experiences combining astrotourism, heritage, and cuisine targeting high-purchasing-power travelers.

The Cuenca Eclipse 2026 cultural program is transforming the Spanish province of Cuenca into a living observatory, blending astronomy with gourmet gastronomy and theatrical heritage routes ahead of the August 12 total solar eclipse.

Spain · Travel & Culture

A Week of Cosmic Gastronomy and Heritage

For residents and expats planning their summer, the festivities begin well before the August 12 total solar eclipse. The ‘Cuenca Eclipse 2026’ program officially launches with a packed weekend from July 10 to 12 in the UNESCO-listed historic capital. Activities include a guided visit that starts from the Fuente del Pilón in the Plaza Mayor on Friday evening, combining astronomical observation with a tasting of provincial products.

The weekend continues with immersive theatrical visits at the Mirador de Florencio Cañas and a family escape room called “La profecía del eclipse” at the Casa del Corregidor on Saturday. The historical-gastronomic route “Cuenca Ruta Historia y Gastronomía” also runs periodically, guiding visitors through the Casco Antiguo to sample tapas and local wines at eateries like Raff San Pedro and Sabvia.

Theatrical Time Travel in the Old Quarter

A standout attraction for culturally curious travelers is ‘Ecos de Cuenca,’ an immersive theatrical visit turning the historic center into a stage for an Inquisition-era mystery. Participants join a fictional company that uses the proximity of the great eclipse to open time portals and investigate old archives. The 60-minute route, available every weekend through August 15, starts at the Mirador de Florencio Cañas and concludes at Bajada de San Miguel.

Tickets for this unique walk cost €6 (about $6.50) and can be reserved via the official cuencaeclipse.com platform. By weaving dark history with visual astronomy themes, the experience offers expatriate Spanish-speakers and international tourists alike an engaging way to connect with local culture beyond standard sightseeing.

Why the Eclipse Matters for Expats and Investors

The August 12, 2026, total solar eclipse is the first of its kind visible from the Iberian Peninsula in over a century, placing Cuenca firmly on the radar of high-spending global travelers. The Provincial Hospitality and Tourism Association reports that foreign reservations are surging, with Americans and Europeans already booking hotels to secure a spot in the path of totality.

The city council is capitalizing on this demand by investing €14,500 (about $15,800) to design exclusive premium experiences that merge astrotourism with regional cuisine. For expats living in Spain, this represents a rare, high-yield tourism window and a massive increase in local cultural activity, making nearby real estate and hospitality services particularly attractive during the summer of 2026.

Province-Wide Activities Beyond the City

Astronomy and nature enthusiasts can explore far beyond the capital’s cobbled alleys. The provincial government is mobilizing mobile planetariums and astronomy kits across dozens of rural towns, including Cañamares and Vega del Codorno. For a more adventurous celestial experience, organizers have scheduled three night-time kayak crossings under the stars in Buendía, Villalba de la Sierra, and the city of Cuenca itself.

The Royal Film Orchestra & DJ Symphonic will also perform a paid concert in Cuenca city on August 7, part of a broader music series. With over 30,000 tickets and invitations expected to be issued for roughly 80 regional activities, the program ensures that the weeks surrounding the eclipse remain vibrant in virtually every corner of the province.

The Main Event: Where to Watch Totality

On August 12, the moon will completely cover the sun for a total eclipse visible across the region. The astronomical event begins at 7:37 p.m. local time, reaches its maximum at approximately 8:44 p.m., and ends at 9:09 p.m. The northern Serranía de Cuenca, certified as a Starlight destination, offers premium low-light conditions.

For those preferring an organized rural viewing, the ‘El Gran Eclipse: Cuenca 2026’ experience sold via Fever will transport ticket holders from the city center to Finca Marlo Embid for a six-hour evening celebration starting at 6:00 p.m. This setup allows visitors to avoid the last-mile logistical hurdles and simply enjoy the rare celestial show.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where exactly does the “Cuenca Eclipse 2026” festival take place?

It takes place in the province and city of Cuenca in Castilla-La Mancha, Spain, not Cuenca, Ecuador. The location is within the path of totality for the August 12 solar eclipse, ensuring a full view of the event.

What combination of activities can visitors expect?

The official programming deliberately blends astronomy with local culture. Visitors can join guided night-sky observations paired with gastronomic tastings, immersive historical theater tours through the old town, family escape rooms themed around the eclipse, and ecotourism routes in the Serranía.

Is this event attracting international tourists?

Yes. Local provincial hospitality groups confirm that hotel reservations from Americans and Europeans have already surged for the eclipse date. The city council is actively designing high-end packages to cater specifically to this influx of international travelers.

Key Facts —ECB Decision The Governing Council announces its policy decision on Thursday, the week’s main global event. —US Tech Earnings Heavyweights Alphabet, Tesla, and IBM report, likely driving risk sentiment. —Copom on Hold Brazil’s next rate-setting meeting is not until August 4-5, leaving the Selic steady for now. —Chile Pause The BCCh meets just after the week ends, on July 27-28, keeping traders in wait-and-see mode. —UK Data Inflation and jobs figures from the UK arrive on Tuesday, offering a read on global price trends. —Quiet LatAm No major domestic data or policy decisions are scheduled in Mexico, Colombia, or Peru.

The European Central Bank’s policy decision on Thursday defines a week otherwise marked by a pause in Latin American monetary policy and a wave of heavyweight US corporate earnings.

The week ahead across Latin American and global markets. (Photo internet reproduction)

Investors face a week where global developed-market signals will dominate, as official calendars show no scheduled central bank meetings in Brazil, Mexico, Chile, Colombia, or Peru. The primary macro catalyst is the ECB’s interest rate announcement on Thursday, which will steer the euro and influence the dollar against emerging-market currencies.

A busy slate of second-quarter earnings from US tech giants, including Alphabet and Tesla, will set the tone for risk appetite. For Latin America, the focus is on the proximity of upcoming policy decisions in Chile and Brazil, making this a period of positioning rather than action.

Three Themes for the Week

The ECB’s Thursday decision is the week’s pivotal moment for global rates and currency markets.

A lull in Latin America’s domestic policy calendar shifts attention to external drivers like US earnings and the dollar.

Markets will position ahead of the next Copom and BCCh meetings, both falling just after the trading week ends.

The Week, Day by Day

Monday, July 20 — A relatively light start features US Leading Indicators and a CPI reading for June, though the date’s primary-source status is unconfirmed.

Tuesday, July 21 — The focus shifts to the UK with the release of June unemployment and inflation data, while no major US or euro-area releases are scheduled.

Wednesday, July 22 — No major global economic releases are listed, leaving the session likely driven by corporate earnings and positioning ahead of the ECB.

Thursday, July 23 — The ECB’s policy decision dominates the day, accompanied by Japan’s CPI and Canadian retail sales, making it the busiest 24 hours for macro traders.

Friday, July 24 — The week closes with US new home sales and a flash S&P Global Services PMI, alongside UK retail sales and Canadian producer price data.

The Week in Context

With Brazil’s Copom not meeting until August 4-5 and Chile’s BCCh gathering on July 27-28, this week is a natural pause in the region’s monetary cycle. Official calendars for Mexico, Colombia, and Peru show no scheduled decisions, leaving Latin American assets highly sensitive to global rate expectations.

The absence of confirmed releases from national statistics agencies like IBGE or INEGI means country-specific risk is low. Instead, the performance of the Brazilian real and Mexican peso will likely hinge on how markets interpret the ECB’s forward guidance and the health of US corporate earnings.

The Bottom Line

For investors in Latin America, this is a week to manage external risks rather than react to local events. The proximity of rate meetings in Chile and Brazil means any sharp moves in the dollar or global yields driven by the ECB could quickly alter the landscape before those decisions land.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Brazilian Copom meeting this week?

No. The next Copom meeting is scheduled for August 4-5, 2026, according to the official central bank calendar.

What is the main event for markets this week?

The European Central Bank’s monetary policy decision on Thursday, July 23, is the most significant scheduled event.

When is Chile’s next monetary policy meeting?

The Banco Central de Chile will hold its next meeting on July 27-28, just after the trading week ends.

World.title: Mexico City’s Feria del Mundo: 40+ Countries, Free Entry
World.content:
Mexico City · Culture

Key Facts —Free Admission The three-day event charges no entry fee, making it a budget-friendly weekend outing for expats and residents in Mexico City. —Global Participation More than 40 countries will present their culture, allowing visitors to experience diverse international traditions without leaving the capital. —Prime Coyoacán Location The fair takes place at the Museo Nacional de Culturas Populares, just steps from the iconic Jardín Centenario in the historic center of Coyoacán. —Culinary and Artistic Variety Attendees can buy international gastronomy, textiles, jewelry, and decorative items directly from native representatives of each nation. —Live Cultural Performances The event features live regional music and traditional dances, offering entertainment beyond the static handicraft and food stalls.

Feria del Mundo returns to Mexico City with free entry, bringing food, crafts, and live performances from more than 40 countries to the Museo Nacional de Culturas Populares in Coyoacán from August 14 to 16, 2026.

Mexico City · Culture

Event Dates, Hours, and Venue Details

The 2026 edition of Feria del Mundo is scheduled for Friday, August 14 through Sunday, August 16. The fair will be open daily from 11:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m., giving visitors ample time to explore the exhibits across all three days.

The venue is the Museo Nacional de Culturas Populares, located at Av. Miguel Hidalgo 289 in the Del Carmen neighborhood of Coyoacán.

The museum is a well-known federal cultural space situated just a few steps from the Jardín Centenario and the Fuente de los Coyotes.

For anyone unfamiliar with the area, Coyoacán is one of Mexico City’s oldest boroughs, famous for its cobblestone streets, colonial architecture, and deep artistic roots. The Jardín Centenario and the adjacent Plaza Hidalgo form the lively heart of the neighborhood, where locals and visitors gather around fountains, street performers, and weekend markets.

The Fuente de los Coyotes, a bronze fountain featuring two coyotes, serves as an unofficial symbol of the borough and a popular meeting point. Arriving early to the fair also lets you enjoy a quieter morning coffee at one of the surrounding historic cafes before the crowds build.

Why This Matters for Expats and Residents

For expats living in Mexico City, this event provides a rare opportunity to connect with communities from over 40 countries in a single location. It serves as a bridge for cultural exchange, allowing attendees to interact directly with native representatives who offer demonstrations and talks.

The free admission policy removes financial barriers, making it an accessible cultural plan for families or solo visitors. The location in Coyoacán also puts attendees in one of the city’s most walkable and historic boroughs, perfect for pairing the fair with a weekend stroll through local bookstores and cafes.

Beyond the immediate enjoyment, events like this matter because they offer a low-pressure setting to practice language skills and build cross-cultural friendships. A conversation started over a shared plate of food or a handcrafted textile can lead to deeper connections that outlast the fair itself.

For newer arrivals still finding their footing in the capital, that kind of organic networking is often more valuable than formal expat meetups.

Food, Handicrafts, and Live Performances

Visitors will find a wide array of international gastronomy and handicrafts. Exhibitors sell textiles, jewelry, cosmetics, perfumes, decorative items, and other representative products, offering a global shopping experience curated by artisans from regions including Asia, Africa, Europe, and Latin America.

The fair is not limited to static stands. Art, music, and dance are central components, with live regional performances scheduled throughout the event. Recent editions have featured countries such as Colombia, India, Turkey, and Nigeria, showcasing the diversity of the lineup.

What makes this format particularly engaging is that the vendors are often the same people performing or demonstrating their craft. A textile seller might also be the weaver explaining the patterns’ meanings, while a food stall might be run by a family cooking recipes passed down through generations.

That direct connection between maker and buyer is increasingly rare in commercial settings, and it turns a simple purchase into a story you carry home.

A Longstanding Cultural Tradition

Feria del Mundo is organized by Francisco Romero of ExpoFest, who also runs other popular festivals in the city. The fair has previously been held at major venues across the capital, including the Plaza externa del Tec de Monterrey Campus CDMX and the Palacio de la Autonomía.

The Museo Nacional de Culturas Populares itself is dedicated to the diffusion of Mexican traditions and frequently hosts large gastronomic fairs, such as the Feria del Tamal. Hosting Feria del Mundo here aligns with its mission to be a hub for both national and international popular culture.

The museum’s regular programming makes it worth a return visit long after the fair ends. Its permanent exhibits document Mexico’s living traditions, from regional sweets and textiles to festival masks and pottery.

Understanding that local context can deepen your appreciation of what the international vendors bring to the same space during Feria del Mundo, creating a dialogue between Mexican popular art and global folk traditions.

What to Watch Next

One open question is whether the fair’s growing popularity will prompt organizers to extend the hours or add an extra day in future editions. As word spreads through expat networks and social media, demand could test the capacity of the museum’s outdoor spaces.

Another point to watch is which new countries might join the lineup. The fair’s appeal depends on fresh representation each year, and the mix of participating nations can shift based on diplomatic and community ties.

Observers may also wonder how the event balances its free-admission model with fair compensation for the artisans who travel to sell their work, a tension common to many cultural festivals.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there an admission fee for the Feria del Mundo?

No. Entry to the Feria del Mundo at the Museo Nacional de Culturas Populares is completely free for all visitors on all three days.

Where exactly in Coyoacán is the venue located?

The fair is held at the Museo Nacional de Culturas Populares on Av. Miguel Hidalgo 289, in the Del Carmen neighborhood.

It is located near the Jardín Centenario in the historic center of Coyoacán.

What items can I buy at the fair?

Vendors sell a range of international goods including traditional foods, handicrafts, textiles, jewelry, decorative items, cosmetics, and perfumes, all produced by representatives from more than 40 countries.

World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Samba no Martinelli if you only have time for ONE place tonight, make it this iconic Sunday samba on the rooftop of the historic Edifício Martinelli. You’ll get live samba, one of the best skyline views in the city, a lively mixed crowd of locals and visitors, and a sunset-to-evening party that captures São Paulo’s downtown soul in a single, unforgettable experience – arrive by 3 pm to grab a good spot and watch the city lights come on.

Tonight at a Glance —Samba no Martinelli – Centro Rooftop samba with the best downtown view; mixed crowd of couples, samba lovers and tourists; Sunday from 2 pm. —Samba da Ephigenia – Centro Classic street roda de samba under the viaduct; raw, local, and free-flowing; perfect for a real grassroots Sunday. —Summer Beats Festival – Santana Huge outdoor EDM festival at Campo de Marte airfield; young festival crowd all afternoon into evening. —Pegada de Gorila at Vila do Samba – Casa Verde Pagode party with guest singer Raquel Tobias in a proper samba house; local crowd, great for mingling. —Ó do Borogodó – Vila Madalena Tiny, samba-forró bar, a magnet for bohemian Brazilians and foreigners; lively music and dancing from 8 pm.

Sunday night in São Paulo is samba’s secret weapon – from rooftop rodas in the Centro to neighbourhood pagode parties, plus a massive electronic festival under the sun. Tonight, 19 July, the city offers the rooftop magic of Samba no Martinelli, the street soul of Samba da Ephigenia, the thump of Summer Beats, and the forró floors of Vila Madalena, letting you chase sunset samba right through to late-night dancing.

Tonight across Sao Paulo. (Photo internet reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Samba no Martinelli – live samba with panoramic rooftop views over the Centro Histórico — at Edifício Martinelli, Rua São Bento, 405 – Centro, from 2 pm. the most cinematic Sunday samba in São Paulo; book ahead, arrive mid-afternoon to catch sunset, and dance as the city lights come on.

Samba da Ephigenia – traditional open-air roda de samba — at Viaduto Santa Ifigênia, 66 – Santa Ifigênia, from 3 pm. raw downtown street samba, very local and relaxed; grab a beer, find a step, and soak up the real Centro vibe.

Summer Beats Festival – outdoor electronic music festival — at Aeroporto do Campo de Marte, Av. Santos Dumont, 1979 – Santana, from 8 am (main acts afternoon/evening). big-stage EDM near the old airfield; arrive mid-afternoon for headline sets, stay into the early evening for the full festival feel.

Pegada de Gorila convida Raquel Tobias – pagode party — at Vila do Samba, Rua João Rudge, 340 – Casa Verde, from 4 pm. a proper Sunday samba-house party with a featured singer; friendly local crowd and an easy, lively pagode atmosphere.

Baile at Beco do Baixo – Sunday forró social dance — at Beco do Baixo, Vila Madalena, from 3:30 pm. partner forró in São Paulo’s bohemian neighbourhood; mixed crowd, all levels, and a warm, welcoming dance-floor culture.

Zais – Forró & Samba dance party — at Zais – A casa mais dançante, Vila Mariana, from 6 pm. two dance floors with forró and samba de gafieira, central and easily reached; great for a structured dance night.

Casa de Francisca – intimate live music (MPB/samba/choro) — at Rua Quintino Bocaiúva, 22, 1º andar – Sé/Centro, 4 pm show. a small, revered listening room with high-quality Brazilian music; perfect for a seated, cosy Sunday evening.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Warm-up (3 pm–6 pm): Start in the Centro with Samba da Ephigenia or the rooftop at Samba no Martinelli – daylight samba with cold beer.

Sunset shift (5 pm–8 pm): Move to Vila Madalena for forró at Beco do Baixo or samba at Ó do Borogodó; the neighbourhood comes alive as the sun drops.

Festival afternoon (3 pm–9 pm): If you’ve got a ticket, head to Summer Beats at Campo de Marte and ride the main-stage energy into the early night.

Evening dance (6 pm–midnight): Hit Zais in Vila Mariana for forró and samba, or stay in the Centro for a refined live show at Casa de Francisca.

Late-night rock & pub (9 pm–late): Slide into The Blue Pub on Paulista or O’Malley’s in Jardins for live rock covers and an expat-friendly crowd.

After midnight: When samba and live music wind down, head to Caos in Baixo Augusta for DJ sets (funk, soul, electro) on the dance floor upstairs.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba & Pagode — the heartbeat of a São Paulo Sunday – street rodas, rooftop parties, and samba houses with live percussion and cold beer. Where: Samba no Martinelli (Centro), Samba da Ephigenia (Centro), Vila do Samba (Casa Verde)

Forró — Northeastern partner-dance with accordion and zabumba; welcoming and easy to learn, even for beginners. Where: Beco do Baixo (Vila Madalena), Zais (Vila Mariana)

MPB & Instrumental — intimate listening rooms and bars with high-quality Brazilian popular music, choro, and samba-jazz. Where: Casa de Francisca (Centro), Bar Brahma (Centro)

Electronic — from large open-air festivals to club DJ sets spinning funk, soul, nu jazz and electro late into the night. Where: Summer Beats Festival (Santana), Caos (Baixo Augusta)

Rock & Pub — English-style pubs and rock bars where expats and locals catch live cover bands and big football matches. Where: The Blue Pub (Paulista), O’Malley’s (Jardins), Kia Ora (Itaim Bibi)

Samba de Gafieira & Social Dance — Rio-style partner samba in dedicated dance studios and clubs; dress smart and bring a partner or find one there. Where: Miliduki (Parque Artur Alvim), Zais (Vila Mariana)

Pick Your Night

Meet locals: Samba da Ephigenia under the viaduct – it’s open-air, classless, and a place where a smile and a beer open conversations naturally.

Date night: Samba no Martinelli rooftop – sunset, skyline, live samba, and a vibrant but not too loud atmosphere; book a table if you can.

Dance till sunrise: Start with Summer Beats Festival in the afternoon, then head to Caos in Baixo Augusta for late-night DJs and a mixed, energetic crowd.

Solo and safe: Casa de Francisca in the Centro – a seated, intimate live-music room with an artsy crowd; book a ticket, enjoy a show, and grab an Uber right outside.

Meet other expats: O’Malley’s or The Blue Pub near Paulista – English-speaking staff, live rock, football on screens, and plenty of foreigners and bilingual Brazilians.

Where to Go

Samba no Martinelli — Centro iconic rooftop samba with one of the best views over downtown São Paulo; mixed crowd of couples, tourists, and samba lovers. Tonight: Samba no Martinelli live samba party from 2 pm. Best time: Sunday afternoons; arrive 3 pm–4 pm to claim a good spot for sunset and the main sets. Cost: from R$80 entry; drinks on comanda; card accepted. Address: Rua São Bento, 405 – Centro Histórico Instagram: @sambanomartinelli Getting there: short walk from São Bento metro (Line 1); use Uber or 99 for a safe pickup right outside the building at night. Good to know: book ahead or buy tickets early; rooftop capacity is limited.

Samba da Ephigenia — Centro classic street roda de samba under Viaduto Santa Ifigênia; very local, open-air, and democratic. Tonight: Sunday roda de samba from 3 pm. Best time: Sunday afternoons; arrive 4 pm–5 pm when the party is warm but not overcrowded. Cost: usually free entry, drinks on comanda; may have a small couvert artístico; card accepted, but carry some cash. Address: Viaduto Santa Ifigênia, 66 – Santa Ifigênia Getting there: walk from São Bento or Anhangabaú metro; use Uber/99 from well-lit corners of the viaduct at night.

Summer Beats Festival — Santana large outdoor EDM festival at the Campo de Marte airfield; young, energetic crowd and big production. Tonight: Summer Beats Festival, gates at 8 am; main DJs afternoon into evening. Best time: afternoon main-stage sets; arrive 3 pm–5 pm to avoid the early sun and catch the peak energy. Cost: tickets typically R$120–R$300, buy in advance; inside, cashless wristband or comanda, card-friendly. Address: Av. Santos Dumont, 1979 – Santana Getting there: near Santana metro (Line 1), but Uber/99 is easier because of festival traffic. Good to know: must buy ticket in advance; not walk-in.

Vila do Samba – Pegada de Gorila convida Raquel Tobias — Casa Verde dedicated samba house with a proper Sunday pagode party and a guest singer; great for an immersed local night. Tonight: Pegada de Gorila convida Raquel Tobias from 4 pm. Best time: Sunday parties; arrive 5 pm–6 pm when the music is going strong. Cost: door cover likely R$30–R$60; drinks on comanda; card accepted. Address: Rua João Rudge, 340 – Casa Verde Getting there: not directly on the metro; take an Uber or 99 from central areas. Good to know: recommended to check availability or buy a ticket earlier in the day.

Ó do Borogodó — Vila Madalena tiny, beloved samba-forró bar packed with bohemian Brazilians and foreigners; close to a popular hostel, so it’s naturally mixed. Tonight: live samba and forró from 8 pm (typical Sunday schedule). Best time: weekends and Sunday evenings; music starts around 8 pm, people pour in from 9 pm onwards. Cost: couvert artístico charged (around R$15–R$30); comanda card system; card accepted. Instagram: @odoborogodo Getting there: short Uber ride from Vila Madalena metro (Line 2); area is busy and safe to walk around in the evening.

Casa de Francisca — Sé / Centro intimate, seated live music house with high-quality MPB, samba, and choro; refined and cosy. Tonight: Sunday show at 4 pm. Best time: weekend evening shows; arrive 30 minutes before showtime; check schedule for the exact artist. Cost: couvert artístico (show cover) charged per person; card accepted. Address: Rua Quintino Bocaiúva, 22, 1º andar – Sé Phone: +55 11 3052-0547 Instagram: @casadefrancisca Getting there: close to Sé metro (Lines 1 and 3); use Uber/99 directly from the door at night.

Caos — Baixo Augusta bar-club on Rua Augusta with a dance floor upstairs spinning funk, soul, nu jazz and electro; young, mixed, and late-night. Tonight: open Sunday night; DJ sets upstairs from late evening. Best time: Friday and Saturday nights; Sunday is quieter but still active; arrive 11 pm–1 am for the peak. Cost: entry around R$30–R$60; comanda card system; card accepted. Instagram: @caossp Getting there: metro Consolação (Line 2) then a short walk along Avenida Paulista/Rua Augusta; Uber is best for late exit.

The Blue Pub — Bela Vista (Paulista) English-style rock pub with live bands, sports on screen, and a strong expat and international crowd. Tonight: regular Sunday rock programming and live sports. Best time: match days and weekend nights; lively from 8 pm onwards. Address: Alameda Ribeirão Preto, 384 – Bela Vista Instagram: @thebluepub Getting there: walk from Trianon-MASP or Brigadeiro metro (Line 2); safe to call an Uber right outside.

O’Malley’s Bar — Jardim Paulista (Jardins) Irish pub with live rock cover bands and a heavy expat presence; a home-from-home for English speakers. Tonight: live music and pub vibe all Sunday evening. Best time: weekday happy hours and weekend live band nights; arrive 7 pm–9 pm. Cost: free entry, drinks on tab; card accepted. Address: Alameda Itu, 1529 – Jardim Paulista Phone: +55 11 3086-0780 Instagram: @omalleysbar Getting there: Uber/99 recommended; a short ride from Paulista and Jardins areas.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Centro (Sé, Santa Ifigênia): historic downtown with raw street samba, rooftop parties, and old-school MPB – the soul of a Sunday.

Vila Madalena: bohemian, artsy, and full of small bars with live forró and samba; a magnet for Brazilians and foreigners alike.

Baixo Augusta / Consolação: the late-night spine of the city; rock, electronic, LGBTQ+ clubs, and a young, no-rules energy.

Jardins / Itaim Bibi: upscale pubs and rock bars with expat crowds, good for English-friendly conversation and live cover bands.

Santana: northern zone hosting São Paulo’s big outdoor festivals and events, reachable by metro but best with a plan.

Vila Mariana: central but residential dance hub; forró and samba de gafieira parties in welcoming, structured settings.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Beco do Baixo (Vila Madalena) — forró dance party with a mixed, open-minded crowd; welcoming to all, great for solo dancers and couples.

Caos (Baixo Augusta) — late-night bar-club with DJs, a mixed sexuality crowd, and the easygoing, anything-goes energy of Rua Augusta.

Consolação / Frei Caneca area — the historical LGBTQ+ hub; while specific Sunday events aren’t listed, several bars and bars in the area stay open Sunday evening – explore Rua Frei Caneca and nearby streets for a friendly drink.

Money & How Paying Works Comanda card: at most bars, clubs and samba houses you’re given a tab card at the door. All drinks are added, and you pay the total when you leave. Losing the card means a heavy fine (often R$200–R$400), so keep it safe and never hand it to strangers. Couvert artístico: a fixed per-person live-music cover, typically R$10–R$40, added to your bill. It does not count as drinks credit – it’s purely for the band. Card or cash? Virtually every venue tonight accepts debit and credit cards, including contactless. Keep a little cash (R$50–R$100) for street drinks, small kiosks, or in case a terminal fails. Tipping: restaurant and bar bills usually include a 10% “serviço” line. Paying it is the norm; extra tips are not expected but are always welcome.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: São Paulo metro closes around midnight on Sundays. If you’re out after 11:30 pm, plan on using a rideshare app.

Use 99 or Uber: they are safer and more predictable than street taxis. Always check the car plate, model, and driver name before getting in.

Safe pickup: call your car from well-lit spots right outside the venue entrance. In the Centro or under viaducts, avoid walking to dark side streets alone – wait inside or near the door until your ride arrives.

Keep your phone and wallet in front pockets or a zipped bag; avoid holding your phone loosely in your back pocket in crowds.

São Paulo at night is about awareness, not fear. Stick to busy, lit streets, stay with the flow of people moving between bars, and trust your gut – the vast majority of nights out end happily.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time should I actually arrive for a Sunday samba?

Brazilians go out late, but Sunday samba is an afternoon-to-evening affair. Arriving 4 pm–5 pm for a 2 pm or 3 pm start means the party is already warm but not yet peak; perfect to find a spot and settle in.

Do I need to book in advance for tonight?

Yes for Samba no Martinelli and Summer Beats Festival – both have limited capacity or require advance tickets. For street rodas like Samba da Ephigenia, Vila do Samba, and pubs, you can just walk in.

Is it safe to go out alone as a foreigner?

Absolutely. São Paulo’s nightlife is used to solo visitors and foreigners. Choose venues like Casa de Francisca, The Blue Pub or Ó do Borogodó where the crowd is naturally social, and use Uber from door to door.

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Samba do Passeio – Canta Djavan If you only have one stop, make it this free open-air samba roda in the historic Passeio Público park where hundreds of locals sing Djavan’s MPB classics. It’s the most welcoming, only-in-Rio Sunday introduction a newcomer can have.

Tonight at a Glance —Bar do Zeca Pagodinho – Barra Sunday feijoada buffet and back-to-back live samba sets from 2 pm; family-friendly Barra crowd and easy for first-timers. —Dominguinho tá como? at 1030 Snooker Bar Late-night Sunday pagode party starting 10 pm in Taquara; proper local West Zone energy, arrive after 11 pm. —Leviano Bar – Lapa Multi-floor mansion open daily until 4 am with live samba, forró and DJs; the safest fallback in Lapa tonight with a mixed local-foreign crowd. —Beco da Cultura RJ – Saúde/Centro Bohemian samba roda from 4 pm on Rua do Mercado; intimate cultural spot loved by samba purists and curious travellers. —Prainha Club com Casa do Naldo – Penha Circular Suburban Sunday ‘baile’ from 2 pm mixing funk, pagode and DJ sets; young, energetic and very local.

Tonight Rio unwinds with a perfect Sunday mix: a free open-air Djavan samba tribute in Lapa’s Passeio Público, late pagode parties in Taquara and Penha Circular, and Zeca Pagodinho’s feijoada-with-samba in Barra. The circuit moves from afternoon park rodas to Lapa bar-hopping and late suburban samba, so pick your zone, grab a comanda, and ease into the city’s most generous night.

Tonight across Rio de Janeiro. (Photo internet reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Samba do Passeio – Canta DJAVAN (free open-air samba/MPB tribute) — at Passeio Público, Rua do Passeio, Lapa/Centro, From 12:00 (midday); peak 15:00–18:00. The most beautiful Sunday introduction to Rio: a free public roda in a historic park, singing Djavan classics with a mixed, welcoming crowd.

Feijoada & Samba: Samba do Gota, Leandro Sapucahy, Cantor LG — at Bar do Zeca Pagodinho, Av. das Américas 8585, Barra da Tijuca, Feijoada 12:00–16:00; samba sets 14:00, 17:00, 20:00. All-you-can-eat feijoada buffet for R$85 plus three live samba acts; the safest family-friendly Sunday immersion in pagode culture.

FRUTA DO PÉ na BATUQ (samba/pagode roda) — at BATUQ Casa de Samba, Rua Belizário Pena 1141, Penha, From 16:00; peak 18:00–22:00. A dedicated North Zone samba house packed with locals who take their pagode seriously; arrive early evening for the best energy.

Beco da Cultura RJ – Samba/Pagode roda — at Beco da Cultura RJ, Rua do Mercado 51, Saúde/Centro, From 16:00; peak 18:00–22:00. Intimate cultural samba in the historic port district with experienced musicians; a bohemian gem where you’ll feel like a discoverer.

Sambinha do Black (samba/pagode party) — at Black Bar, Rua Francisco Real 1641, Campo Grande, From 12:00; peak 17:00–21:00. A true West Zone Sunday samba at a neighbourhood bar; go if you want zero tourists and pure local weekend vibes.

Dominguinho tá como? (late-night samba/pagode) — at 1030 Snooker Bar, Av. dos Mananciais 1030, Taquara, From 22:00; peak 23:30–02:00. The rare Sunday late-night pagode where the party starts when others are closing; snooker tables and cold beer keep things loose and local.

Prainha Club com Casa do Naldo (day-into-night Baile/funk/pagode) — at Prainha Club, Rua Caroen 171, Penha Circular, From 14:00; peak 18:00–23:00. Suburban Sunday party with DJ sets and live acts blending funk and pagode in a beach-club atmosphere; young, energetic and unpolished.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Midday–sunset (12:00–19:00): Start at Samba do Passeio in Lapa/Centro (free, open-air, relaxed) then take an Uber to Bar do Zeca in Barra for feijoada and afternoon samba sets.

Late afternoon–evening (16:00–22:00): Roda-hoppers should hit Beco da Cultura in Saúde or BATUQ Casa de Samba in Penha; both are real neighbourhood rodas peaking around 18:00–20:00.

Sunset–early night (18:00–23:00): Head to Lapa and base yourself at Leviano Bar (Av. Mem de Sá 47) for live samba and forró, then bar-hop the Lavradio strip.

Late-night (22:00–02:00): Dedicated dancers should rideshare to 1030 Snooker Bar in Taquara for Dominguinho tá como? – the only verified late-Sunday samba party on tonight.

All-day suburban (12:00–late): Campo Grande’s Black Bar (Sambinha do Black from noon) and Penha Circular’s Prainha Club (from 2 pm) run marathon Sunday parties; pick one and commit.

Worth checking direct: Rio Scenarium (Lavradio 20) and Leviano (Mem de Sá 47) normally open Sundays from early evening; their Instagrams will confirm tonight’s exact line-up.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba & Pagode — The heartbeat of a Rio Sunday: large rodas, cold beer, and spontaneous singing. From open-air parks to dedicated samba houses. Where: Passeio Público (free outdoor), Bar do Zeca (Barra, feijoada+samba), BATUQ (Penha), Beco da Cultura (Saúde), 1030 Snooker Bar (Taquara, late-night)

MPB (Brazilian Popular Music) — Sophisticated songbook tributes – tonight dedicated to Djavan – with a mixed crowd singing every lyric; more seated and musical than samba. Where: Samba do Passeio – Canta Djavan at Passeio Público; also check Rio Scenarium and Leviano for MPB sets on a typical Sunday

Forró — Accordion-driven Northeastern dance music with close partner dancing; lively but welcoming to beginners who want to try. Where: Leviano Bar in Lapa frequently programmes forró sets among its live-music rotation

Funk Carioca & Baile Funk — Heavy bass, MCs and street-energy dancefloors; the sound of Rio’s suburbs at full volume. Where: Prainha Club (Penha Circular) tonight with ‘Casa do Naldo’; also look for baile-style Sundays in suburban clubs across North and West Zones

Electronic & DJ Sets — House, tech and Brazilian bass after midnight in multi-room clubs; smaller scene on Sunday but Lapa’s late bars hold their own. Where: Leviano Bar’s upper floors and Portal Club (Lapa, LGBTQ+) when open; check D-Edge or Lapa dance bars for rare Sunday electronic nights

Sertanejo — Brazilian country-pop with big singalongs; not the dominant Sunday sound but pops up in larger Barra and West Zone bars. Where: Multi-space bars in Barra da Tijuca sometimes host sertanejo weekends; confirm individual line-ups on Instagram

Pick Your Night

Date night: Bar do Zeca Pagodinho in Barra – afternoon feijoada, live samba, well-lit shopping-centre setting, easy conversation before the music gets loud.

Solo and safe: Leviano Bar in Lapa – open every day, multi-floor, lots of solo travellers and a central location where you can join the bar crowd without feeling out of place.

Dance till sunrise: Dominguinho tá como? at 1030 Snooker Bar in Taquara is the only verified late-Sunday samba party tonight; stay until 2 am then consider Lapa’s late bars.

Meet locals: BATUQ Casa de Samba in Penha or Beco da Cultura in Saúde – neighbourhood rodas where most people are local regulars, and a foreign face is a conversation starter.

Chill and conversation: Boa Praça (Leblon or Ipanema branches open until 1 am) – boteco-style, outdoor tables, craft beers and snacks; a low-key Sunday wind-down.

Meet other expats and digital nomads: Lapa bars along Av. Mem de Sá between Leviano and Lapa’s main strip – the area is the natural expat gravity well, especially on Sundays when everyone drifts there.

Where to Go

Samba do Passeio (Passeio Público) — Lapa/Centro Free, open-air samba roda in a historic park; the most democratic Sunday party in Rio with a crowd of all ages. Tonight: Samba do Passeio – Canta DJAVAN from 12:00; free entry, peak 15:00–18:00. Best time: Sundays from 12:00; arrive 15:00 for full energy; usually winds down by early evening. Cost: Free entry; drinks and food from vendors (bring cash or card). Address: Passeio Público, Rua do Passeio, Centro/Lapa, Rio de Janeiro Getting there: Metro Line 1 to Cinelândia station, then 5-minute walk; or Uber/99 to ‘Passeio Público’. Good to know: No booking needed; open public event.

Bar do Zeca Pagodinho – Barra da Tijuca — Barra da Tijuca Pagode legend Zeca’s official bar with guaranteed Sunday samba and a famous feijoada buffet; tourist-friendly, shopping-centre setting. Tonight: Feijoada 12:00–16:00 (R$85); samba sets: 14:00 Samba do Gota, 17:00 Leandro Sapucahy, 20:00 Cantor LG; couvert artístico R$40. Best time: Sundays for feijoada+samba; arrive 14:00–15:00 for the full afternoon or 17:00 for the evening sets. Cost: Couvert artístico R$40 per person; feijoada buffet R$85; drinks extra; cards widely accepted. Address: Avenida das Américas 8585, Loja SS101, Barra da Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro Getting there: Uber/99 recommended; in a shopping-centre complex with safe pickup area. Good to know: Book ahead for feijoada at weekends; casual dress, no strict door.

Leviano Bar — Lapa Multi-floor mansion-bar with live samba, forró and DJs; open daily until 4 am and the most reliable Lapa fallback for any night including Sunday. Tonight: Open from 18:00 to 04:00; live music and DJs (exact Sunday line-up on Instagram); mixed local-foreign crowd peaks 22:00–02:00. Best time: Any night from 18:00; arrive 21:30–22:30 for the best balance of energy and space. Cost: Cover varies (typically R$20–R$50); drinks extra; comanda system; cards accepted. Address: Avenida Mem de Sá 47, Centro/Lapa, Rio de Janeiro, 20230-150 Phone: +55 21 2507-5779 Getting there: Uber/99 to door; or metro Line 1 to Cinelândia then 10-minute walk along Mem de Sá. Good to know: No booking for bar entry on a Sunday; groups of 6+ may want to WhatsApp ahead; casual but neat.

BATUQ Casa de Samba — Penha (North Zone) Dedicated samba house in Penha with serious rodas and a local crowd that lives for pagode; very few tourists make it here. Tonight: FRUTA DO PÉ na BATUQ from 16:00; samba/pagode roda, entry from R$28. Best time: Sundays from 16:00; arrive 18:00–19:00 for the peak atmosphere. Cost: Entry from R$28; drinks extra; expect card or cash. Address: Rua Belizário Pena 1141, Penha, Rio de Janeiro Getting there: Rideshare (Uber/99) strongly recommended for North Zone at night. Good to know: Check Instagram for reservation link; door policy is relaxed but full, so arrive early.

Beco da Cultura RJ — Saúde/Centro A bohemian samba spot on a historic Centro street with experienced musicians; feels like a secret backyard roda even though it’s central. Tonight: Samba/pagode roda from 16:00; no specific event name beyond the roda, check their Instagram. Best time: Sundays from 16:00; arrive by 18:00 for the best music and crowd. Cost: Often free entry with consumption or small couvert; confirm exact price at door. Address: Rua do Mercado 51, Saúde/Centro, Rio de Janeiro Getting there: Uber/99 to Rua do Mercado; or VLT (light rail) to Parada dos Museus then walk. Good to know: No booking typically needed for Sunday roda; check Instagram for special events.

1030 Snooker Bar — Taquara (West Zone) Snooker hall by day, late Sunday pagode party by night; the rare place where the samba starts at 10 pm on a Sunday. Tonight: Dominguinho tá como? from 22:00; samba/pagode, entry from R$24. Best time: Sunday late-night from 22:00; arrive 23:00–23:30 for peak energy. Cost: Entry from R$24; drinks extra; cash and card. Address: Avenida dos Mananciais 1030, Taquara, Rio de Janeiro Getting there: Rideshare only (Uber/99); Taquara is not on the metro. Good to know: No booking; casual dress, local bar atmosphere.

Black Bar — Campo Grande (West Zone) West Zone neighbourhood bar running all-day Sunday samba/pagode from noon; zero tourists, pure suburban weekend spirit. Tonight: Sambinha do Black from 12:00; samba/pagode event, exact entry price not specified. Best time: Sunday from noon; arrive 17:00–18:00 for the busiest vibe. Cost: Likely paid entry or couvert, price not verified; drinks extra. Address: Rua Francisco Real 1641, Campo Grande, Rio de Janeiro Getting there: Rideshare (Uber/99) from central Rio; Campo Grande is far West Zone. Good to know: No booking info; check their Instagram for details.

Prainha Club — Penha Circular (North Zone) Suburban party venue mixing funk, pagode and DJs in a beach-club style; young crowd and all-day Sunday energy from 2 pm. Tonight: Prainha Club com Casa do Naldo from 14:00; entry from R$30. Best time: Sundays from 14:00; peak 18:00–23:00. Cost: Entry from R$30; drinks extra; cards and cash. Address: Rua Caroen 171, Penha Circular, Rio de Janeiro Getting there: Rideshare (Uber/99) only; safe pickup at venue entrance. Good to know: Check Instagram for advance tickets; casual/suburban party wear.

Boa Praça (Ipanema/Leblon branches) — Leblon / Ipanema Polished boteco chain with craft beers, outdoor tables and a relaxed Sunday vibe; ideal for a quiet pre-game or a low-key night. Tonight: Open Sunday; Leblon branch: Rua Dias Ferreira 420, store E, Leblon, from 11:30 to 01:00. Best time: Weekday late afternoons and Sunday early evenings; arrive before 21:00 for a good table. Cost: Craft beers R$15–R$25; snacks R$30–R$60; cards widely accepted. Address: Rua Dias Ferreira 420, Loja E, Leblon, Rio de Janeiro Getting there: Metro Line 1 to Antero de Quental then 12-minute walk; or Uber to door. Good to know: No booking needed on a Sunday; casual-chic Zona Sul dress.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Lapa / Centro: The beating heart: colonial streets full of samba bars, street parties and a chaotic mix of locals, tourists and bohemians. Dense, loud, and essential.

Barra da Tijuca: Sprawling, modern and shopping-centre-based; family-friendly Sunday samba with feijoada, safer streets and a more car-dependent lifestyle.

Saúde / Porto Maravilha: Revitalised port district with cultural spaces, intimate rodas and a more curated, less touristy Centro atmosphere.

Penha / Penha Circular (North Zone): Working-class suburban samba headquarters; dedicated casas de samba with serious rodas and few foreign faces – the most authentic pagode experience.

Taquara / Campo Grande (West Zone): Deep West Zone: massive suburban bars, snooker halls turned samba clubs, and all-day Sunday parties where everyone knows the lyrics.

Leblon / Ipanema (Zona Sul): Upscale beach neighbourhoods with polished botecos, craft cocktails and a more European pace on a Sunday night; good for a quiet one.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Portal Club – Lapa — The LGBTQ+ club in central Rio with multiple dancefloors playing pop, funk and Brazilian hits; young crowd (18–25). Check their Instagram for Sunday opening – historically Fri/Sat are main nights.

Up Turn – Barra da Tijuca — Majority-gay Barra club with pulsating dancefloors and lounge areas; 25–45 crowd. Listed among weekend clubs – confirm Sunday status directly.

Lapa strip bars (Galeria Café, La Cueva area) — Iconic LGBTQ+ spots near Cinelândia/Glória; some host late-night parties. Sunday specific programming often only on Instagram day-of.

Money & How Paying Works Comanda card: At most clubs and samba houses you get a tab card at the door. Every drink and snack is added to it. You pay the total on exit. Losing the comanda means a heavy fine (often R$150–R$300), so guard it like cash. Couvert artístico: This is a live-music cover charge added to your bill when you sit or enter the music area – R$28–R$40 is typical for Sunday samba. It’s separate from entry but works on the same comanda. Cash vs card: Cards are widely accepted in Lapa, Barra and Zona Sul bars; some suburban and street vendors are cash-only. Carry at least R$100 in cash as backup, especially for West Zone samba parties. Tipping: A 10% service charge (serviço/garçom) is usually included on the bill – check before adding extra. If not included, 10% is the standard gesture; tip in cash or add it when paying by card.

Getting Home Safe

Metro closes around midnight on Sundays (Lines 1 and 2). If you are out past 23:30, plan on using a rideshare app – don’t rely on the metro.

Use 99 or Uber, not street taxis. Order from inside the venue or at the well-lit entrance. In Lapa, walk to the main strip (Mem de Sá or Av. Gomes Freire) to meet your car rather than waiting on a dark side street.

Late-night surge: Sunday after midnight sees fewer drivers, so expect surge pricing of 1.5x–2.5x in Lapa and Barra. Budget R$40–R$80 for Zona Sul returns, R$80–R$150+ from West Zone or Penha at 2 am.

Stick to main bar streets in Lapa (Av. Mem de Sá, Rua do Lavradio) after dark and avoid wandering into empty backstreets. Keep your phone in a front pocket or zipped bag, especially in crowded rodas.

In suburban areas like Penha, Taquara and Campo Grande, arrive and leave by rideshare directly at the venue door. These neighbourhoods are safe around the party but not designed for street-wandering at night if you don’t know the area.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time should I actually arrive at a Sunday samba roda?

For afternoon rodas (12:00 or 16:00 start), arrive 2–3 hours after the listed start for the full crowd – so 15:00–16:00 for a noon roda, 18:00–19:00 for a 16:00 roda. Late-night parties from 22:00 really fill up 23:30–00:00. Brazilians are fashionably late; being first means an empty room.

Can I go out on Sunday without speaking Portuguese?

In Lapa and Barra, you’ll manage with English and gestures at bigger venues like Leviano and Bar do Zeca. Suburban samba houses (BATUQ, Black Bar, Prainha Club) operate almost entirely in Portuguese – keep Google Translate handy and a smile goes a long way.

Is Sunday a proper night out or just a wind-down?

Sunday is Rio’s secret weapon: it starts with huge afternoon samba rodas and feijoada, then transitions to late-night pagode in the suburbs while Lapa stays lively until 4 am. It’s less club-heavy than Friday/Saturday but absolutely a full night out – just with more samba and less electronic.

World.title: ‘Experiencia Queen’ Brings a Symphonic Tribute to Montevideo
World.content:
Uruguay · Entertainment

Key Facts —Date and City The ‘Experiencia Queen – Greatest Hits Tour 2026’ will stage a major international performance in Montevideo on August 9, 2026, marking a key cultural date for the capital. —High-Fidelity Production The show is not a standard cover band; it uses authentic-style costumes and original instruments to meticulously recreate Queen’s music, stage design, and the distinct personas of each original member. —Proven Regional Success This is an established international tour with 2026 stops already confirmed in Paraguay, Argentina, and a previous sold-out demand for past Montevideo shows, signaling a reliable professional production. —Setlist and Duration Fans can expect a full concert experience lasting nearly two hours, featuring a repertoire of definitive anthems like ‘Bohemian Rhapsody,’ ‘We Are the Champions,’ and ‘Radio Ga Ga.’ —Robust Tribute Scene Montevideo is a thriving hub for major tribute productions, also hosting ‘God Save the Queen’ and ‘Candlelight: Queen vs. The Beatles’ in 2026, offering investors insight into the city’s live entertainment market.

Experiencia Queen Montevideo will bring a high-fidelity tribute to the British rock legends to Uruguay’s capital on August 9, 2026, as part of its international ‘Greatest Hits Tour 2026.’

Uruguay · Entertainment

A Meticulous Recreation of Queen’s Legacy

‘Experiencia Queen’ is widely promoted across the region as far more than a conventional tribute act. The production uses authentic-style costumes and original instruments to deliver an immersive experience inspired directly by the iconic band fronted by Freddie Mercury.

A local television feature described the spectacle as a faithful concert recreation that represents each original member, including Brian May, Roger Taylor, and John Deacon, with notable accuracy. The stage design is meticulously crafted to replicate the visual power of a classic Queen performance.

What to Expect on August 9 in Montevideo

While the specific venue for the August 9 show has not yet been confirmed by the organizers, the tour’s format is well established. Audiences can expect a program packed with non-negotiable rock anthems, including ‘Bohemian Rhapsody,’ ‘Love of My Life,’ ‘Somebody to Love,’ ‘Radio Ga Ga,’ ‘I Want to Break Free,’ and ‘We Are the Champions.’

Regional performers have stated that the full musical set runs between 1 hour 40 minutes and 1 hour 50 minutes. In previous Montevideo presentations, the experience was expanded to include a traveling museum featuring Queen-related objects and memorabilia, offering fans a pre-show immersion into the band’s history.

The 2026 International Tour Context

‘Experiencia Queen’ is staging a significant South American tour this year, reinforcing the production’s scale ahead of its Montevideo stop. The tour was recently promoted for a show at the Auditorio Belgrano in Buenos Aires on May 21, with tickets sold via Ticketek.

Montevideo’s Tribute Scene and Ticket Demand

The Uruguayan capital has demonstrated a strong appetite for Queen tributes in 2026, providing a lively night-out option for expats and residents. The separate concert ‘God Save the Queen’ is scheduled for Teatro Metro on April 16, with tickets previously listed from 13,865 Uruguayan pesos.

Frequently Asked Questions

What kind of performance is Experiencia Queen?

It is an international tribute show that recreates the music, authentic costumes, and stage design of the legendary British rock band Queen. It uses original instruments to accurately mimic a live Queen concert led by Freddie Mercury.

What songs will likely be played at the Montevideo show?

The standard ‘Greatest Hits’ setlist for this tour includes major anthems such as ‘Bohemian Rhapsody,’ ‘Somebody to Love,’ ‘Radio Ga Ga,’ ‘I Want to Break Free,’ ‘Love of My Life,’ and ‘We Are the Champions,’ among other classics.

Are tickets for the August 9 Montevideo event available now?

Specific ticket prices and the official sales platform for the August 9 Montevideo performance have not been published yet. Regional tours typically use platforms like Ticketek or Ticketea, but buyers should wait for the venue confirmation to purchase from the official source.

World.title: Carin León Headlines Feria de las Flores Super Concert

Key Facts —Event Date The Super Concierto takes place on Saturday, August 8, 2026, at 7 p.m., during the second weekend of the 68th Feria de las Flores, which runs from July 31 to August 9. —Ticket On-Sale Tickets go on sale Friday, May 29, 2026, at 10 a.m. local time exclusively via Tuboleta.com, with pre-sale prices available until 50% of capacity in each section is sold. —Price Range Pre-sale grandstand tickets start at COP 90,000 (about US$22), while 10-person box seats range from COP 4 million to COP 17 million (about US$950 to US$4,040), plus service fees. —Age Restrictions Most sections require attendees to be 18 or older; designated family grandstands allow guests aged 12 and up when accompanied by a responsible adult. —Festival Scale The Feria de las Flores draws over 2 million attendees overall, with the Super Concierto hosting more than 50,000 fans at Estadio Atanasio Girardot.

Carin León headlines the Feria de las Flores Super Concierto 2026 as the Mexican regional music icon anchors Colombia’s premier flower-festival concert alongside five other Latin stars on Saturday, August 8, in Medellín.

A Six-Act Latin Powerhouse at Atanasio Girardot

The Súper Concierto Feria de las Flores 2026 will transform Estadio Atanasio Girardot into a major Latin music arena on August 8. Headliner Carín León, the chart-topping Mexican singer, leads a bill that also features Colombian vallenato giant Silvestre Dangond, legendary salsa orchestra Grupo Niche, música popular star Luis Alfonso, rising urbano artist Aria Vega, and vallenato-pop singer-songwriter Felipe Peláez.

The official tour page for Carín León lists the Super Concierto as his confirmed Medellín performance, lending international weight to the festival’s biggest paid musical event.

For readers unfamiliar with these genres, vallenato is a folk style born on Colombia’s Caribbean coast, built around the accordion, caja drum, and guacharaca scraper. It tells stories of love, land, and daily life, and Silvestre Dangond is one of its most electrifying modern voices.

Grupo Niche, meanwhile, represents the hard-swinging, brass-heavy salsa tradition that has defined Cali and the Pacific region for decades. Música popular, the lane Luis Alfonso occupies, blends ranchera sentiment with Colombian street-level storytelling, often called “music for drinking and healing.” Aria Vega’s urbano tag signals a younger, reggaeton- and trap-influenced sound that connects with streaming-era audiences.

Together, the lineup deliberately spans generations and regions, making the stadium feel like a compressed tour of Latin America’s musical map.

Ticket Pricing and How to Buy Safely

Official ticket sales open on Friday, May 29, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. local time exclusively through Tuboleta.com. The event operates under PULEP code SVK619.

A pre-sale window runs until 50 percent of capacity in each section is sold; after that, full prices apply. The cheapest grandstand seat, Norte Baja, starts at COP 90,000 (about US$22) pre-sale.

Mid-range grandstand options include Occidental Alta Oro at COP 450,000 (about US$107) and PMU at COP 500,000 (about US$119).

The PULEP code is a unique event identifier used by Tuboleta, Colombia’s dominant ticketing platform. It helps buyers confirm they are on the correct official page and not a resale or scam site.

Because large concerts in Colombia routinely attract counterfeit ticket operations, purchasing only through the Tuboleta portal and double-checking the PULEP code is the single most reliable way to avoid fraud. International buyers should also note that Colombian ticket platforms typically display prices in Colombian pesos, and the final charge on a foreign card will reflect the exchange rate applied by the buyer’s bank on the transaction date.

Age Policy and Family-Friendly Zones

A strict age policy divides the stadium into adult-only and family-accessible sections. All standard localities require attendees to be 18 or older, with no exceptions.

Tuboleta explicitly warns that minors holding tickets for these areas will be denied entry with no refund. This rule is strictly enforced, making it essential for families to select the correct section at purchase.

The designated family grandstands—Gradería Occidental Baja Familiar and Oriental Baja Familiar—allow guests aged 12 and up when accompanied by a responsible adult. This setup reflects a broader trend at large Colombian stadium events, where organizers balance the demand for adult-oriented nightlife with the reality that the Feria de las Flores is, at its core, a citywide family celebration.

Parents planning to attend should factor in the concert’s late-night schedule when deciding whether the family section suits younger teenagers.

Where the Super Concierto Fits in the Feria de las Flores

The Super Concierto stands as the signature paid musical event within the 68th Feria de las Flores, scheduled from July 31 to August 9, 2026. Local media call it “un espectáculo que ya es un símbolo de la Feria de Flores y una cita obligada para Medellín y Colombia.” While most festival activities are free and scattered across public spaces, this stadium show anchors the second festival weekend, placing it right before the iconic Desfile de Silleteros.

The Desfile de Silleteros is the emotional climax of the entire Feria. It is a parade in which campesinos from the flower-growing village of Santa Elena carry enormous, intricately arranged flower displays on their backs—some weighing over 70 kilograMs These silletas are living artworks, and the parade draws hundreds of thousands of spectators to Medellín’s streets.

Positioning the Super Concierto on the eve of that parade means the concert serves as a high-energy, modern counterpoint to a deeply traditional event. Visitors who attend both get the full sweep of what the Feria represents: rooted rural heritage alongside a cosmopolitan, music-obsessed city.

Why This Matters for Expats and Music Fans in Medellín

The Super Concierto offers a concentrated dose of A-list Latin music that would normally require multiple separate concerts. Carín León’s appearance places a global Mexican music phenomenon on a Colombian stage, while Silvestre Dangond and Grupo Niche guarantee strong local turnout with sounds deeply woven into Antioquia’s social fabric.

For English-speaking expats, this event is a rare opportunity to experience a top-tier Colombian mega-concert with clear ticketing procedures, predefined pricing, and a well-documented venue—reducing the uncertainty that sometimes accompanies local cultural events.

Beyond the music itself, the Super Concierto functions as a cultural entry point. Attending means navigating the same ticket platform, stadium entry protocols, and crowd rhythms that locals know well.

For newcomers still building their Medellín routines, that practical knowledge transfers to other large events in the city. It also offers a shared experience with tens of thousands of paisa families and friend groups, creating a sense of participation in the city’s calendar rather than observation from the outside.

Several open questions remain worth watching. Will the pre-sale allocation sell out within hours, as has happened with past Feria headliners, pushing late buyers into higher price tiers?

How will the stadium manage the flow between adult-only and family sections given the strict age enforcement? And with Carín León’s international profile still rising, could his Medellín appearance draw a noticeable contingent of Mexican regional music fans from across Latin America, shifting the audience mix compared to previous years?

None of these can be answered yet, but they will shape the on-the-ground experience for anyone holding a ticket.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time does the Super Concierto 2026 start and when can I enter?

Doors open at 4:00 p.m., and the concert begins at 7:00 p.m. on Saturday, August 8, 2026. The event is expected to run late into the night, so plan for a multi-hour show.

Can I bring my teenager to see Carin León at the Super Concierto?

Yes, but only in designated family sections (Gradería Occidental Baja Familiar or Oriental Baja Familiar). These sections allow guests 12 and older when accompanied by a responsible adult.

All other sections are restricted to 18 and older with no exceptions.

How do I buy official tickets from outside Colombia?

Tickets are sold exclusively online through Tuboleta.com, starting May 29, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Colombian time. International credit cards are generally accepted on the platform, but ensure you select a section that matches your group’s ages to avoid being denied entry.
