Should Abkhazia’s MPs be required to speak Abkhaz?

World.title: Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from Council of Europe: sovereignty strategy and possible consequences
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from the Council of Europe

On 13 July, speaking at the opening ceremony of the 4th Global Media Forum in Shusha, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev said the country was considering a complete withdrawal from the Council of Europe (CoE). His remarks came after the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) decided in January 2024 not to ratify the credentials of the Azerbaijani delegation, effectively suspending its voting rights.

Azerbaijan joined the Council of Europe voluntarily in 2001. According to the government’s official position, it sought membership to make use of international mechanisms and secure support for resolving the Karabakh conflict. Relations between Baku and the organisation, however, gradually deteriorated. After Azerbaijan restored full control over its internationally recognised territory in 2023, the authorities described PACE’s decisions as unfair and politically motivated. Aliyev’s latest statement reflects a broader reassessment of sovereignty in Azerbaijan’s foreign policy and its approach to international organisations.

This article draws on official statements, independent analysis and international sources to examine Azerbaijan’s position, the criticism it has faced, and the potential consequences of leaving the Council of Europe.

Official position and arguments

Speaking at the 4th Global Media Forum in Shusha, President Ilham Aliyev said Azerbaijan was seriously considering leaving the Council of Europe altogether.

“I openly say that Azerbaijan is considering the possibility of completely withdrawing from the organisation. This is not about suspending or freezing our membership. We are definitely considering leaving this institution.”

Aliyev also argued that if Azerbaijan were to leave the Council of Europe, ordinary citizens would not notice any significant changes and the situation could even improve. State officials and pro-government media framed the issue as one of protecting national sovereignty and accused international institutions of treating Azerbaijan unfairly.

According to the government’s official position, Azerbaijan joined the Council of Europe in 2001 in the hope of securing international support for resolving the Karabakh conflict. Officials argue that those expectations were never fulfilled. They also describe PACE’s January 2024 decision not to ratify the credentials of the Azerbaijani delegation and suspend its voting rights as punishment for Azerbaijan’s restoration of its territorial integrity in 2023.

“We did not take part in the vote on the election of judges and have been subjected to discrimination for the past two years,” Aliyev said.

The Council of Europe’s leadership, including Secretary General Alain Berset, has contacted Aliyev and urged Azerbaijan not to leave the organisation, while calling for a way to resolve the dispute.

Baku maintains that the next step should come from the Council of Europe. According to the government, PACE should first restore the Azerbaijani delegation’s voting rights, after which the delegation could return to its work in the Assembly. Officials argue that leaving the organisation would have little impact on the country’s domestic situation because Azerbaijan already has its own institutional mechanisms in place and regards sovereignty as a top priority. Analysts close to the government have echoed this position, saying Azerbaijan should reject what they describe as bias by international organisations and put national interests first.

Critical assessments and the international perspective

In reports and video coverage published on 13 July, Meydan TV argues that Aliyev’s statement signals preparations for Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from both PACE and the jurisdiction of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). The outlet published its coverage under the headline: “Aliyev is preparing to withdraw Azerbaijan from PACE and the ECtHR – who will lose out?” It focuses primarily on the risk that Azerbaijani citizens could lose their right to file individual applications with the ECtHR.

According to Meydan TV, such a move would weaken human rights protections, particularly against the backdrop of cases involving the arrests of journalists from AbzasMedia and Meydan TV, as well as the broader state of media freedom. In contrast to the government’s position, the outlet argues that withdrawing from the Council of Europe and ending the ECtHR’s jurisdiction would have significant consequences for ordinary citizens. It notes that the ECtHR dealt with 2,180 cases involving Azerbaijan in 2025 alone, arguing that this reflects the large number of people who turned to the international court after failing to obtain justice in the country’s domestic courts.

RFE/RL places the issue in a broader context. It notes that PACE imposed sanctions on Azerbaijan amid a wave of arrests that began in 2023, a growing number of political prisoners and continued concerns over media freedom. The outlet also points to Azerbaijan’s refusal to invite PACE observers to monitor the presidential election held in February 2024.

RFE/RL also recalls that, as part of the process of joining the Council of Europe between 1996 and 2002, Azerbaijan introduced a number of reforms, including abolishing the death penalty, reforming its penitentiary system and acceding to the European Convention on Human Rights.

The outlet further compares Aliyev’s claim that “little will change, and things may even improve” after withdrawal with Russia’s departure from the Council of Europe in 2022. It argues that Russia’s experience suggests such a move can deprive citizens of access to international human rights protection mechanisms. According to RFE/RL, any Azerbaijani withdrawal from the Council of Europe would primarily affect people seeking justice for human rights violations.

From an international perspective, the possible consequences of Azerbaijan’s full withdrawal from the Council of Europe include greater international isolation and reputational damage, although the Azerbaijani authorities reject this assessment. At the same time, the Council of Europe’s leadership has publicly expressed its desire for Azerbaijan to remain a member of the organisation.

Alternative platforms and a long-term strategy

Azerbaijan’s foreign policy has traditionally been based on a multi-vector approach that seeks to balance relations with different international partners. This strategy allows the country to engage selectively with international organisations in line with its national interests. According to the government’s official position, regional and international bodies such as the Organization of Turkic States, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation offer forms of cooperation that place greater emphasis on sovereignty and equal partnership. Officials argue that these organisations provide opportunities to expand cooperation in areas including the economy, energy, culture and security.

At the same time, Azerbaijan continues to deepen its energy partnership with European countries. Projects such as the Southern Gas Corridor and natural gas exports operate independently of the country’s membership in the Council of Europe. As a result, Baku argues that a stronger focus on sovereignty can coexist with pragmatic economic and energy cooperation with Europe.

In the longer term, this diversification is intended to give Azerbaijan greater flexibility in its foreign policy and allow it to maintain balanced relations with different partners. Critics warn that leaving the Council of Europe could weaken international human rights safeguards available to Azerbaijani citizens. The government, however, argues that alternative international platforms can offset any gaps in economic and political cooperation. Overall, officials present this strategy as part of a broader effort to pursue an independent foreign policy based on Azerbaijan’s national interests.

Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from the Council of Europe

World.title: Russian MFA spokeswoman: ‘West cannot stomach Georgia’s independence’
World.content:
Maria Zakharova on Georgia and OSCE

Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze‘s assessment of Western institutions required no further confirmation from Moscow, adding that the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly had long pursued a course of “aggression, aggressive rhetoric and destructive actions”.

Zakharova’s remarks came in response to a question at a news conference on whether the Russian Foreign Ministry shared Kobakhidze’s assessment. Kobakhidze had earlier accused the OSCE and European institutions of involvement in attempts to bring about a violent change of government in Georgia.

Maria Zakharova: “The Georgian prime minister’s remarks require no confirmation from us. We are talking about the leader of a sovereign state who knows and loves his country and represents its people.

Modern Georgia is a clear example of brazen, and at times unprecedented, external interference in the affairs of a state that possesses all the attributes of sovereignty

Tbilisi’s determination to pursue an independent and nationally oriented policy — meaning one focused on its own people, who are themselves multi-ethnic — is perceived by the ‘collective West’ as a direct challenge. To put it in plain Russian, it sticks in their throat.

This irritates Western representatives so much that they are prepared to use every lever at their disposal to remove the current government simply because it serves the interests of its own people, thinks about them, understands them and their history, and builds the country’s future on that basis, rather than serving those who have nothing to do with the Georgian people or their history.

The Georgian prime minister’s remarks apparently relate to the adoption of the Hague Declaration at the annual session of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly. The declaration includes a number of resolutions, including one concerning Georgia’s ‘undemocratic’ elections.

Such destructive activity by the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly comes as no surprise to us. The assembly long ago chose the path of aggression. A number of states use the OSCE platform to launch unrestrained criticism not only of Russia but also of other countries, including through the use of the ‘Moscow Mechanism’ — an outdated, pseudo-human-rights and non-consensual instrument.

Everything they allege against Georgia, including the accusations you have asked about, is false.”

OSCE resolution

On 8 July, the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly adopted a critical resolution on Georgia calling on the country’s authorities to release political prisoners, repeal legislation restricting civil liberties and uphold democratic standards.

The resolution, entitled Protecting Electoral Integrity and Fundamental Freedoms in Georgia, forms part of the Hague Declaration, the final document adopted at the assembly’s 33rd annual session, held in the Netherlands from 4 to 8 July.

Representatives of Georgia’s ruling Georgian Dream party attended the session but walked out in protest at the adoption of the resolution.

World.title: Armenia begins ratifying TRIPP agreement with US: foreign minister outlines key details
World.content:
Armenia begins ratifying the TRIPP agreement

Armenia has begun the process of ratifying the framework agreement on strategic cooperation with the United States under the TRIPP project.

The agreement concerns the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a transit route linking Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhichevan. The project forms part of the Armenian government’s Crossroads of Peace initiative, which aims to reopen regional transport links.

The government has approved the agreement and submitted it to the Constitutional Court. The court must now determine whether it complies with Armenia’s constitution.

“If the Constitutional Court finds that the obligations set out in this international agreement are compatible with Armenia’s constitution, we will submit it to the National Assembly in accordance with the established procedure and bring it before parliament for discussion,” Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said, outlining the next steps. Parliament must ratify the agreement before it can take effect.

Mirzoyan said Armenia must also finalise two more documents before it can complete the TRIPP project. They include a shareholders’ agreement and the charter of the TRIPP Development Company.

The foreign minister also commented on reports about the TRIPP+ fund. Britain’s The Guardian reported on the fund a day earlier, prompting questions in Armenia about the new structure. Mirzoyan said it was an American investment fund and would have only “an indirect connection” with the company that Armenia plans to establish.

Armenia and the United States initialled the framework agreement on strategic cooperation under the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity project on 26 May 2026. Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio took part in the initialling ceremony in Yerevan. They signed the agreement shortly afterwards through a remote procedure. Rubio signed it in Washington on 1 June, while Mirzoyan signed it in Yerevan on 4 June. “To dispel any possible questions, I would like to note that international practice and Armenian legislation both provide for the signing of such non-simultaneous, remote agreements, and this is a widely accepted practice,” Ararat Mirzoyan said during today’s government meeting. On 8 August 2025, the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed a joint declaration at a summit in Washington, marking the launch of the regional connectivity project. The declaration mentioned the Trump Route project for the first time. Before that, Armenia and Azerbaijan had failed to reach agreement on the issue. Azerbaijan had demanded a route it called the “Zangezur Corridor”. Armenia said it was ready to reopen all transport links. At the same time, it firmly rejected the term “corridor”, arguing that it implied the loss of sovereign rights over its territory. The parties reached a compromise only in Washington. They agreed that Armenia would retain sovereign control over the route, while the United States would join the project as a business partner.

“Armenia and the US will help strengthen peace in the South Caucasus”

According to Armenia’s foreign minister, the TRIPP project will help bring peace, stability and prosperity to the South Caucasus. He said it would achieve this by promoting:

transport connectivity;

infrastructure development; and

regional and global trade.

Under the framework agreement, Armenia and the United States will establish the TRIPP Development Company. The company will have the authority to create special purpose entities and bring in additional partners to implement individual projects in Armenia.

“The entire process, from the establishment of the development company to its future operations, will fully respect Armenia’s sovereignty, jurisdiction and territorial integrity,” Ararat Mirzoyan said.

He recalled that the development company would receive land use and development rights for the relevant areas. The parties have set the initial term at 49 years. The United States will hold a 74% stake in the company, while Armenia will own the remaining 26%. If the partnership continues for another 50 years, Armenia’s share will automatically increase to 49% after the first 49-year term.

“If the term is extended, Armenia will not need to take any additional steps to obtain its 49% stake,” the minister said.

Armenia will retain control over border, customs and migration procedures

The foreign minister again stressed that, in line with Armenia’s domestic legislation and international agreements, the Armenian authorities will continue to oversee:

security and the protection of rights;

border control and border security;

customs and migration procedures;

the collection of taxes and customs duties for the state budget;

state information systems; and

public administrative functions.

He said these guarantees should address public concerns about Armenia retaining its sovereign rights over the territory.

What is the link between the TRIPP Development Company and TRIPP+?

Britain’s The Guardian reported that the US State Department had appointed Konstantin Sokolov to lead the TRIPP+ trade fund. Sokolov is a US investor who was born in the Soviet Union and now lives in Chicago.

Armenian media quickly picked up the report. However, questions remained about the nature of the fund and its relationship with the company that Armenia plans to establish to implement the Trump Route project.

Journalists raised the issue during the government meeting. Ararat Mirzoyan replied that the agreement between Yerevan and Washington provides for the creation of the TRIPP Development Company.

“Its founders will be the Armenian government and the TRIPP Development Company-USA, which will be established in the United States,” Mirzoyan said.

As for TRIPP+, he said it is an American company established under the TRIPP Development Company-USA. Its role will be to attract investment for the project.

“From a legal perspective, TRIPP+ has only an indirect relationship with the TRIPP Development Company that will be established in Armenia,” the minister said..

Armenia begins ratifying the TRIPP agreement

World.title: Breaking: 'ISIS bride' Rayann El Houli granted bail by Melbourne court
World.content:
A Victorian woman facing terror charges after living under Islamic State rule in Syria will be freed on bail.

Rayann El Houli has been in custody for about two months after being charged with being a member of a terrorist organisation and entering a declared area.

Her lawyers say she will fight the charges, which carry a maximum 10-year jail term.

Police argued against bail, saying there was an unacceptable risk she would spread extremist ideology.

But today a Melbourne magistrate concluded the risk to the community was low.

He said there were "exceptional circumstances" that warranted her release, including potential legal delays and her poor health.

World.title: Breakthrough win for Bernard Tomic after lean tennis times
World.content:
Bernard Tomic is back in the winner's circle with the Australian veteran cracking his first Challenger Tour title in eight years.

Reaching the final of the Lincoln Challenger tournament in Nebraska, the 33-year-old showed some grit to save a championship point before downing Estonian Mark Lajal 4-6, 7-6 (4), 7-6 (3).

With a world ranking at 206, down from a career-high of number 17 back in 2016, Tomic started as underdog against 23-year-old Lajal, who is ranked world number 159.

The crafty Queenslander nailed his service games, on target with 72 per cent of first serves as well as nine aces to cause headaches for his rival.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Tomic also had a three-set battle to book his place in the final, downing American wildcard Spencer Johnson 6-7 (5), 6-3, 6-2.

It was his fourth Challenger Tour title, with the last coming in Mallorca in Spain in 2018.

A quarter-finalist at Wimbledon back in 2011 and former junior champion, Tomic recently lost in the second round of qualifying, falling to fellow Australian Chris O'Connell 6-4, 6-4.

On the main ATP Tour, his fourth and last singles title was at the 2015 Colombia Open in Bogota.

AAP

World.title: Wintry one-pot meals, from cheat's chicken soup to creamy butter beans
World.content:
Short, wintry days can induce a case of the "can't be bothereds" when it comes to dinner.

If this sounds like you, these tasty one-pot recipes will help you get a meal on the table fast, so you can snuggle up on the couch with a blanket and get warm.

From butter beans with jammy leaks to a quick chicken soup, there's an option here for all palates.

Serve one-pot chicken and tomato rice with yoghurt, pickles and salad for a delicious midweek meal. (ABC News: Lina Jebeile)

This Lebanese-style chicken and tomato rice dish comes together with minimal fuss.

Hints of cumin, paprika and cinnamon, combined with the rich taste of tomato and the fluffy texture of basmati rice, make for a tasty and satisfying meal.

Pan-fry your chicken and onion, add your tomatoes, spices and rice, simmer in stock for 15 minutes — and you're done.

Delicious chicken soup needn't take hours to cook. (ABC News: Edwina Storie)

This recipe delivers on its promise.

Made with shredded rotisserie chicken and thin, ready-to-eat egg noodles, it also takes just 30 minutes to make.

But its tasty combo of fresh herbs and veggies will leave you feeling satisfied and nourished.

This simple meal comes from gluten-free cook and recipe developer Helen Tzouganatos. (Supplied: Ben Dearnley/Plum)

Butter beans are the star of this simple dish that ticks a lot of boxes.

You can have it on the table in 15 minutes, it's packed with protein, and it's free of gluten and dairy.

Miso and butter bean brine (from the tin) give this dish a lovely creaminess, even though it's dairy free.

The store-bought gnocchi in this tasty tray bake does not need pre-boiling. (ABC Life: Hetty McKinnon)

This one uses one tray, rather than a pot, but the vibe is right.

The person who discovered store-bought gnocchi can be used in a tray bake deserves a medal. There's no pre-cooking required for gnocchi in this dish, and the whole thing is done in 30 minutes, including prep time.

The charred lemon and fennel seeds make this low-effort dish feel a little bit fancy, while a good helping of grated pecorino on top adds a delicious layer of comfort.

World.title: Boy, 15, bailed a week after northern Queensland school stabbing
World.content:
A 15-year-old boy charged with stabbing another teen at a Cairns school has been given bail, with a magistrate finding new information "paints a different picture" to police statements.

The injured boy, also 15, was released from Cairns Hospital over the weekend.

He spent last week being treated for a wound on his right side which pierced his liver, plus "six small lacerations or scratches".

The court heard surgery was not required.

The injured boy spent a week in Cairns Hospital after the alleged stabbing. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

The boys were involved in a fight at a high school a week ago during the first break on the first day of the new school term.

Cairns Children's Court heard today police have an 18-second video of the fight and that witnesses separated the boys after they saw blood.

The accused, who appeared in the dock, was represented by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Legal Services lawyer Steven Baso on a charge of acts intended to cause grievous bodily harm.

Mr Baso said a disagreement in social media messages between the boys started early in the winter school holidays and escalated the night before the fight.

Mr Baso said a sworn police statement alleging the accused arranged for the knife to be brought to school was "overstated" and not supported by evidence.

"The providence of the knife is a key aspect," Mr Baso told the court.

However, the court heard the defendant told police in his statement he got the knife from "someone at school" when asked where it came from.

"Rather than demonstrating malicious intent, there may be a defensive mindset," Mr Baso said.

Mr Baso presented Acting Magistrate Kellie Walker with 18 images of a conversation between the defendant and the complainant.

"The first reference to any sort of physical violence comes from the complainant and has a message where he's threatening to gang up on him," he said.

Ms Walker agreed the defendant did not challenge the complainant, was not the aggressor, had not arranged someone to bring the knife, and that the fight was not over a girl.

"I accept the text messages in these proceedings paint a different picture in relation to the background leading up to the fight than that deposed in the bail affidavit," Ms Walker told the court.

The court heard a conversation between the boys on the social media application TikTok. (ABC News: Phoebe Pin)

Ms Walker said there were discrepancies in the police's bail objection.

"At no time in the text messages do you say to the complainant things such as, 'I will bash you', or 'I will fight you', which is an allegation made by the complainant in his statement to police," she said.

"The prosecution case with respect to the premeditation of the attack has been weakened by the statements tendered today," she said.

The magistrate accepted the defendant had felt paranoid after he was threatened, and that he was distressed after the fight.

Police prosecutor Marie Griffiths said she opposed bail because the child posed an unacceptable risk to the community.

She told the court she expected the boy would be sentenced to between three and six years in prison if found guilty.

But Ms Walker told the court she was not convinced a lengthy period of detention would inevitably follow a successful conviction.

Acting Magistrate Kellie Wilson said the text messages presented "painted a different picture" to the police affidavit. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

His bail conditions mean he will be under a 24-hour curfew, is unable to attend school or use social media, and cannot contact the other teenager or other witnesses from school.

The case returns to the children's court in early September.

World.title: UK YouTuber Yung Filly violently sexually assaulted young fan, court hears
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains details some readers may find distressing, including descriptions of alleged sexual assault.

British social media personality Yung Filly violently and repeatedly sexually assaulted a young fan in a hotel room during his tour of Australia, a court has heard.

The alleged victim, who cannot be identified, had a "celebrity crush" on the YouTuber and rapper, the court heard, and had consensual sex with him in his Perth hotel after a nightclub performance in September 2024.

But the encounter soon became "non-consensual", and she found herself being physically assaulted, the court was told.

The court heard the sexual activity became increasingly violent. (Facebook: Yung Filly)

Yung Filly, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, 30, is on trial in the District Court, accused of sexually assaulting the 20-year-old woman.

Prosecutor Danielle Clarke said the woman was looking forward to seeing his performance at Bar1 at Hillarys Boat Harbour, with her cousin.

The prosecutor said she had recorded a video saying she "loved Yung Filly and wanted him to be her future husband".

The woman wore her "lucky" white top but, the prosecutor said it "turned out to be anything but lucky" for the alleged victim.

'You're coming home with me'

The woman was allowed into the club's VIP lounge, where free drinks were available, and she was approached by Mr Barrientos, who seemed interested in her.

Ms Clarke said the rapper told her "you're coming home with me tonight", with the woman believing she was going to a party.

Yung Filly has millions of followers across his multiple social media profiles. (Instagram: yungfilly)

Soon after they arrived at the Intercontinental Hotel in Hay Street, Mr Barrientos's bodyguard took her phone.

Inside the hotel room, the woman had consensual sex with him. But the prosecutor said the rapper became more aggressive, biting her neck, right cheek and breast.

The alleged victim had told him to stop, but he continued, the court heard.

Ms Clarke told the jury he held his hand tightly around her neck for a few seconds and slapped her, telling her to say derogatory things.

YouTube rapper accused of rape allowed to fly home on bail British YouTube content creator Yung Filly, who's facing trial in Perth on sex assault charges, is granted permission to travel home.

The woman refused, the court was told, and started to cry.

The court heard Mr Barrientos then allegedly anally raped her.

After the alleged rape, she was given back her phone and overheard Mr Barrientos saying to his bodyguard that she "wasn't good in bed".

The court heard the alleged victim took photos of her injuries and reported it to police the next day.

Mr Barrientos is charged with six counts of sexual penetration without consent, three counts of assault causing bodily harm and one count of impeding someone's normal breathing.

UK rapper and YouTuber Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, known as Yung Filly, pictured in June last year. (ABC News: Grace Burmas)

Defence lawyer David Edwardson did not give an opening statement.

The alleged victim is set to testify this afternoon.

The trial is set down for two weeks.

Large following

Yung Filly's social media channels boast millions of followers while his videos have amassed more than 100 million views.

He has also found success in music, charting two top 40 singles in the UK, including one that was certified silver for selling more than 200,000 units.

Yung Filly performs on songs as a rapper, with his musical projects prompting the 2024 tour of Australia.

World.title: Brisbane MP says tax figures show 'AirTrain's foreign owners are ripping us all off'
World.content:
Brisbane's "rip-off" airport shuttle service paid zero income tax to Australia while parking its assets overseas, Greens MP Michael Berkman has said.

Financial reports by USS Axle, which owns the Brisbane AirTrain service, show the company paid zero income tax between 2015 and 2025 financial years.

USS Axle's parent company, Universities Superannuation Scheme, is based in the United Kingdom and holds significant international assets.

Michael Berkman says AirTrain is ripping off Queensland taxpayers. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

"It looks like AirTrain's owner has set up complex financial arrangements including taking out a loan from its own parent company to dodge tax," Mr Berkman said.

"While Queenslanders are working hard, paying their taxes and struggling with fuel and transport costs, the AirTrain's foreign owners are ripping us all off."

AirTrain is a private service running on public infrastructure, meaning it can set its own fares and that Queensland's 50 cent fares do not apply.

A standard one-way AirTrain ticket costs $23.30 per person, with concessions for children.

AirTrain's exclusive deal with the state government prohibits any other form of direct public transport to the airport until 2036.

The only other public transport option is taking a shuttle service to the DFO mall on the outskirts of the airport, and then catching connecting buses and trains into the city.

This method typically takes two to three times longer than the AirTrain.

Plans are underway to build a Metro bus line to the DFO mall and connect passengers to the terminal via a shuttle bus, since the line is not allowed to go directly to the airport.

DFO Brisbane is just outside AirTrain's exclusion zone. (ABC News: Jim Malo)

Under USS Axle's contract, AirTrain is not due to return to public hands until 2036.

Mr Berkman said the state government should try to nationalise AirTrain, offering to buy it back for $45 million.

He said if the owners refused the offer, the state government should legislate to force it on the grounds it was "an unacceptably bad deal for Queensland" ahead of the 2032 Olympics.

Under the existing contract, AirTrain will be the only direct public transport option for international visitors when the 2032 Olympics rolls around.

Mr Berkman said nationalising AirTrain would allow the state government to reduce tickets to 50 cents and extend the Gold Glider bus line into the airport.

"Ditching the AirTrain contract sends exactly the right message: that we won't let corporations hold Queenslanders to ransom anymore," Mr Berkman said.

"By ending the private contract we could also get to work building a new station at DFO, and boost frequency from 30 minutes to every 15 minutes."

AirTrain and Brisbane Airport were contacted for comment.

World.title: 'Good night, sweet dreams': Derryn Hinch farewelled at state funeral
World.content:
Australian broadcaster and former senator Derryn Hinch has been remembered as a prolific journalist with a kind heart.

Hinch died aged 82 on July 10 after several years of declining health.

At a state funeral service in Melbourne today his family, friends and colleagues from the entertainment and media realms remembered a rich life, lived to the full.

Derryn Hinch holds his official Senate portrait in July 2026. (Facebook: Derryn Hinch)

A moving tribute from Hinch's brother, Desmond "Des" Hinch, read by broadcaster and announcer Craig Willis, invited attendees to remember the man once nicknamed the "human headline" as a "pesky little brother".

Des recalled that in their youth the brothers separated their bedroom with a line and that Derryn's side was always a "chaotic jumble" of his possessions.

Prized among them was a kaleidoscope.

Derryn Hinch dies aged 82 Hinch was known for his distinctive broadcast style, his time in the Senate, and his law-breaking crusades to expose sex offenders that earned him several stints in jail.

Des then asked everyone at the service to think of "at least one special memory you will keep of my brother".

"It could be something he said, something he did, something he wrote. It could be a book, an interview or a recipe.

"If we could all gather those memories together they would fill that bedroom from our youth.

"You could look at them through a kaleidoscope, and with each twist of the tube you as the observer would see the colourful, constantly changing multifaceted mosaic that was his life."

His former wife, Australian actress Jacki Weaver, was among those to deliver eulogies.

Hinch was famously married five times, and at the end of his life had reunited with former partner Lynda Stoner.

Weaver could not attend the state funeral in person, so her eulogy was played as a video.

She began by describing herself as "Derryn's third wife and close friend for almost half a century".

Jacki Weaver delivered a tribute via video at Derryn Hinch's funeral. (ABC News)

She paid tribute "sincerely and warmly" to all the women Hinch had loved.

"I won't mention you individually. We don't have the time," she said.

"And in the immortal words of Steven Spielberg, 'We're going to need a bigger boat.'"

Weaver became emotional at the end of her tribute, saying she loved him "from the very start to the very end".

She became tearful as she wished him a "good night, sweet dreams".

Look back at our live coverage of the state funeral service for Derryn Hinch to read more tributes to the legendary broadcaster.

Colleagues remember a loud voice for justice who was always likeable

Starting his career in newspapers in New Zealand, Hinch later moved to Australia, working at numerous newspapers and radio stations.

The larger-than-life media figure often told people he was sacked from "16 or 17" of his high-profile jobs.

But today, his former colleagues only had fond memories and anecdotes to share.

Ray Martin was among those to speak at Derryn Hinch's eulogy. (ABC News)

Veteran journalist Ray Martin, who worked as a foreign correspondent for the ABC in New York at the same time Hinch worked in the US city for Fairfax, prompted mourners to give Hinch a standing ovation.

Martin said there was nothing subtle about Hinch or his "endless" opinions.

"He was born with a megaphone for a voice. His typewriter was just about as loud," Martin said.

"He was brave and brash with an ego that could light up a small city."

He said Hinch was also very likeable, and had written multiple books.

"Two of them were about Scrabble because he loved words," Martin said.

"Six were about himself … because he quite liked himself as well," he laughed.

Derryn Hinch was a former chair and ambassador of the children's charity, Variety. (Facebook: Variety)

A common theme was Hinch's strong sense of justice. The broadcaster became infamous throughout his career for flouting contempt of court laws regarding sex offenders.

He was convicted three times and even jailed.

Tony Tardio, the longtime newsreader at radio station 3AW where Hinch worked, said there would "never be another one like" Derryn Hinch.

"He interviewed the famous, locked horns with the powerful, romanced the most beautiful women, wrote millions of words, became a radio star, a television star," he said.

"Took on big and sometimes unpopular causes, went to jail, was put under home detention, founded a political party, sat in the Australian Senate.

"Drank too much, was within weeks of death [then] got someone else's liver, got an extra 16 years of precious life, and had a bloody good time doing it all," he said.

The service featured musical performances from Rhonda Burchmore who sang They Can't Take That Away From Me, Bob Valentine sang That's Life, and Nikki Nicholls performed one of Hinch's favourite songs, You Are So Beautiful.

Hinch's goddaughter Ellie O'Connell also performed the national anthem at the start of the service, returning to sing an original song for her godfather near its conclusion.

World.title: Man admits to making 'menacing' phone call to Age journalist
World.content:
A man has been ordered to complete an anger management course after he was caught making a "menacing" phone call to award-winning journalist Nick McKenzie.

The Melbourne Magistrates Court heard David Scholes, 32, called McKenzie on Christmas Eve in 2025 and called him a "f***ing scumbag".

It came after McKenzie, a reporter at The Age, had written about Mr Scholes's employer, MA Services Group.

The stories related to allegations of suspected tax evasion, worker exploitation and sexual harassment involving the company's founder, court documents said.

The security company collapsed in late 2025, leaving up to 1,700 people out of work.

According to a summary of allegations read to the court, Mr Scholes used software from his work to track down McKenzie's phone number, which was not publicly listed.

The MA Services Group manager switched off his phone's caller ID and rang McKenzie, boasting that the reporter was easy to find.

David Scholes has been placed on a good behaviour bond for 12 months. (Supplied)

"Bro I f***ing hope you sleep well at night … you're a rat," Mr Scholes said during the two-minute call.

During a police interview, Mr Scholes said he made the call because he blamed McKenzie for job losses at the company, where several of his family members worked.

He was also concerned an article would be written about him and his wife.

Prosecutor Annina Tropea said the incident left McKenzie feeling "rattled and under attack".

"Journalists and the media play an important role in the community and this type of menacing behaviour is designed to intimidate them performing that role," she said.

Defence lawyer Alastair Grigor said his client made full admissions and had written an apology letter to the reporter.

Mr Scholes, from Fraser Rise in Melbourne's north-west, was charged with using a carriage service to harass or menace.

The Age welcomes 'people being held accountable'

On Monday, Magistrate Donna Bakos described the phone call as "menacing" and "distressing to receive", and placed Mr Scholes on a diversion order.

The order means Mr Scholes has taken responsibility for making the call but no formal finding of guilt will be entered against him, nor a conviction recorded.

Mr Scholes was supported by family in court, and the magistrate said six character references had been tendered on his behalf.

She ordered him to complete an anger management program and be placed on a good behaviour bond for 12 months.

McKenzie is one of Australia's most-decorated reporters and has won 20 Walkley awards for journalistic excellence.

Since 2024, he has reported extensively allegations of corruption and criminality within Victoria's building industry.

In a statement, The Age editor Patrick Elligett said: "It is pleasing to see people being held accountable for threatening journalists, which could have a chilling effect on public interest reporting if left unchecked."

McKenzie's house was targeted in an unrelated incident in October 2025, when an offender climbed onto his roof and tried to disable a security system.

World.title: From code red to unstoppable: How your AFL team is placed in the chase for the top 10
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 From code red to unstoppable: How your AFL team is placed in the chase for the top 10 Jon Pierik July 20, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With five rounds remaining in the 2026 AFL home-and-away season, the sprint to September is officially on. Fremantle appear a lock for top spot, but from there it’s anyone’s guess. Josh Treacy fired for the Dockers against Port Adelaide. AFL Photos Sydney’s hold on second place is under siege from Hawthorn, Collingwood are pressing, while five would-be wildcard aspirants have taken a hit – although all remain in the race. The introduction of the wildcard round – extending the number of clubs who can make finals from eight to 10 – has ensured more teams remain in the race at this point of the campaign. We take a look at what awaits for your team.



What we say: The locked-and-loaded Dockers are an unstoppable force, the Power the latest to falter. They now sit three games clear on top of the ladder, and are all but certain to remain there despite what, on paper at least, is a challenging run home. The Eagles have improved, while the Bulldogs, Melbourne and Crows are flag contenders. Best-case finish: First. Worst-case finish: First.



What we say: We asked last week if the Swans’ indifferent form was something to ponder. The answer to that is yes. There was the loss to the Brisbane Lions, the fade-out against Fremantle, and now their first home defeat of the season, against Adelaide. That’s three defeats to premiership contenders. Isaac Heeney has slipped from being the No.1-ranked player in the league to 66th since round 14. The Giants await this week. Are the Swans tumbling from a top-two position? We’ll see. Best-case finish: Second. Worst-case finish: Fifth. Connor Macdonald and Nick Watson celebrate the Hawks’ big win over Richmond. AFL Photos What we say: Completed another clinical win, this time over Richmond, and are pressing for second spot on the ladder with the Swans faltering. Nick Watson continues to deliver wizardry acts, but co-captain James Sicily needs to harness his emotions, for he would not want to blow a fuse when a key game is on the line. The Hawks surely account for Essendon this week (please, no references to 1983-85), but the Brisbane Lions and Collingwood await.



Best-case finish: Second. Worst-case finish: Fourth. What we say: The Lions have won six straight, and there is no reason not to think this run won’t continue for at least another fortnight. Coach Chris Fagan has made no secret of his team’s aim. “Everyone knows the ladder and percentage and all that sort of stuff, so why shy away from it,” he said. “We’ve definitely used that as motivation over the last two or three weeks. It’s so tight. We’ve got to stay in the hunt, and we want to get that top four spot.” The chance to play at least two finals at home will have the Lions primed for a premiership three-peat. Best-case finish: Second. Worst-case finish: Eighth.



What we say: Last week we said the Crows were humming. Make that roaring after their sterling win in Sydney on Friday night, inflicting the Swans’ first loss at home this season. They have six wins from their past seven games, with Richmond and Essendon among their run home. Best-case finish: Second. Worst-case finish: Sixth. Kysaiah and Latrelle Pickett bask in victory after the Demons rolled over the Kangaroos. Getty Images What we say: Coach Steven King says the Demons are far from the finished product, a statement which should worry opponents after they have won five of their past six games. We said their best-case finish was third – that’s been re-rated to second. They will embrace the Friday night lights against a banged-up Geelong this week, and appear well-placed to even claim a top-four berth amid a potentially challenging run home.



Best-case finish: Second. Worst-case finish: Sixth. What we say: Last week we asked whether the Bulldogs were for real? We still can’t answer that question. Yes, it was an impressive victory against Gold Coast, but recent defeats to Adelaide and Sydney, and a less-than-convincing win over the Eagles, continue to gnaw away. Will take care of the Tigers this week, but the Dockers – and a serious litmus test – awaits. Best-case finish: Fourth. Worst-case finish: 11th.



What we say: That’s five straight wins for the Magpies, who are firmly in the hunt for a top-six finish. Is there a better team in the competition at filling selection holes and maximising their on-field performance? Now comes a season-defining month, for heavyweights Adelaide, Geelong, Hawthorn and the Brisbane Lions are on the agenda (and West Coast in Perth). Probably need to win at least three to avoid the wildcard round. On the march: The Magpies have momentum, and can sniff a top six finish. Getty Images Best-case finish: Fourth. Worst-case finish: 14th. What we say: As we said last week, the Cats have arguably the easiest run home, although their growing injury list, particularly to prime movers Jeremy Cameron and Max Holmes, may negate this. It’s a toss-of-the-coin job against Melbourne and Collingwood over the next fortnight (both games at the MCG), before expected wins over the final three rounds. Is the wildcard round the Cats’ best hope?



Best-case finish: Seventh. Worst-case finish: Ninth. Connor O’Sullivan of the Cats is tackled by Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera of the Saints. AFL Photos What we say: The Saints have arguably been the biggest disappointment of the season. A weakened Geelong was there for the taking on Thursday night, and what did the Saints do? They barely got moving for most of the night. They are no lock to knock over North Melbourne this week, then comes Sydney. They are suddenly in a major fight just to make the wildcard round. What has their off-season recruiting splurge really achieved? Not much to date. Best-case finish: 10th. Worst-case finish: 14th.



What we say: This was the shocker of the weekend, and sums up where the Giants really are. Internally, they had been frustrated by their lacklustre efforts against weaker sides, and that was reinforced against the Bombers. Terrible. Now they’ll be without injured skipper Toby Greene. We had the Giants finishing as high as seventh. That’s been downgraded to 10th. Ouch. Best-case finish: 10th. Worst-case finish: 14th. What we say: Has the bubble burst at Ikon Park? The seven straight wins under caretaker coach Josh Fraser are slowly receding into memory, for two defeats to serious September aspirants have shown where the Blues are really at. Still, they remain in wildcard contention. A win over the Suns at Marvel Stadium this weekend is a must.



Best-case finish: Seventh. Worst-case finish: 14th. Max Gawn of the Demons and Tristan Xerri of the Kangaroos contest the ruck. Getty Images What we say: It’s code red at Arden St. The Kangaroos had club royalty in the stands on Saturday, but blew a promising start against the Demons. That’s three straight defeats, their bid for a wildcard round in peril. Their best-case finish has been re-rated from eighth to 10th, for they have a potentially bruising run home. They need to get the job done against St Kilda this weekend otherwise their campaign is dead. Best-case finish: 10th. Worst-case finish: 14th.



What we say: We called the Suns a train wreck last week. Now we are not even sure they even were on the final line, such is the bewilderment over eight straight defeats. Yes, eight straight, from a team that should be contending for a flag. The Blues, at Marvel awaits, but we’ll be tipping Fraser’s men to rebound. The Suns face a painstaking post-season review. Ouch. Best-case finish: 10th. Worst-case finish: 15th. What we say: As we said last week, the Power are a mathematical chance to make the top 10, but there is little hope they will make it. They fought well against the Dockers, but their run home is arduous, the Lions up next.



Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 ‘A bloody good feeling’: Essendon bask in the glow of landing a win, climbing off the bottom Best-case finish: 14th. Worst-case finish: 15th. Not in the running West Coast (4-14) The Eagles did well to push the Lions in Perth, and have taken some important strides this season. They would love nothing better than knocking over the Dockers this weekend in the derby, but their best chance of another win in the remaining weeks of the season is against the Tigers.

World.title: Rodri touched the heavens, descended into hell, then won the Golden Ball
World.content:
Analysis SportSoccerFIFA World Cup Rodri touched the heavens, descended into hell, then won the Golden Ball Emma Kemp July 20, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a well-worn cliché about the merits of patience. Something about it being a highly regarded moral trait. One that helps a person tolerate frustrating delays and maintain focus on the long-term goal. Resilience and endurance win the day, and Rodri wins the Golden Ball. Just ask the oracle, Pep Guardiola, who held his Manchester City player back from returning too soon after rupturing his right anterior cruciate ligament. Loading “I said to him – and he maybe struggled to understand – it’s not about six, seven, eight months out, then playing and being the Rodri of before,” Guardiola said last October, with the wisdom of having observed the midfielder return for June’s Club World Cup just eight months after the initial injury, only to re-aggravate it. “No. Do you know when Rodri will be good? At the World Cup with Spain. At the World Cup, he will be the best Rodri.”



Even when Rodri finally returned properly in January, and City were visibly the better for his presence, there was a sense that the 2024 Ballon d’Or winner had not yet matched his previous heights. Plenty wondered if he ever would rediscover the form that helped Spain win the 2024 European Championship (and him win player of the tournament) and City to a record 74-match unbeaten streak with him in the side. After Spain’s opening match at the World Cup – that shock group-stage draw with Cape Verde – the criticism was loud enough for manager Luis de la Fuente to publicly defend his player. Rodri kisses his Golden Ball trophy. Getty Images “It seems incredibly insulting to me that people would say that about the best player in the world,” de la Fuente said last after last month’s scoreless result. “… Rodri is the best player in the world. Even at 50 per cent, he is better than most other midfielders in the world. He brings clarity, vision, balance. Rodri is an inspiration for us.” Then the rest of Spain’s tournament happened. They conceded a single goal en route to winning the trophy, and goalkeeper Unai Simon made a total 14 saves across their eight games – Argentina’s Emi Martinez made 11 in the final alone – demonstrating just how well he has been shielded.



Spain’s defensive line has been miserly, but Rodri has been the midfield anchor, cutting off supply to opponents’ attacks and playing almost every minute. The campaign was collective, but this 30-year-old was the commander. The reference point. And yet, the announcement of Rodri as player of the 2026 World Cup was met with as much disdain as it was nods of agreement. Lionel Messi was robbed, they said. Messi was named player of the match five times; Rodri once. Messi had eight goals and four assists; Rodri had none of either. Many believe Messi should have won the Golden Ball. SBS The MetLife Stadium crowd chanted Messi’s name as Rodri collected his Golden Ball trophy, as if the voting had somehow been rigged. Others mentioned Kylian Mbappe, Erling Haaland and Jude Bellingham as more worthy candidates. In reality, the identity of the official recipient said more about how much the world values individualism over teamwork. It also revealed how sometimes the most meaningful contributions can be the quietest.



The defensive midfield role is on the less sexy end of the spectrum, and the hallmark of those who thrive in it is that they often go unnoticed. They operate in service of structure and passes that allow others to steal the limelight. It isn’t glitzy, but it is as necessary as a goalscorer in a team in pursuit of greatness. Rodri completed a tournament-high 747 passes at a 93 per cent accuracy rate. In the final, he rendered Messi invisible. The all-time GOAT recorded one touch in the opening 15 minutes, and that was the kick-off. Argentina became the first World Cup finalists to fail to register a single shot in the regulation 90 minutes. By the end of extra time they had two, neither on target. Related Article Analysis

FIFA World Cup Spanish domination shows the limitations of ‘suffering’ in football And yes, Messi’s tournament has been a smorgasbord of logic-defying moments of which a 39-year-old should not be capable. And so it stands to reason that such a talent could also be squeezed out by one performing more efficiently. Rodri, back at his best. Joining Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Muller and Zinedine Zidane as the only men to win the World Cup and European Championships with their country, the European Cup/Champions League with club, and the Ballon d’Or.



“It feels like the perfect script. I certainly didn’t expect this,” Rodri said upon receiving the Golden Ball trophy. “I’d love for the younger generations to see that a player who touches the heavens, then descends into hell, can come back. It’s a lesson in overcoming adversity.” Patience is a virtue, and good things come to those who wait.

World.title: ‘We got good ... we never got near perfect’: Schmidt’s verdict on Wallabies tenure
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies ‘We got good ... we never got near perfect’: Schmidt’s verdict on Wallabies tenure Jonathan Drennan July 20, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The signs that it was Joe Schmidt’s last day at Rugby Australia were obvious on Monday. The outgoing head coach had swapped his regulation Wallabies polo for an open-necked light blue one. He had also pulled an all-nighter – not to review game tape, but to watch compatriot Ryan Fox, the son of All Blacks great Grant Fox, win golf’s British Open. Outgoing Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt thanks his captain, Harry Wilson, after Saturday’s victory over Italy in his final Test. Getty Images Schmidt’s 31st and final Wallabies Test ended with a 47-point win over Italy in Perth on Saturday. His successor, Les Kiss, will name his first squad on Thursday. The handover is all but done and while there is a good deal of pride in the Wallabies team he passes on to Kiss, Schmidt is not without regrets about his tenure. “There will always be regrets and there’s always going to be frustrations, because I think anyone involved in that level of performance is trying to aim at perfection [while] knowing that it’s unattainable,” Schmidt said.



“So I think we got good, we certainly never got near perfect. But we’re in a better place, in my humble opinion, than we were when I arrived. “On the dark days, in the last two games of the year [against Italy and France in November], when the boys were only just hanging in there, we were all really tired. I spent four days in bed at the end of that tour, because I think I’d run myself down so much I got a serious dose of man flu. Angus Bell and Joe Schmidt leave the field in Perth. Getty Images “Despite being resilient, that sort of ended me for a while. But I have no regrets about my commitment. I have regrets that we didn’t quite finish a few chances. And convert those and get the result that I felt the players had earned.” Details of those 31 Tests – tries, tackles, penalties conceded – remain fresh in Schmidt’s mind. The drought-breaking Ellis Park victory over South Africa and the third Test win against the British and Irish Lions were savoured, but the Lions series loss and the close defeat to New Zealand at Eden Park still sting.



Still, the coach remains proud of his achievements in rebuilding the side from the rubble of the calamitous 2023 World Cup under Eddie Jones. “I probably would [rate this job as his most challenging], just because it was the first time I came in, I knew no one,” he said. “There were two other members of staff, so we had no coaches. We had no real support staff, because it was a total clean-out after the World Cup. Schmidt is confident incoming coach Les Kiss will inherit a happier and more confident Wallabies squad. Getty “And a lot of the players, even post-World Cup, either weren’t available or there had been some guys who’d been left out and were teetering on the edge of heading overseas. So it was about convincing them that we could still get together and be competitive. “It was challenging, but I’ve learnt a heck of a lot in this window, and I’ve loved the challenge. I’ve loved the results sometimes, [but] in fact, I’ve also been depressed about the results in some of those games.”





“I think rugby league is always going to be a contest, particularly around the loose forward, midfield, wing positions,” Schmidt. “I used to look from the outside and think: why don’t Rugby Australia just grab all those really good kids out of school and give them academy scholarships? “But academy scholarships, compared to what some of the competitors can offer, it’s very tough going.” Schmidt hugs Max Jorgensen after the Italy Test. Getty Images The victory in Perth was followed by emotional scenes in which the Wallabies queued up to hug the departing coach with whom they had formed such a close bond. What was Schmidt’s final message to the players he will now watch from afar? “They take the mickey out of me sometimes with some of the phrases I use, but one of the ones they probably haven’t taken the mickey out of is that belief is the base and trust is the glue. I really believe that,” Schmidt said.



“When we build our self-belief and we genuinely know we’re good enough, then we can trust ourselves and each other, and that trust is the glue. That is the connective tissue. “So I’ll probably try to leave them with a message that: trust yourself, trust each other and build that belief in among some skill sets and some strategy around the game.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘One in 15 million’: Mum gives birth to identical quadruplets in likely Australian first
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPregnancy ‘One in 15 million’: Mum gives birth to identical quadruplets in likely Australian first Courtney Kruk July 20, 2026 — 3:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Brisbane woman has given birth to identical quadruplets – an extremely rare “one in 15 million” event – with doctors saying the pregnancy could be an Australian first. Jenitar Sau Na’amoana, 34, was raising four young children and had not planned another child with her husband Jortham when she naturally fell pregnant with the quadruplets. Dr Alexa Bendall, a fetal medicine specialist and obstetrician at Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, cared for Sau Na’amoana throughout the pregnancy. The healthy identical quadruplets were born at 28 weeks and four days. She said the now mum-of-eight handled the news well, taking “everything in her stride from day one”.



This included acknowledging the high-risk nature of a quadruplet pregnancy. “Whenever you have a multiple pregnancy – which is usually twins, not quads – where the babies are sharing a placenta, there’s a very high risk of complications,” Bendall said. The four girls – Emily, Harriet, Alexa and Catherine – were delivered via caesarean section. “Babies can be growth-restricted … there can be a high risk of mortality and morbidity for these babies and for mum. “So the fact that we’ve got four beautiful, healthy babies born at 28 weeks and four days is incredible, and we’re very happy to be apart of it.”



Monozygotic quadruplets – identical quadruplets split from one singular fertilised egg – are one of the rarest types of pregnancies in the world. Related Series

Fertility Australia’s baby bust Adding to Sau Na’amoana’s extraordinary odds was the fact that her quadruplets shared the same placenta. “This is unheard of,” Bendall said. “So four sacs, one placenta – we think the figures are about one in every 15 million for a case like this, to be spontaneously conceived. We don’t think it’s ever happened in Australia.



“There may have been a couple of cases elsewhere in the world, and when I say a couple, literally a couple; two. But this is the only case we know about in Australia.” Sau Na’amoana has been cared for by a team of experts at the RBWH since 10 weeks, and was admitted as an inpatient at 25 weeks for close monitoring. The family named one of the girls after RBWH Maternal Fetal Medicine Specialist and Obstetrician Dr Alexa Bendall. The four girls – Emily, Harriet, Alexa and Catherine – were delivered by caesarean section on July 14. Alexa is named after Bendall. “I’m incredibly honoured that they decided to name one of their girls after me,” she said.



The four babies are currently doing “extremely well” and will remain in the hospital’s specialist Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) to grow to full term. “We always said that is we could get her to 28 weeks, we would be doing well, so we are happy she could make it to this gestation,” Bendall said. World.title: Blues seek clarity from prominent commentator over McKay injury; Magpies and premiership forward preparing to split
World.content:
AFL Briefing SportAFLAFL 2026 Blues seek clarity from prominent commentator over McKay injury; Magpies and premiership forward preparing to split Jon Pierik Updated July 20, 2026 — 3:09pm ,first published 12:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In today’s AFL briefing: Carlton have sought clarity from prominent commentator David King after he questioned Harry McKay’s pain threshold on Saturday night.

The Magpies and premiership forward Bobby Hill are set to part ways.

Essendon star Nate Caddy has been discharged from hospital and is expected to play this week. Carlton have sought clarity from prominent commentator David King after he questioned Harry McKay’s pain threshold when the star forward went off injured in Saturday’s loss to Collingwood at the MCG. King, a dual North Melbourne premiership player and Fox Footy analyst, said on his breakfast radio show on SEN on Monday that the Blues had called him on Sunday to discuss his comments. “I took the call from Carlton [on Sunday] … and had a lot of [public] feedback about it [his commentary]. Look, my thoughts are my thoughts. I am not necessarily going to back over it too much,” King said. Out of the game: Carlton lost Harry McKay to a knee injury in the opening term against Collingwood on Saturday. AFL Photos



“I think we have spoken about players that go off a little bit easy in the past. I am not saying that’s Harry on this occasion. Clearly, he has got an issue, and they are telling me he will miss two weeks. I was basically referring to an old Denis Paganism which you will know if you listened to what I said earlier.” Asked to elaborate, King said: “All good. They [Blues] disagree with what the discussion was about, which is fine. That’s footy. I am happy to move on from that.” A Blues spokesman confirmed the Blues had spoken with King, but the club did not want to elaborate. On Sunday Carlton said McKay would be tested this week and might play against Gold Coast at Marvel Stadium next Saturday. King was contacted for comment by this masthead.





When it became clear McKay would take no further part in the game, King said: “Looks like he’s put a line through himself, putting the jacket on, that’s it, night over. Incredible disappointment. You wonder whether there’s any structural issue there or is it just a pain tolerance discussion?” In the box: Fox Footy commentator David King. Getty Images “This Harry McKay discussion will rage. There’s nothing worse than when a player of that significance is not there. It changes the whole game.” In reference to his former coaches, including premiership great Denis Pagan, King said: “My old coaches would say: ‘I hope that’s a two or three-week [injury]. If that’s a 15-20 minute [injury], you lose a lot of respect’.” Carlton said on the night that McKay had been ruled out by club doctors.



King added at half-time: “If that’s just a bit of pain management then you’ve got a lot more to answer for. I hope that’s not the case with Harry and time will tell.” Related Article AFL 2026 ‘We’ll be hard to play against’: How first Devils coach Ken Hinkley won the job McKay, the 2021 Coleman medallist, has battled mental health problems through his career. In the AFL Players Association’s annual insights and impact report released last week, 34 per cent of players said they felt a level of disrespect by broadcast media. This included concerns about a focus on negativity and hyperbole. After seven-straight wins under caretaker coach Josh Fraser, the Blues have lost their past two games, against Hawthorn and Collingwood, but remain in contention for a wildcard berth. They host the Gold Coast at Marvel Stadium on Saturday.



Magpies and star premiership forward preparing to split Jon Pierik Collingwood are working towards parting ways with premiership star Bobby Hill. The 2023 Norm Smith medallist is contracted until the end of 2030 on a deal reportedly worth about $750,000 a season.



Industry sources have confirmed conversations between the Magpies and Hill’s management at Mac’s Sports Promotions are ongoing. The Magpies and Mac’s Sports Management were contacted for comment. Uncertain future: Bobby Hill and Collingwood are working towards a split. Getty Images Hill has not played a senior game since round 21 last year, largely because of personal issues. He had an extended break over summer but was welcomed back into the fold earlier this season. He had been training at suburban grounds with a trainer before returning to the club. The dynamic small forward has played three VFL games, but has not been a consistent presence at the club.



Coach Craig McRae has repeatedly said he was excited about Hill’s potential return, but there was always the caveat of the unknown. McRae said in June that Hill was still working through his personal issues. “Truthfully, battling,” McRae replied when asked about Hill. Loading “He has a bit going on, let’s be really clear. He has a lot going on. He’s a work in progress, but it’s nice to have him in the building.



“He’s a long way away from playing footy ... but again, when he’s in our building, at least we get some opportunities to make him feel that he’s loved and appreciated.” Hill and his partner Georgia Devlin welcomed their third child in May. Seven reported on Monday that Hill was keen for a move to the Brisbane Lions, Gold Coast or Port Adelaide. Hill was originally drafted by Greater Western Sydney with pick No.24 in 2018. He has played 102 senior games across eight seasons.



Bombers confident Caddy will face Hawks Jon Pierik Essendon are confident Nate Caddy will be available for selection this week after he was hospitalised with an irregular heart rate during Sunday’s three-point win over Greater Western Sydney. Ready to go: Essendon star Nate Caddy is expected to be available to face the Hawks on Saturday. AFL Photos via Getty Images



Caddy was taken to hospital for assessment, having collapsed to the turf when he got to the interchange bench in the first quarter. He had further tests but was given the all clear and discharged on Sunday night. Essendon’s general manager of football Daniel McPherson said he expected Caddy to train this week ahead of a clash against arch-rival Hawthorn on Saturday. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 ‘A bloody good feeling’: Essendon bask in the glow of landing a win, climbing off the bottom “There was some concern in the first quarter when Nate’s heart rate became elevated,” McPherson said on Monday. “He was removed from the game, and our medical team assessed him at the ground before sending him to hospital for further assessment. He was discharged last night and is back at home.



“He is expected to be able to train and play without concern this week.” Caddy recently signed a contract extension until the end of 2031 in a huge boost for the battling Bombers, who no longer sit in last spot on the ladder. Wingman Xavier Duursma (hamstring) faces a spell on the sidelines. The Bombers were able to sing the club song for only the second time in 31 games after edging the shocked Giants. It was their first win since beating Melbourne in Gather Round in Adelaide on April 11, while they had not tasted victory in Victoria since May last year. It was Dean Solomon’s first win as caretaker coach since replacing Brad Scott in May.



While only 14,601 fans attended the game, the scenes of joy for the Bombers were palpable. “It’s a bloody good feeling. Our footy club’s been on its knees for a period of time, and the footy world’s jumped on that, and they enjoy us sitting at the bottom,” Solomon said. “We’ve felt that, and we don’t like that, so to push back a little bit and get one win, albeit one win, I’m just really happy for these players.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: As Kiss’s first Wallabies signing is revealed, a boom rookie is next on the radar
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies As Kiss’s first Wallabies signing is revealed, a boom rookie is next on the radar Nick Wright Updated July 20, 2026 — 3:06pm ,first published 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Reds boss Sam Cordingley has declared Australian rugby was well positioned to retain boom teenager Treyvon Pritchard, despite the wounded phenom courting interest from rival codes. Speaking from the club’s headquarters at Ballymore to announce the signing of Wallabies centre Izaia Perese, Cordingley was quietly confident Pritchard would not be swayed by an NRL defection, having held talks with the incoming Papua New Guinea Chiefs for their 2028 launch. The 19-year-old would have been a chance of earning a Wallabies or Australia A call-up as former Reds coach Les Kiss takes the national reins this week, having shown impressive signs in his maiden Super Rugby Pacific campaign. Treyvon Pritchard World Rugby His highlights reel included his dazzling footwork to bamboozle Chiefs and All Blacks superstar Damian McKenzie, while he had dominated the World Rugby Under-20s Championships in Georgia before suffering a broken leg and syndesmosis injury after being subjected to a ‘hip-drop’ tackle.



Cordingley – the Reds’ general manager of high performance – confirmed Pritchard would undergo surgery on Monday, and stressed there was no rush on his return to play. “I think he’s had a really good progression, he’s played a lot of Super Rugby this year and the 20s was an important rite of passage for him, and he was pretty keen to be a part of that,” Cordingley said. “I’m sure he would’ve been part of discussions. I daresay once he’s back on deck, those discussions will happen pretty quickly around where he sits in the Wallabies framework.” Treyvon Pritchard suffered serious injuries in this hip drop tackle against Wales at the Junior World Championship. Stan Sport Cordingley said Pritchard’s setback would not have any influence on the Reds’ desire to extend his contract beyond the end of his 2027 deal, while suggesting the club may be forced to contend with global interest after his Junior Wallabies exploits.



While the interest from the Chiefs, equipped with tax-free salary incentives, looms as an enticing carrot for the youngster who grew up in rugby league, Cordingley believed Rugby Australia held the upper hand. “He’s an elite talent, so I’m not surprised with the interest. He’s played over in the Junior World Cup against countries like France, and we know they have very strong recruitment processes as well – clubs certainly would have been watching his games over there,” Cordingley said. Loading “In terms of the injury, I don’t see it as detracting from our capacity to retain him, I think where that sits, it’s pretty well-placed for rugby to retain Trey. “I’m confident we’re going to put our best foot forward to retain him.”



Related Article Wallabies Australia’s top rugby schools revealed – including one ‘beast’ in Brisbane Cordingley’s revelations came as Perese became the first Rugby Australia signing of Kiss’ Wallabies tenure, with the powerful centre returning to his debut club after a two-year stint in England with Leicester. The six-time Test centre will rejoin the Reds through to the end of 2028, and will seek to fill the void left by departing No.13 Josh Flook (Benetton). Fellow Wallabies Hunter Paisami and Jock Campbell have also been heavily linked to Japanese rugby defections. “Decisions around Hunter and Jock, they’re sort of future [decisions], the focus of today is to really celebrate Izzy’s signing,” Cordingley said.



“He’s a great signing for the club, obviously we’ve lost Josh Flook to Benetton – hopefully that’s in the short-term, and hopefully, we can plan around the future and get Flooky back – but we’re trading a Wallaby for a Wallaby.” Perese confirmed the allure of the home World Cup in 2027 drew him and his family – including four young children – back to Australian shores, admitting he felt he would finish his career abroad. The 29-year-old, who briefly switched to rugby league and managed two games for the Brisbane Broncos, laughed when asked if the Chiefs ever appealed to him as an option, before expressing he was never going to be swayed from the 15-man code. Izaia Perese has returned to the Queensland Reds. Getty Images “There was no temptation there, I don’t know too much about that, but I wouldn’t have my family locked in a compound for nine months – it’d drive my missus and kids crazy,” Perese quipped.



“The World Cup’s always in the back of my mind, but the main reason to sign was I wanted to come back to the Reds for my family, wife and kids … but to also propel myself into Wallabies contention. “The longer season [in England], you definitely tend to learn more about yourself with the highs and lows, good times and bad. It’s time to come back and apply diligently.” Perese threw his hand up to come back into the Wallabies fold ahead of Kiss’s first Test in charge against Japan on August 8, provided he got himself back to peak fitness and overcame a minor knee issue.
