World.title: Investors bark. Coles backpedals on ‘peak pooch’ price for pet business
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMergers & acquisitions Opinion Investors bark. Coles backpedals on ‘peak pooch’ price for pet business Elizabeth Knight Business columnist July 20, 2026 — 3:00pm

July 20, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was roughly 20 years ago when supermarket bosses had their pet epiphany. The beginning of the trend towards pet (mainly dog) anthropomorphism that, perversely, had supermarket chief executives drooling over a retailing category with a hockey-stick-shaped growth potential. Forget the days when the pet isle in stores consisted of cans of Pal, rather supermarkets were ushering in an era in which shelves were stocked with expensive designer pooch treats, doggy apparel, vitamins and more. Coles’ boss Leah Weckert decided to abandon late-stage negotiations to spend nearly $4 billion to buy Greencross. Arsineh Houspian Against this backdrop it might appear counterintuitive that Coles’ boss Leah Weckert decided to abandon late-stage negotiations to spend nearly $4 billion to buy Greencross – the owner of Petbarn and City Farmer retail chains, hundreds of vet clinics and 24 vet hospitals. But there are plenty of reasons that Coles’ investors were lukewarm to the prospect of Coles making a major investment into Greencross – not the least of which was the price.



The widely speculated price of $3.9 million is a big lick of capital – an amount that could represent “peak pooch”. Related Article Updated

Private equity Private equity boss keeps his job despite guilty plea as $4 billion deal looms Coles called its decision disciplined – albeit the decision was reached after some shareholder pressure to reserve its capital. Four years ago, Woolworths spent $586 million for a foothold in Petstock – a provider of petfood, toys, vet clinics, grooming salons and even animal adoption hubs. The Woolworths deal valued Petstock at (what at the time seemed to be) a staggering $1 billion. To provide some context, the Petstock deal was done in the same week that private equity operator Anchorage Capital bought 100 per cent of high-end department store group David Jones for a mere $130 million. In the intervening years David Jones has financially struggled and Petstock has grown, so the valuation disparity now makes sense.



Woolworths’ then chief executive Brad Banducci was all smiles when posing for celebratory photos with his beloved Cavalier Cocker Spaniel cross, Juno. Meanwhile, Greencross inks $2 billion in annual revenue and it’s reported to be making $400 million profit before interest, tax and depreciation. It is difficult to deny that the growth in the provision of pet goods and services is a trend that retains some steam. Its current owner TPG Capital paid $675 million for the business seven years ago, so had the Coles deal been consummated, it would have been a massive payday for this private equity vendor, which is now contemplating a public float of the business. It is difficult to deny that the growth in the provision of pet goods and services is a trend that retains some steam, but there is a strong argument to be made for the supermarket industry spending its capital and management resources focusing on the current and not insignificant challenges it faces.



The sector will remain capital thirsty as the major players continue to integrate technology into supply chain and logistics to better manage digital distribution channels that are increasingly adopted by customers. They are up against the masters of online logistics and fulfillment, Amazon, whose infiltration into grocery retailing continues to grow. Brad Banducci with his dog Juno. Louise Kennerley The big supermarket operators are currently also in a highly contested fight for market share – and one that has come with an expensive investment into lowering prices. And despite Woolworths’ successful foray into the pet business, the two large supermarket groups have a checkered history of success when they have strayed outside their core competence.



Woolworths exited the last of its bottle shop and pubs investments in 2024, its ownership of Big W has been largely patchy, and its foray 10 years ago into establishing a hardware big box chain, Masters, was a legendary and very costly disaster. And then there is the legion of yield obsessed investors who would rather see profits pumped into dividends ahead of dogs. World.title: Safety authority grilled over pilot drug-testing gaps
World.content:
NationalQueenslandInquest Safety authority grilled over pilot drug-testing gaps Robyn Wuth July 20, 2026 — 2:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pilots on Sea World joy flights were breath-tested for alcohol before every shift but faced no mandated routine testing for illicit drugs ahead of a fatal crash, a coroner has heard. Four people – including pilot Ashley Jenkinson – were killed in a fatal midair collision between two Sea World helicopters outside the Gold Coast theme park on January 2, 2023. Ashley Jenkinson, the pilot who died in the Gold Coast helicopter crash. Facebook Earlier evidence revealed Jenkinson, 40, returned a post-mortem positive test for cocaine metabolites. Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) was quizzed about drug and alcohol rules for aviation operators at the ongoing inquest into the fatal crash in Brisbane on Monday.



CASA’s national manager for regulatory services Niels Bunte was asked how the rules were applied to Drug and Alcohol Management Plans, which set out how companies test “safety-sensitive” staff such as helicopter pilots. He confirmed that operators like Sea World Helicopters could require daily alcohol breath tests before flights under their own policies and arrangements. The Sea World helicopters in the aftermath of the crash. AAP But civil aviation safety regulations did not specify how often pilots must be tested for illicit drugs, beyond trigger points such as CASA random tests, new hires, serious incidents and suspected impairment, Bunte said. “There is no prescribed frequency for routine drug testing in the regulations,” Bunte told coroner Carol Lee.



“The legislation identifies when testing must occur but not how often an operator has to run those checks.” He told the court CASA expected operators to ensure “all individuals conducting safety-sensitive activities are managed appropriately” under their drug and alcohol plans. Emergency workers at the scene of the helicopter collision near Sea World. AAP The inquest has heard that Sea World Helicopters’ written drug and alcohol plan, and its later revisions, were intended to comply with the regulations and could be audited by CASA. Witnesses earlier told the inquest they saw Jenkinson take cocaine at a New Year’s Eve party before the collision.



Jenkinson was flying an EC130 helicopter with six passengers when it collided midair with another Sea World aircraft near the theme park and plunged about 40 metres onto a sandbar. He was killed along with British newlyweds Ronald and Diane Hughes, aged 65 and 67, and Sydney mother Vanessa Tadros, 36. The second helicopter, flown by pilot Michael James, made an emergency landing on the same sandbar. Nine people in total were injured, including Tadros’s son Nicholas, who spent months in hospital and lost his leg. The inquest is examining pilot impairment, cockpit visibility, Sea World Helicopters’ safety systems and CASA’s oversight of drug and alcohol use in the industry. AAP

World.title: From code red to unstoppable: How your AFL team is placed in the chase for the top 10
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 From code red to unstoppable: How your AFL team is placed in the chase for the top 10 Jon Pierik July 20, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With five rounds remaining in the 2026 AFL home-and-away season, the sprint to September is officially on. Fremantle appear a lock for top spot, but from there it’s anyone’s guess. Josh Treacy fired for the Dockers against Port Adelaide. AFL Photos Sydney’s hold on second place is under siege from Hawthorn, Collingwood are pressing, while five would-be wildcard aspirants have taken a hit – although all remain in the race. The introduction of the wildcard round – extending the number of clubs who can make finals from eight to 10 – has ensured more teams remain in the race at this point of the campaign. We take a look at what awaits for your team.



What we say: The locked-and-loaded Dockers are an unstoppable force, the Power the latest to falter. They now sit three games clear on top of the ladder, and are all but certain to remain there despite what, on paper at least, is a challenging run home. The Eagles have improved, while the Bulldogs, Melbourne and Crows are flag contenders. Best-case finish: First. Worst-case finish: First.



What we say: We asked last week if the Swans’ indifferent form was something to ponder. The answer to that is yes. There was the loss to the Brisbane Lions, the fade-out against Fremantle, and now their first home defeat of the season, against Adelaide. That’s three defeats to premiership contenders. Isaac Heeney has slipped from being the No.1-ranked player in the league to 66th since round 14. The Giants await this week. Are the Swans tumbling from a top-two position? We’ll see. Best-case finish: Second. Worst-case finish: Fifth. Connor Macdonald and Nick Watson celebrate the Hawks’ big win over Richmond. AFL Photos What we say: Completed another clinical win, this time over Richmond, and are pressing for second spot on the ladder with the Swans faltering. Nick Watson continues to deliver wizardry acts, but co-captain James Sicily needs to harness his emotions, for he would not want to blow a fuse when a key game is on the line. The Hawks surely account for Essendon this week (please, no references to 1983-85), but the Brisbane Lions and Collingwood await.



Best-case finish: Second. Worst-case finish: Fourth. What we say: The Lions have won six straight, and there is no reason not to think this run won’t continue for at least another fortnight. Coach Chris Fagan has made no secret of his team’s aim. “Everyone knows the ladder and percentage and all that sort of stuff, so why shy away from it,” he said. “We’ve definitely used that as motivation over the last two or three weeks. It’s so tight. We’ve got to stay in the hunt, and we want to get that top four spot.” The chance to play at least two finals at home will have the Lions primed for a premiership three-peat. Best-case finish: Second. Worst-case finish: Eighth.



What we say: Last week we said the Crows were humming. Make that roaring after their sterling win in Sydney on Friday night, inflicting the Swans’ first loss at home this season. They have six wins from their past seven games, with Richmond and Essendon among their run home. Best-case finish: Second. Worst-case finish: Sixth. Kysaiah and Latrelle Pickett bask in victory after the Demons rolled over the Kangaroos. Getty Images What we say: Coach Steven King says the Demons are far from the finished product, a statement which should worry opponents after they have won five of their past six games. We said their best-case finish was third – that’s been re-rated to second. They will embrace the Friday night lights against a banged-up Geelong this week, and appear well-placed to even claim a top-four berth amid a potentially challenging run home.



Best-case finish: Second. Worst-case finish: Sixth. What we say: Last week we asked whether the Bulldogs were for real? We still can’t answer that question. Yes, it was an impressive victory against Gold Coast, but recent defeats to Adelaide and Sydney, and a less-than-convincing win over the Eagles, continue to gnaw away. Will take care of the Tigers this week, but the Dockers – and a serious litmus test – awaits. Best-case finish: Fourth. Worst-case finish: 11th.



What we say: That’s five straight wins for the Magpies, who are firmly in the hunt for a top-six finish. Is there a better team in the competition at filling selection holes and maximising their on-field performance? Now comes a season-defining month, for heavyweights Adelaide, Geelong, Hawthorn and the Brisbane Lions are on the agenda (and West Coast in Perth). Probably need to win at least three to avoid the wildcard round. On the march: The Magpies have momentum, and can sniff a top six finish. Getty Images Best-case finish: Fourth. Worst-case finish: 14th. What we say: As we said last week, the Cats have arguably the easiest run home, although their growing injury list, particularly to prime movers Jeremy Cameron and Max Holmes, may negate this. It’s a toss-of-the-coin job against Melbourne and Collingwood over the next fortnight (both games at the MCG), before expected wins over the final three rounds. Is the wildcard round the Cats’ best hope?



Best-case finish: Seventh. Worst-case finish: Ninth. Connor O’Sullivan of the Cats is tackled by Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera of the Saints. AFL Photos What we say: The Saints have arguably been the biggest disappointment of the season. A weakened Geelong was there for the taking on Thursday night, and what did the Saints do? They barely got moving for most of the night. They are no lock to knock over North Melbourne this week, then comes Sydney. They are suddenly in a major fight just to make the wildcard round. What has their off-season recruiting splurge really achieved? Not much to date. Best-case finish: 10th. Worst-case finish: 14th.



What we say: This was the shocker of the weekend, and sums up where the Giants really are. Internally, they had been frustrated by their lacklustre efforts against weaker sides, and that was reinforced against the Bombers. Terrible. Now they’ll be without injured skipper Toby Greene. We had the Giants finishing as high as seventh. That’s been downgraded to 10th. Ouch. Best-case finish: 10th. Worst-case finish: 14th. What we say: Has the bubble burst at Ikon Park? The seven straight wins under caretaker coach Josh Fraser are slowly receding into memory, for two defeats to serious September aspirants have shown where the Blues are really at. Still, they remain in wildcard contention. A win over the Suns at Marvel Stadium this weekend is a must.



Best-case finish: Seventh. Worst-case finish: 14th. Max Gawn of the Demons and Tristan Xerri of the Kangaroos contest the ruck. Getty Images What we say: It’s code red at Arden St. The Kangaroos had club royalty in the stands on Saturday, but blew a promising start against the Demons. That’s three straight defeats, their bid for a wildcard round in peril. Their best-case finish has been re-rated from eighth to 10th, for they have a potentially bruising run home. They need to get the job done against St Kilda this weekend otherwise their campaign is dead. Best-case finish: 10th. Worst-case finish: 14th.



What we say: We called the Suns a train wreck last week. Now we are not even sure they even were on the final line, such is the bewilderment over eight straight defeats. Yes, eight straight, from a team that should be contending for a flag. The Blues, at Marvel awaits, but we’ll be tipping Fraser’s men to rebound. The Suns face a painstaking post-season review. Ouch. Best-case finish: 10th. Worst-case finish: 15th. What we say: As we said last week, the Power are a mathematical chance to make the top 10, but there is little hope they will make it. They fought well against the Dockers, but their run home is arduous, the Lions up next.



Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 ‘A bloody good feeling’: Essendon bask in the glow of landing a win, climbing off the bottom Best-case finish: 14th. Worst-case finish: 15th. Not in the running West Coast (4-14) The Eagles did well to push the Lions in Perth, and have taken some important strides this season. They would love nothing better than knocking over the Dockers this weekend in the derby, but their best chance of another win in the remaining weeks of the season is against the Tigers.

World.title: Rodri touched the heavens, descended into hell, then won the Golden Ball
World.content:
Analysis SportSoccerFIFA World Cup Rodri touched the heavens, descended into hell, then won the Golden Ball Emma Kemp July 20, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a well-worn cliché about the merits of patience. Something about it being a highly regarded moral trait. One that helps a person tolerate frustrating delays and maintain focus on the long-term goal. Resilience and endurance win the day, and Rodri wins the Golden Ball. Just ask the oracle, Pep Guardiola, who held his Manchester City player back from returning too soon after rupturing his right anterior cruciate ligament. Loading “I said to him – and he maybe struggled to understand – it’s not about six, seven, eight months out, then playing and being the Rodri of before,” Guardiola said last October, with the wisdom of having observed the midfielder return for June’s Club World Cup just eight months after the initial injury, only to re-aggravate it. “No. Do you know when Rodri will be good? At the World Cup with Spain. At the World Cup, he will be the best Rodri.”



Even when Rodri finally returned properly in January, and City were visibly the better for his presence, there was a sense that the 2024 Ballon d’Or winner had not yet matched his previous heights. Plenty wondered if he ever would rediscover the form that helped Spain win the 2024 European Championship (and him win player of the tournament) and City to a record 74-match unbeaten streak with him in the side. After Spain’s opening match at the World Cup – that shock group-stage draw with Cape Verde – the criticism was loud enough for manager Luis de la Fuente to publicly defend his player. Rodri kisses his Golden Ball trophy. Getty Images “It seems incredibly insulting to me that people would say that about the best player in the world,” de la Fuente said last after last month’s scoreless result. “… Rodri is the best player in the world. Even at 50 per cent, he is better than most other midfielders in the world. He brings clarity, vision, balance. Rodri is an inspiration for us.” Then the rest of Spain’s tournament happened. They conceded a single goal en route to winning the trophy, and goalkeeper Unai Simon made a total 14 saves across their eight games – Argentina’s Emi Martinez made 11 in the final alone – demonstrating just how well he has been shielded.



Spain’s defensive line has been miserly, but Rodri has been the midfield anchor, cutting off supply to opponents’ attacks and playing almost every minute. The campaign was collective, but this 30-year-old was the commander. The reference point. And yet, the announcement of Rodri as player of the 2026 World Cup was met with as much disdain as it was nods of agreement. Lionel Messi was robbed, they said. Messi was named player of the match five times; Rodri once. Messi had eight goals and four assists; Rodri had none of either. Many believe Messi should have won the Golden Ball. SBS The MetLife Stadium crowd chanted Messi’s name as Rodri collected his Golden Ball trophy, as if the voting had somehow been rigged. Others mentioned Kylian Mbappe, Erling Haaland and Jude Bellingham as more worthy candidates. In reality, the identity of the official recipient said more about how much the world values individualism over teamwork. It also revealed how sometimes the most meaningful contributions can be the quietest.



The defensive midfield role is on the less sexy end of the spectrum, and the hallmark of those who thrive in it is that they often go unnoticed. They operate in service of structure and passes that allow others to steal the limelight. It isn’t glitzy, but it is as necessary as a goalscorer in a team in pursuit of greatness. Rodri completed a tournament-high 747 passes at a 93 per cent accuracy rate. In the final, he rendered Messi invisible. The all-time GOAT recorded one touch in the opening 15 minutes, and that was the kick-off. Argentina became the first World Cup finalists to fail to register a single shot in the regulation 90 minutes. By the end of extra time they had two, neither on target. Related Article Analysis

FIFA World Cup Spanish domination shows the limitations of ‘suffering’ in football And yes, Messi’s tournament has been a smorgasbord of logic-defying moments of which a 39-year-old should not be capable. And so it stands to reason that such a talent could also be squeezed out by one performing more efficiently. Rodri, back at his best. Joining Franz Beckenbauer, Gerd Muller and Zinedine Zidane as the only men to win the World Cup and European Championships with their country, the European Cup/Champions League with club, and the Ballon d’Or.



“It feels like the perfect script. I certainly didn’t expect this,” Rodri said upon receiving the Golden Ball trophy. “I’d love for the younger generations to see that a player who touches the heavens, then descends into hell, can come back. It’s a lesson in overcoming adversity.” Patience is a virtue, and good things come to those who wait.

World.title: ‘We got good ... we never got near perfect’: Schmidt’s verdict on Wallabies tenure
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies ‘We got good ... we never got near perfect’: Schmidt’s verdict on Wallabies tenure Jonathan Drennan July 20, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The signs that it was Joe Schmidt’s last day at Rugby Australia were obvious on Monday. The outgoing head coach had swapped his regulation Wallabies polo for an open-necked light blue one. He had also pulled an all-nighter – not to review game tape, but to watch compatriot Ryan Fox, the son of All Blacks great Grant Fox, win golf’s British Open. Outgoing Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt thanks his captain, Harry Wilson, after Saturday’s victory over Italy in his final Test. Getty Images Schmidt’s 31st and final Wallabies Test ended with a 47-point win over Italy in Perth on Saturday. His successor, Les Kiss, will name his first squad on Thursday. The handover is all but done and while there is a good deal of pride in the Wallabies team he passes on to Kiss, Schmidt is not without regrets about his tenure. “There will always be regrets and there’s always going to be frustrations, because I think anyone involved in that level of performance is trying to aim at perfection [while] knowing that it’s unattainable,” Schmidt said.



“So I think we got good, we certainly never got near perfect. But we’re in a better place, in my humble opinion, than we were when I arrived. “On the dark days, in the last two games of the year [against Italy and France in November], when the boys were only just hanging in there, we were all really tired. I spent four days in bed at the end of that tour, because I think I’d run myself down so much I got a serious dose of man flu. Angus Bell and Joe Schmidt leave the field in Perth. Getty Images “Despite being resilient, that sort of ended me for a while. But I have no regrets about my commitment. I have regrets that we didn’t quite finish a few chances. And convert those and get the result that I felt the players had earned.” Details of those 31 Tests – tries, tackles, penalties conceded – remain fresh in Schmidt’s mind. The drought-breaking Ellis Park victory over South Africa and the third Test win against the British and Irish Lions were savoured, but the Lions series loss and the close defeat to New Zealand at Eden Park still sting.



Still, the coach remains proud of his achievements in rebuilding the side from the rubble of the calamitous 2023 World Cup under Eddie Jones. “I probably would [rate this job as his most challenging], just because it was the first time I came in, I knew no one,” he said. “There were two other members of staff, so we had no coaches. We had no real support staff, because it was a total clean-out after the World Cup. Schmidt is confident incoming coach Les Kiss will inherit a happier and more confident Wallabies squad. Getty “And a lot of the players, even post-World Cup, either weren’t available or there had been some guys who’d been left out and were teetering on the edge of heading overseas. So it was about convincing them that we could still get together and be competitive. “It was challenging, but I’ve learnt a heck of a lot in this window, and I’ve loved the challenge. I’ve loved the results sometimes, [but] in fact, I’ve also been depressed about the results in some of those games.”





“I think rugby league is always going to be a contest, particularly around the loose forward, midfield, wing positions,” Schmidt. “I used to look from the outside and think: why don’t Rugby Australia just grab all those really good kids out of school and give them academy scholarships? “But academy scholarships, compared to what some of the competitors can offer, it’s very tough going.” Schmidt hugs Max Jorgensen after the Italy Test. Getty Images The victory in Perth was followed by emotional scenes in which the Wallabies queued up to hug the departing coach with whom they had formed such a close bond. What was Schmidt’s final message to the players he will now watch from afar? “They take the mickey out of me sometimes with some of the phrases I use, but one of the ones they probably haven’t taken the mickey out of is that belief is the base and trust is the glue. I really believe that,” Schmidt said.



“When we build our self-belief and we genuinely know we’re good enough, then we can trust ourselves and each other, and that trust is the glue. That is the connective tissue. “So I’ll probably try to leave them with a message that: trust yourself, trust each other and build that belief in among some skill sets and some strategy around the game.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘One in 15 million’: Mum gives birth to identical quadruplets in likely Australian first
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPregnancy ‘One in 15 million’: Mum gives birth to identical quadruplets in likely Australian first Courtney Kruk July 20, 2026 — 3:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Brisbane woman has given birth to identical quadruplets – an extremely rare “one in 15 million” event – with doctors saying the pregnancy could be an Australian first. Jenitar Sau Na’amoana, 34, was raising four young children and had not planned another child with her husband Jortham when she naturally fell pregnant with the quadruplets. Dr Alexa Bendall, a fetal medicine specialist and obstetrician at Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, cared for Sau Na’amoana throughout the pregnancy. The healthy identical quadruplets were born at 28 weeks and four days. She said the now mum-of-eight handled the news well, taking “everything in her stride from day one”.



This included acknowledging the high-risk nature of a quadruplet pregnancy. “Whenever you have a multiple pregnancy – which is usually twins, not quads – where the babies are sharing a placenta, there’s a very high risk of complications,” Bendall said. The four girls – Emily, Harriet, Alexa and Catherine – were delivered via caesarean section. “Babies can be growth-restricted … there can be a high risk of mortality and morbidity for these babies and for mum. “So the fact that we’ve got four beautiful, healthy babies born at 28 weeks and four days is incredible, and we’re very happy to be apart of it.”



Monozygotic quadruplets – identical quadruplets split from one singular fertilised egg – are one of the rarest types of pregnancies in the world. Related Series

Fertility Australia’s baby bust Adding to Sau Na’amoana’s extraordinary odds was the fact that her quadruplets shared the same placenta. “This is unheard of,” Bendall said. “So four sacs, one placenta – we think the figures are about one in every 15 million for a case like this, to be spontaneously conceived. We don’t think it’s ever happened in Australia.



“There may have been a couple of cases elsewhere in the world, and when I say a couple, literally a couple; two. But this is the only case we know about in Australia.” Sau Na’amoana has been cared for by a team of experts at the RBWH since 10 weeks, and was admitted as an inpatient at 25 weeks for close monitoring. The family named one of the girls after RBWH Maternal Fetal Medicine Specialist and Obstetrician Dr Alexa Bendall. The four girls – Emily, Harriet, Alexa and Catherine – were delivered by caesarean section on July 14. Alexa is named after Bendall. “I’m incredibly honoured that they decided to name one of their girls after me,” she said.



The four babies are currently doing “extremely well” and will remain in the hospital’s specialist Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) to grow to full term. “We always said that is we could get her to 28 weeks, we would be doing well, so we are happy she could make it to this gestation,” Bendall said. World.title: Blues seek clarity from prominent commentator over McKay injury; Magpies and premiership forward preparing to split
World.content:
AFL Briefing SportAFLAFL 2026 Blues seek clarity from prominent commentator over McKay injury; Magpies and premiership forward preparing to split Jon Pierik Updated July 20, 2026 — 3:09pm ,first published 12:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In today’s AFL briefing: Carlton have sought clarity from prominent commentator David King after he questioned Harry McKay’s pain threshold on Saturday night.

The Magpies and premiership forward Bobby Hill are set to part ways.

Essendon star Nate Caddy has been discharged from hospital and is expected to play this week. Carlton have sought clarity from prominent commentator David King after he questioned Harry McKay’s pain threshold when the star forward went off injured in Saturday’s loss to Collingwood at the MCG. King, a dual North Melbourne premiership player and Fox Footy analyst, said on his breakfast radio show on SEN on Monday that the Blues had called him on Sunday to discuss his comments. “I took the call from Carlton [on Sunday] … and had a lot of [public] feedback about it [his commentary]. Look, my thoughts are my thoughts. I am not necessarily going to back over it too much,” King said. Out of the game: Carlton lost Harry McKay to a knee injury in the opening term against Collingwood on Saturday. AFL Photos



“I think we have spoken about players that go off a little bit easy in the past. I am not saying that’s Harry on this occasion. Clearly, he has got an issue, and they are telling me he will miss two weeks. I was basically referring to an old Denis Paganism which you will know if you listened to what I said earlier.” Asked to elaborate, King said: “All good. They [Blues] disagree with what the discussion was about, which is fine. That’s footy. I am happy to move on from that.” A Blues spokesman confirmed the Blues had spoken with King, but the club did not want to elaborate. On Sunday Carlton said McKay would be tested this week and might play against Gold Coast at Marvel Stadium next Saturday. King was contacted for comment by this masthead.





When it became clear McKay would take no further part in the game, King said: “Looks like he’s put a line through himself, putting the jacket on, that’s it, night over. Incredible disappointment. You wonder whether there’s any structural issue there or is it just a pain tolerance discussion?” In the box: Fox Footy commentator David King. Getty Images “This Harry McKay discussion will rage. There’s nothing worse than when a player of that significance is not there. It changes the whole game.” In reference to his former coaches, including premiership great Denis Pagan, King said: “My old coaches would say: ‘I hope that’s a two or three-week [injury]. If that’s a 15-20 minute [injury], you lose a lot of respect’.” Carlton said on the night that McKay had been ruled out by club doctors.



King added at half-time: “If that’s just a bit of pain management then you’ve got a lot more to answer for. I hope that’s not the case with Harry and time will tell.” Related Article AFL 2026 ‘We’ll be hard to play against’: How first Devils coach Ken Hinkley won the job McKay, the 2021 Coleman medallist, has battled mental health problems through his career. In the AFL Players Association’s annual insights and impact report released last week, 34 per cent of players said they felt a level of disrespect by broadcast media. This included concerns about a focus on negativity and hyperbole. After seven-straight wins under caretaker coach Josh Fraser, the Blues have lost their past two games, against Hawthorn and Collingwood, but remain in contention for a wildcard berth. They host the Gold Coast at Marvel Stadium on Saturday.



Magpies and star premiership forward preparing to split Jon Pierik Collingwood are working towards parting ways with premiership star Bobby Hill. The 2023 Norm Smith medallist is contracted until the end of 2030 on a deal reportedly worth about $750,000 a season.



Industry sources have confirmed conversations between the Magpies and Hill’s management at Mac’s Sports Promotions are ongoing. The Magpies and Mac’s Sports Management were contacted for comment. Uncertain future: Bobby Hill and Collingwood are working towards a split. Getty Images Hill has not played a senior game since round 21 last year, largely because of personal issues. He had an extended break over summer but was welcomed back into the fold earlier this season. He had been training at suburban grounds with a trainer before returning to the club. The dynamic small forward has played three VFL games, but has not been a consistent presence at the club.



Coach Craig McRae has repeatedly said he was excited about Hill’s potential return, but there was always the caveat of the unknown. McRae said in June that Hill was still working through his personal issues. “Truthfully, battling,” McRae replied when asked about Hill. Loading “He has a bit going on, let’s be really clear. He has a lot going on. He’s a work in progress, but it’s nice to have him in the building.



“He’s a long way away from playing footy ... but again, when he’s in our building, at least we get some opportunities to make him feel that he’s loved and appreciated.” Hill and his partner Georgia Devlin welcomed their third child in May. Seven reported on Monday that Hill was keen for a move to the Brisbane Lions, Gold Coast or Port Adelaide. Hill was originally drafted by Greater Western Sydney with pick No.24 in 2018. He has played 102 senior games across eight seasons.



Bombers confident Caddy will face Hawks Jon Pierik Essendon are confident Nate Caddy will be available for selection this week after he was hospitalised with an irregular heart rate during Sunday’s three-point win over Greater Western Sydney. Ready to go: Essendon star Nate Caddy is expected to be available to face the Hawks on Saturday. AFL Photos via Getty Images



Caddy was taken to hospital for assessment, having collapsed to the turf when he got to the interchange bench in the first quarter. He had further tests but was given the all clear and discharged on Sunday night. Essendon’s general manager of football Daniel McPherson said he expected Caddy to train this week ahead of a clash against arch-rival Hawthorn on Saturday. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 ‘A bloody good feeling’: Essendon bask in the glow of landing a win, climbing off the bottom “There was some concern in the first quarter when Nate’s heart rate became elevated,” McPherson said on Monday. “He was removed from the game, and our medical team assessed him at the ground before sending him to hospital for further assessment. He was discharged last night and is back at home.



“He is expected to be able to train and play without concern this week.” Caddy recently signed a contract extension until the end of 2031 in a huge boost for the battling Bombers, who no longer sit in last spot on the ladder. Wingman Xavier Duursma (hamstring) faces a spell on the sidelines. The Bombers were able to sing the club song for only the second time in 31 games after edging the shocked Giants. It was their first win since beating Melbourne in Gather Round in Adelaide on April 11, while they had not tasted victory in Victoria since May last year. It was Dean Solomon’s first win as caretaker coach since replacing Brad Scott in May.



While only 14,601 fans attended the game, the scenes of joy for the Bombers were palpable. “It’s a bloody good feeling. Our footy club’s been on its knees for a period of time, and the footy world’s jumped on that, and they enjoy us sitting at the bottom,” Solomon said. “We’ve felt that, and we don’t like that, so to push back a little bit and get one win, albeit one win, I’m just really happy for these players.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: As Kiss’s first Wallabies signing is revealed, a boom rookie is next on the radar
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies As Kiss’s first Wallabies signing is revealed, a boom rookie is next on the radar Nick Wright Updated July 20, 2026 — 3:06pm ,first published 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Reds boss Sam Cordingley has declared Australian rugby was well positioned to retain boom teenager Treyvon Pritchard, despite the wounded phenom courting interest from rival codes. Speaking from the club’s headquarters at Ballymore to announce the signing of Wallabies centre Izaia Perese, Cordingley was quietly confident Pritchard would not be swayed by an NRL defection, having held talks with the incoming Papua New Guinea Chiefs for their 2028 launch. The 19-year-old would have been a chance of earning a Wallabies or Australia A call-up as former Reds coach Les Kiss takes the national reins this week, having shown impressive signs in his maiden Super Rugby Pacific campaign. Treyvon Pritchard World Rugby His highlights reel included his dazzling footwork to bamboozle Chiefs and All Blacks superstar Damian McKenzie, while he had dominated the World Rugby Under-20s Championships in Georgia before suffering a broken leg and syndesmosis injury after being subjected to a ‘hip-drop’ tackle.



Cordingley – the Reds’ general manager of high performance – confirmed Pritchard would undergo surgery on Monday, and stressed there was no rush on his return to play. “I think he’s had a really good progression, he’s played a lot of Super Rugby this year and the 20s was an important rite of passage for him, and he was pretty keen to be a part of that,” Cordingley said. “I’m sure he would’ve been part of discussions. I daresay once he’s back on deck, those discussions will happen pretty quickly around where he sits in the Wallabies framework.” Treyvon Pritchard suffered serious injuries in this hip drop tackle against Wales at the Junior World Championship. Stan Sport Cordingley said Pritchard’s setback would not have any influence on the Reds’ desire to extend his contract beyond the end of his 2027 deal, while suggesting the club may be forced to contend with global interest after his Junior Wallabies exploits.



While the interest from the Chiefs, equipped with tax-free salary incentives, looms as an enticing carrot for the youngster who grew up in rugby league, Cordingley believed Rugby Australia held the upper hand. “He’s an elite talent, so I’m not surprised with the interest. He’s played over in the Junior World Cup against countries like France, and we know they have very strong recruitment processes as well – clubs certainly would have been watching his games over there,” Cordingley said. Loading “In terms of the injury, I don’t see it as detracting from our capacity to retain him, I think where that sits, it’s pretty well-placed for rugby to retain Trey. “I’m confident we’re going to put our best foot forward to retain him.”



Related Article Wallabies Australia’s top rugby schools revealed – including one ‘beast’ in Brisbane Cordingley’s revelations came as Perese became the first Rugby Australia signing of Kiss’ Wallabies tenure, with the powerful centre returning to his debut club after a two-year stint in England with Leicester. The six-time Test centre will rejoin the Reds through to the end of 2028, and will seek to fill the void left by departing No.13 Josh Flook (Benetton). Fellow Wallabies Hunter Paisami and Jock Campbell have also been heavily linked to Japanese rugby defections. “Decisions around Hunter and Jock, they’re sort of future [decisions], the focus of today is to really celebrate Izzy’s signing,” Cordingley said.



“He’s a great signing for the club, obviously we’ve lost Josh Flook to Benetton – hopefully that’s in the short-term, and hopefully, we can plan around the future and get Flooky back – but we’re trading a Wallaby for a Wallaby.” Perese confirmed the allure of the home World Cup in 2027 drew him and his family – including four young children – back to Australian shores, admitting he felt he would finish his career abroad. The 29-year-old, who briefly switched to rugby league and managed two games for the Brisbane Broncos, laughed when asked if the Chiefs ever appealed to him as an option, before expressing he was never going to be swayed from the 15-man code. Izaia Perese has returned to the Queensland Reds. Getty Images “There was no temptation there, I don’t know too much about that, but I wouldn’t have my family locked in a compound for nine months – it’d drive my missus and kids crazy,” Perese quipped.



“The World Cup’s always in the back of my mind, but the main reason to sign was I wanted to come back to the Reds for my family, wife and kids … but to also propel myself into Wallabies contention. “The longer season [in England], you definitely tend to learn more about yourself with the highs and lows, good times and bad. It’s time to come back and apply diligently.” Perese threw his hand up to come back into the Wallabies fold ahead of Kiss’s first Test in charge against Japan on August 8, provided he got himself back to peak fitness and overcame a minor knee issue. World.title: Investors bark. Coles backpedals on ‘peak pooch’ price for pet business
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMergers & acquisitions Opinion Investors bark. Coles backpedals on ‘peak pooch’ price for pet business Elizabeth Knight Business columnist July 20, 2026 — 3:00pm

July 20, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was roughly 20 years ago when supermarket bosses had their pet epiphany. The beginning of the trend towards pet (mainly dog) anthropomorphism that, perversely, had supermarket chief executives drooling over a retailing category with a hockey-stick-shaped growth potential. Forget the days when the pet isle in stores consisted of cans of Pal, rather supermarkets were ushering in an era in which shelves were stocked with expensive designer pooch treats, doggy apparel, vitamins and more. Coles’ boss Leah Weckert decided to abandon late-stage negotiations to spend nearly $4 billion to buy Greencross. Arsineh Houspian Against this backdrop it might appear counterintuitive that Coles’ boss Leah Weckert decided to abandon late-stage negotiations to spend nearly $4 billion to buy Greencross – the owner of Petbarn and City Farmer retail chains, hundreds of vet clinics and 24 vet hospitals. But there are plenty of reasons that Coles’ investors were lukewarm to the prospect of Coles making a major investment into Greencross – not the least of which was the price.



The widely speculated price of $3.9 million is a big lick of capital – an amount that could represent “peak pooch”. Related Article Updated

Private equity Private equity boss keeps his job despite guilty plea as $4 billion deal looms Coles called its decision disciplined – albeit the decision was reached after some shareholder pressure to reserve its capital. Four years ago, Woolworths spent $586 million for a foothold in Petstock – a provider of petfood, toys, vet clinics, grooming salons and even animal adoption hubs. The Woolworths deal valued Petstock at (what at the time seemed to be) a staggering $1 billion. To provide some context, the Petstock deal was done in the same week that private equity operator Anchorage Capital bought 100 per cent of high-end department store group David Jones for a mere $130 million. In the intervening years David Jones has financially struggled and Petstock has grown, so the valuation disparity now makes sense.



Woolworths’ then chief executive Brad Banducci was all smiles when posing for celebratory photos with his beloved Cavalier Cocker Spaniel cross, Juno. Meanwhile, Greencross inks $2 billion in annual revenue and it’s reported to be making $400 million profit before interest, tax and depreciation. It is difficult to deny that the growth in the provision of pet goods and services is a trend that retains some steam. Its current owner TPG Capital paid $675 million for the business seven years ago, so had the Coles deal been consummated, it would have been a massive payday for this private equity vendor, which is now contemplating a public float of the business. It is difficult to deny that the growth in the provision of pet goods and services is a trend that retains some steam, but there is a strong argument to be made for the supermarket industry spending its capital and management resources focusing on the current and not insignificant challenges it faces.



The sector will remain capital thirsty as the major players continue to integrate technology into supply chain and logistics to better manage digital distribution channels that are increasingly adopted by customers. They are up against the masters of online logistics and fulfillment, Amazon, whose infiltration into grocery retailing continues to grow. Brad Banducci with his dog Juno. Louise Kennerley The big supermarket operators are currently also in a highly contested fight for market share – and one that has come with an expensive investment into lowering prices. And despite Woolworths’ successful foray into the pet business, the two large supermarket groups have a checkered history of success when they have strayed outside their core competence.



Woolworths exited the last of its bottle shop and pubs investments in 2024, its ownership of Big W has been largely patchy, and its foray 10 years ago into establishing a hardware big box chain, Masters, was a legendary and very costly disaster. And then there is the legion of yield obsessed investors who would rather see profits pumped into dividends ahead of dogs. World.title: Safety authority grilled over pilot drug-testing gaps
World.content:
NationalQueenslandInquest Safety authority grilled over pilot drug-testing gaps Robyn Wuth July 20, 2026 — 2:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pilots on Sea World joy flights were breath-tested for alcohol before every shift but faced no mandated routine testing for illicit drugs ahead of a fatal crash, a coroner has heard. Four people – including pilot Ashley Jenkinson – were killed in a fatal midair collision between two Sea World helicopters outside the Gold Coast theme park on January 2, 2023. Ashley Jenkinson, the pilot who died in the Gold Coast helicopter crash. Facebook Earlier evidence revealed Jenkinson, 40, returned a post-mortem positive test for cocaine metabolites. Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) was quizzed about drug and alcohol rules for aviation operators at the ongoing inquest into the fatal crash in Brisbane on Monday.



CASA’s national manager for regulatory services Niels Bunte was asked how the rules were applied to Drug and Alcohol Management Plans, which set out how companies test “safety-sensitive” staff such as helicopter pilots. He confirmed that operators like Sea World Helicopters could require daily alcohol breath tests before flights under their own policies and arrangements. The Sea World helicopters in the aftermath of the crash. AAP But civil aviation safety regulations did not specify how often pilots must be tested for illicit drugs, beyond trigger points such as CASA random tests, new hires, serious incidents and suspected impairment, Bunte said. “There is no prescribed frequency for routine drug testing in the regulations,” Bunte told coroner Carol Lee.



“The legislation identifies when testing must occur but not how often an operator has to run those checks.” He told the court CASA expected operators to ensure “all individuals conducting safety-sensitive activities are managed appropriately” under their drug and alcohol plans. Emergency workers at the scene of the helicopter collision near Sea World. AAP The inquest has heard that Sea World Helicopters’ written drug and alcohol plan, and its later revisions, were intended to comply with the regulations and could be audited by CASA. Witnesses earlier told the inquest they saw Jenkinson take cocaine at a New Year’s Eve party before the collision.



Jenkinson was flying an EC130 helicopter with six passengers when it collided midair with another Sea World aircraft near the theme park and plunged about 40 metres onto a sandbar. He was killed along with British newlyweds Ronald and Diane Hughes, aged 65 and 67, and Sydney mother Vanessa Tadros, 36. The second helicopter, flown by pilot Michael James, made an emergency landing on the same sandbar. Nine people in total were injured, including Tadros’s son Nicholas, who spent months in hospital and lost his leg. The inquest is examining pilot impairment, cockpit visibility, Sea World Helicopters’ safety systems and CASA’s oversight of drug and alcohol use in the industry. AAP
