World.title: Auckland's biggest sewer pipe up and running
World.content:
Auckland's biggest sewer pipe officially in action Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

After seven years and $1.66 billion, Auckland's second most anticipated tunnel is up and running.

The Central Interceptor is an enormous sewer pipe running from Herne Bay, in central Auckland, down to the Mangere Wastewater Plant.

Watercare describes it as the backbone of Auckland's sewer system, but some of the ribs won't be built until well beyond 2030.

Deputy Mayor Desley Simpson said it would take some time for Aucklanders to enjoy the project's benefits.

"They won't see it straight away... It's a start though. It enables all these things to happen because it takes more pressure off the older infrastructure," she said.

In recent years, Aucklanders had become well acquainted with wastewater overflows.

Black flags on the council's Safeswim website warning beachgoers to stay out of the water had been a regular sight across the Waitematā Harbour.

Watercare chief executive Jamie Sinclair said the Central Interceptor was already making a difference.

"One of the great things about the Central Interceptor is it does take a lot of pressure off some of that older infrastructure, like the Orakei main sewer, which is very old, so we'll be able to do some rehabilitation of those interceptors."

But he warned that overflows wouldn't disappear overnight.

"The Central Interceptor does create more capacity into our overall network, so it'll help with that resilience," he said.

"It doesn't fix the problem. There will still be overflows, but this will dramatically improve our ability to reduce overflows over time."

Watercare chief executive Jamie Sinclair says the Central Interceptor is already making a difference. Supplied

Deputy Mayor Desley Simpson said it was the first bullet point on a long to-do list, now that Watercare was financially independent from Auckland Council.

"Projects like this make a huge difference for the future, but more important, they are the start. They are the enabler for even more investment for the future," she said.

"I think one of the great things about Watercare, now being able to stand on its own two feet, and borrow more money, you will see a faster growth programme."

One of the projects still clogging the pipeline was the Newmarket Gully, originally pencilled for 2016 but now marked for 2034.

Hobson Bay local Margot Nicholson had been waiting for that project.

She said Hobson Bay had endured a steady flow of sewage for years.

"Whenever there's enough rain for your hair to get wet, there's untreated sewage going in," she said.

"Watercare try to have spills happening no more than twice a year, [but] we've got quite a significant number of points that are high volume, high frequency, 50 times a year."

She said the central interceptor would help, but while she was holding her nose, she wasn't holding her breath.

"It reduces some of the load on the Orakei main, so that is a positive, but until the infrastructure projects are done in the local network... The central interceptor is the motorway, but the big roads coming into that, there's major problems with those," she said.

"The Central Interceptor won't fix that."

World.title: Dave Letele to 'step back' from NZ Muscle
World.content:
Dave Letele has announced he will 'step back' from NZ Muscle a week after he was appointed as the new chief executive of the supplement company.

"I came in with the best of intentions, to help a business front up and fix things properly. I've realised I can't help in the way it needs, and the right thing to do is be honest about that," he posted to his Brown Buttabean social media page.

NZ Muscle hit strife after a former employee posted a YouTube video making claims of questionable practices. The company recalled some creatine products that could contain undeclared dairy.

That prompted the Commerce Commission and Ministry of Primary Industries to investigate.

Letele had wanted to give it his "best shot of trying to turn it around" and protect the jobs of its 35 staff.

"The better I can turn it around, it's only going to help myself and my family," he said last Tuesday.

The former boxer turned social activist wished the NZ Muscle team well and said "there are good people there working hard to get it right".

"Back to the work I've always done. Thank you to everyone who backed me."'

Shortly after taking on the role, Letele said he faced criticism and death threats for taking the role.

Posting on his Brown Butterbean Facebook page, he said he had been receiving racist hate mail.

"People want answers which I fully understand. But I need time to find out what's actually happened. It's now hard to do this with so much noise and now I have to worry for my family's safety.

"I've entered this with my eyes wide open. I've taken on a company that has f**ked up and it's my job to come fix it and make it better than before.

World.title: Creative NZ to cut a third of workforce
World.content:
Creative New Zealand says it's cutting staff by about a third as it looks to implement a new operating model.

The arts funding agency has announced it will be reducing overall staff numbers from 84 to 55 roles.

It said 13 of those roles were currently vacant, meaning 16 people could lose their jobs.

Creative NZ is a Crown entity governed by the Arts Council, which "encourages, promotes and support New Zealand arts".

Its staff are spread across three cities: Wellington, Auckland and Dunedin.

Arts Council chair Kent Gardner said the change in headcount was "not a reaction to short-term pressures" - which include required savings of $1.3 million over four years in Budget 2026.

"Over the past two years, the Arts Council has deliberately reset Creative New Zealand for the future. We appointed a new Chief Executive, worked together to develop a new long-term strategy, and have now aligned the organisation's structure to deliver it," Gardner said.

Creative NZ chief executive Gretchen La Roche. Supplied

Creative NZ chief executive Gretchen La Roche said the arts and funding environment was dynamic, and continually evolving.

"This review and change has been about ensuring we're organised and resourced to deliver on our strategic priorities, and effectively support artists, communities and the wider arts sector into the future.

"Our focus is on supporting our people through the transition and ensuring our work with the artists, organisations and communities we serve is maintained, including retaining valuable experience, expertise and institutional knowledge," La Roche said.

However, Public Service Association national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons labelled the move "cultural vandalism".

"These are experienced, essential specialists in New Zealand art, literature, dance and visual arts," she said.

World.title: Bird flu: What is the threat to NZ's pet cats?
World.content:
A Wairarapa vet who has had an onslaught of calls from cat owners worried about their felines catching bird flu says it is rare when cats get the H5 strain of the virus, but there is a high mortality rate.

It was confirmed on Friday that a native kāhu - or swamp harrier hawk - in the region was the country's second confirmed case of the deadly H5 strain of the virus.

MPI has increased monitoring and says there is no evidence of mass mortality in wildlife, and there has been no detection in poultry.

Several countries that have had cases of the virus have also had domestic cat deaths due to the H5 strain.

Onslaught of cat owners worried about pets catching bird flu Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Wairarapa vet Dr Louisa Broughton told Checkpoint cat owners in her area had been "pretty worried, understandably" about the situation.

She said they were asking if their cats needed to be kept indoors, and what they need to do to lower the risks to their cats.

Dr Broughton said cats can catch bird flu, although cases were considered rare.

"Unfortunately, if they do get it, it can have a reasonably high mortality rate, so I understand peoples' concerns about it.

"So we've mostly been communicating that it's up to each individual cat owner as to how much prevention they want to do.

"Some people decide to make them indoor cats, or patio cats, that don't go outside. And a lot of it is about trying to reduce the amount of time they are near sick or dead birds."

She said the symptoms presented like many other respiratory symptoms, such as high fever, depression, lethargy and loss of appetite.

There was no vaccination to deal with infected cats, said Dr Broughton.

"Treatment is very much symptomatic, so they might need intravenous fluids or help eating, those sort of things."

But she said if a cat was showing those symptoms, it was "probably not going to be bird flu".

World.title: Greens promises to cut power bills and make solar more affordable with $980m 'KiwiPower' plan
World.content:
The Green Party has pledged to set up a publicly-owned entity to boost investment in renewable energy and ensure affordable power and energy security.

Co-leaders Chlöe Swarbrick and Marama Davidson unveiled the party's energy policy at the Dunedin Gasworks Museum on Monday, the site of the country's first and last place to manufacture coal gas.

They promised to make power bills more affordable by making it easier for renters and homeowners to generate their own power, and set up and fund the new entity called KiwiPower using $980 million from the party's "super-rich tax" over four years.

KiwiPower would start with $100m a year for operating costs and $142m a year for new investment.

The policy also includes zero-interest clean energy loans to install solar and batteries for up to 90 percent of homeowners, legalising plug-in solar and investing $80m into renewable energy for Māori housing.

It would also expand government grant programme Warmer Kiwi Homes to offer more upgrades to make more low-income homes warm, dry and energy efficient, costing $969.8m over four years for 50,000 upgrades.

The party promised for solar to be installed on more than half of all public homes within four years at a cost of $460m and to invest $200m for community energy projects, which the party said would be funded by reallocating subsidies for fossil fuel companies.

Swarbrick said the market and successive governments had failed to deliver affordable, secure, renewable power.

"200,000 households are unable to afford to heat their homes while four big power companies control over 85 percent of the market and rake in massive profits," she said.

"A warm, dry home powered by clean energy should be within everyone's reach. That is the country we can build, and this is how we do it."

The plan would lower bills, cut emissions and put power back in the hands of New Zealanders and could be funded by making corporations and the super rich "pay their fair share", Swarbrick said.

"KiwiPower will invest directly in new renewable generation and sort out our dry-year problem sensibly, without a billion-dollar LNG facility, and support new, independent players coming into the market."

Swarbrick said the Greens had chosen to launch the plan at the Dunedin Gasworks Museum because gas belonged in a museum rather than in modern policy.

She believed plug-in solar could make a difference for renters.

"We're looking at a saving of around $300 per year for an average household's energy consumption," she said.

She acknowledged that the industry currently did not have enough workers to meet the needs of the policy in the long run, and said The Greens would soon have an announcement about improving workforce investment and planning.

But she believed the policy was feasible and could help New Zealanders.

Marama Davidson, said there were Fast-track pathways to attract overseas workers while the local workforce grew.

"We're good to go and get it started in as little time as six months," she said.

"At the moment, we are putting up a good 10,000 installations a year already."

Davidson said the number of households who could not heat their homes had doubled in the last five years.

"We are held hostage to dirty fossil fuels and unaffordable power bills," she said.

"I don't want to forget what it was like for my tamariki before becoming an MP, trying to heat our draughty home in the middle of winter. My baby wearing a wollen beanie and socks to bed. Being able to see my breath in her cold room. Our doctor telling me my house was making my kids sick.

"The guilt because I chose to feed them rather than keep them warm."

That was about a decade ago, and she said the situation had gotten worse.

Davidson said the Greens' plan gave back ownership to communities and invested in Māori and public housing.

"Tangata whenua are two to three times more likely to face energy hardship," she said.

"This is about rangatiratanga over energy and it is part of our enduring commitment to Te Tiriti o Waitangi."

World.title: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon speaks on Resource Management Act reforms
World.content:
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says Resource Management Act reforms will make building infrastructure easier, faster and more affordable.

But opposition parties warn the changes could make the system more unworkable, and dilute environmental protections.

The select committee reports also pointed to an independent report finding the regulatory relief scheme it sets up could cots up to about $2b.

The reports detail 142 pages of changes to the government's proposed reforms to the Resource Management Act which includes a "regulatory relief" scheme that would see landowners compensated by councils for changes that affect them.

This included the removal of a clause requiring that use and development of the environment must be kept "within environmental limits".

Changes agreed by Cabinet would also mean existing agreements between councils and iwi - known as Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreements - would be scrapped and replaced with "new narrowly scoped iwi participation agreements".

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop pointed to independent analysis showing that by 2050, the changes were expected to increase GDP annually by 0.56 percent.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop. (File photo) RNZ / Calvin Samuel

"A cost benefit analysis estimates $13.3 billion in savings over 30 years through reduced administrative and compliance costs."

He said the removal of the existing iwi agreements had been because of the government's concern about the growing number of agreements, with the legislation previously allowing for existing agreements to continue but preventing new ones.

"Eight [agreements] existed when the Bills were introduced late last year. Since then, several dozen more have been agreed or initiated," he said.

"Instead, councils will have the option of entering into new narrowly scoped iwi participation agreements to record how iwi authorities will participate in statutory planning processes and processes required to give effect to Treaty settlement redress. Clear guardrails will be included in the legislation to prevent scope creep."

Changes to the purpose and goals of the legislation would "give stronger recognition to people's enjoyment of their land and the importance of food and fibre production", he said.

Labour in its minority report raised a number of concerns, saying the party supported the legislation - which somewhat resembled the bills it passed in the last Parliament - through its first reading in the hope that improvements could be made.

"Unfortunately, almost all policy decisions made during the select committee process have made the bills even more unpalatable and unworkable," the party said.

"The bills are an embarrassment-National could have worked with us to amend Labour's legislation but instead they chose to start again with something full of campaign slogans that will end up costing all New Zealanders and the environment."

The Greens raised similar concerns, particularly over what they said was the dismantling of environmental protections.

Regulatory relief

The regulatory relief scheme would see councils paying out to landowners where their property was

The reports show a ministry-commissioned report by consultancy Martin Jenkins puts the cost of that scheme at between $7 million and $1.99 billion - the huge range reflecting "that local authorities may take a range of approaches".

Labour said councils had told the committee the regulatory relief scheme would be expensive and they were "unlikely to be able to afford the cost of compensation, particularly in light of other government work that will further restrict councils' ability to raise funds," referring to the proposed rates cap of between 2-4 percent a year.

"Ratepayers would have to pay landowners for protecting something that is not their land - that is, biodiversity," Labour said.

The party said this was likely to result in a cottage industry of valuers

The Greens said they opposed the regulatory relief regime "in its entirety".

"We were deeply concerned that despite the only report the committee received on the matter outlining the novelty, uncertainty and potential for crippling costs to local councils and ratepayers of up to two billion dollars, that the committee proceeded to retain regulatory relief."

Green Party environment spokesperson Lan Pham singled out the regulatory relief framework as particularly irresponsible.

"This is not only going to cause a chilling effect in terms of councils simply not being able to meet these costs and therefore unable to protect things that matter to the community like biodiversity, but the costs could actually be much greater."

Green Party environment spokesperson Lan Pham. (File photo) RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Environmental protections

Labour's previous legislation aimed to set system-wide bottom limits for the degradation of the environment - for things like air pollution or water quality - based on scientific assessment.

The party said that although the legislation looked to retain that approach, the methods used would rely on national standards which "must not determine an ecosystem health limit itself".

"This does not make much sense and presumably comes from a desire to appease lobbyists who do not want nationally applied limits - yet they will likely get them through all the methodologies and minimum acceptable levels."

They also raised concern about the removal of the environmental limit clause.

"The Natural Environment Bill's goal of 'no net loss' of indigenous biodiversity is unworkable and lacks ambition. There is no definition of or baseline for measuring 'no net loss'," the party said of the replacement.

The Greens said this was dismantling the environmental protections under the current system.

They said the Minister now had discretion over whether developments needed to be within environmental limits or not, and another clause requiring caution when the science was uncertain had also been removed.

"The ecosystem health limits do not even have to be set at a level that would 'prevent significant or irreversible harm', in the way that human health limits must be," the party said.

The Greens also raised concern about timeframes for achieving interim limits had been shortened to five years, that Freshwater Farm plans were set to become self-certified, and mechanisms to address the overallocation of freshwater had been scrapped.

Pham said the changes to environmental limits were "beyond a joke".

"For the government to insist this is going to be an enduring framework, it's absolutely laughable," she said.

"They've not only removed the environmental limit thing, but they've also put in place essentially a shout-out to their favourite lobby groups - you know, big agriculture and aquaculture - and they've inserted them in the goals instead.

"This is an outrage and it certainly has no standing for a decent future for the country."

Conflicting goals and ministerial overrides

Labour and the Greens both pointed to the legislation being split into two bills, saying the overarching goals and purpose of them appeared to be at odds in some places.

Labour said there had been "no cogent explanation" for the separation.

"We suspect the reason is an attempt to end the 'integrated management' approach of the RMA. This is both dangerous and foolish. Our environment exists everywhere; including urban environments."

The party - which also had its reforms split into two - said its approach did not affect integrated management and had been split to ensure the spatial plans in their legislation could work with different infrastructure development approaches.

"These two replacement bills will result in a lot of duplication and cause unnecessary uncertainty and inefficiency."

Labour pointed to the "funnel" approach taken under the new version which would see lower-level planning overruled by higher-level planning, with national directions from the ministers able to override council plans, for example.

"When goals conflict with each other, the Minister will determine how the conflict is resolved - this is in effect the Minister establishing a hierarchy. This is a lot of power and leaves no wiggle room should a poor decision be made at the top of the funnel."

The Greens echoed the concerns of the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, saying the powers granted to ministers had the potential for "endless church following every change of government", and with Te Rūnanga o Toa Rangatira which said the new system would be top heavy and centralise decision making.

Iwi, Treaty changes

Labour said the bills' removal of a clause guaranteeing Māori culture and traditions within their ancestral lands, water, sites, wāhi tapu and other taonga was to be recognised and provided for would degrade Māori rights.

"There will be Treaty Settlement litigation around these changes that downgrade mana whenua participation because these settlements were reliant on the general settings of the RMA."

The party - whose response came before the government announced its plans to remove Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreements - noted feedback that those agreements "assist with the timeliness and efficiency of the resource management system, so it is not in anyone's interests to remove them".

The Greens' report said Treaty obligations and the rights and interests of Māori had been "weakened and narrowed", pointing to the Waikato River Authority's comments to the select committee that the bills would be "eviscerating" Crown-Māori relationships.

The party said a proposed two-year timeframe - during which the bills would be enacted and post-settlement iwi organisations would need to agree on how their Treaty redress could have "the same or equivalent" effect was "a retrograde insult to iwi and hapū.

Bishop said the bills had retained an approach to provide for Māori interests "through a system goal and iwi participation in national instruments and plan-making rather than relying on broad, open-ended Treaty provisions."

World.title: Non-executive director pay gap falls but remain at chair level
World.content:
A new report shows the non-executive director pay gap has fallen to just 0.5 percent, while the gap for board chairs is also significantly lower.

The survey by Strategic Pay showed female non-executive directors earned median fees of $55,433 dollars, $290 lower than their male counterparts.

The 0.5 percent gap was significantly lower than the near 6 percent gap last year.

The gender gap for non-executive chairs has reduced from 18 percent to 8 percent.

Female non-executive chairs earned median fees of $90,000, compared to $98,004 for males.

The annual survey analysed 382 organisations, covering 329 chairs and 1648 directors.

"While gaps still remain at chair level, the movement among non-executive directors represents a notable step toward greater fee equity," Strategic Pay managing director Cathy Hendry said.

Hendry said growth in public sector fees was probably the key driver, as public sector fees were stagnant for a long time.

She said the increases in the public sector were "overdue".

Strategic Pay's report said public sector director fees increased by around 9 percent over the past year, while private sector fees declined by almost 3 percent.

The report said it was particularly relevant as public sector boards historically had stronger female representation than private sector boards, meaning the previous fee disparity may have disproportionately affected female directors.

"Public sector organisations have generally experienced greater stability over recent years, while many private sector organisations have continued operating in a constrained economic environment," she said.

World.title: Tears and excitement as Spain win Football World Cup
World.content:
"Vamos" was heard from both of those cheering for Argentina and Spain.

But Spain came out on top, winning the Football World Cup final 1-0.

Inside central Auckland's Wynyard Pavilion, the whole crowd was singing, stamping.

Hundreds of people, dressed in red, knew their team were just minutes away from being world champions.

Finally, the ball found the back of the net, and the bar erupted. The loud cheering was accompanied by a person banging on a drum.

People hugged and kissed. A couple even threw their dog in the air. A man went outside to video call a family member, tears streaming down his face. The crowd of Spain supporters sang, danced, exalted.

They had watched for long, long minutes as their team had done everything bar beat Argentina.

Spain fans in Auckland CBD. RNZ / Jeremy Rees

Wearing the Iberian red of the Spanish strip, they had been exuberant, excited, then tense and silent as minutes ticked by.

"This is a team that can do everything except we don't have a Messi," said one red shirt at 80 minutes.

That was true. There were still three quarters of an hour of tension and worry to go as the game ticked down to injury time, then extra time.

It was heart stopping stuff. Endless Spanish attacks had the crowd on their feet. Then seconds later that exhalation, "Oooooh" as the shot was wide or blocked.

"España! España!", they chanted to will their team to victory.

But football is a terrible stark game. All that beauty and passing the ball through the eye of the needle means nothing when the score stands at 0-0.

And then, in minute 106, it came.

And the crowd erupted in relief, in joy, in fury, in pent up energy.

An Argentina fan reacts to Spain's game-winning goal. RNZ / Nick Monro

Up on the North Shore, there were also tears - but for a different reason at the Argentina watch party.

About 200 supporters crammed into a warehouse at Pachamama Latino Store in Glenfield to watch the game.

Proudly sporting blue and white and their Argentina kits, they cheered on their team all throughout the nail-biting game.

Fans earlier said they were confident Argentina had what it took to become back-to-back men's World Cup champions after winning the competition in 2022.

But it was not their day.

Football fans packed out Locker Room in Queenstown. RNZ / Katie Todd

Many in the crowd burst into tears at the result and embraced each other to cope with the loss of not only the title but Lionel Messi, who has indicated this would be his last World Cup match.

In Queenstown, the Locker Room sports bar erupted into scenes of equal elation and devastation as Spain locked in the win.

More than 280 fans from both sides had arrived as early as 6am, equipped with face paint and flags.

Spanish fans told RNZ they could not be more relieved or happy, while Argentinian fans said they felt their team had given it all.

Beeping and chants of "Yo soy español" could be heard all through the main streets.

'One of the happiest days of my life'

It was estimated that 1.8 billion people - or more than 20 percent of the world's population - watched the match, and Paloma Argüelles was one of those in Auckland.

"I don't have words. I don't have words, but I'm so happy. One of the happiest days of my life."

Paloma Argüelles. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Javier Yebenes, from Albacete in Spain, said the bar felt like home.

"It's a great opportunity for the Spanish community to get together, celebrate."

Yebenes was also grateful to be able to share a little bit of his culture with New Zealand after living in Auckland for 14 years.

Nacho Fernandez (left) and Javier Yebenes (right). RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

He told RNZ's Afternoons that he had since lost his voice.

"I've got a little bit of difficulty talking at the moment. It's been a lot of screaming, and then dancing, and hugging, and cheering.

"We watched it with a group of about 120 Spaniards in Auckland, in the Wynyard Pavilion, and the atmosphere was bustling."

Spain for the win! We celebrate with a fan Afternoons Download MP3 7m

Yebenes said it was nice to be able to spend time with other people from Spain.

"We're in the Antipodes. We are a very small community and we don't get together as often. We don't celebrate things as often. So this really brings people together and seeing people from different parts of the country with many, many different political views and this, all of us cheering for our country. Pretty amazing, you know, pretty amazing feeling."

Arrate and Alberto, from Bilbao, agreed.

"We are so far from home, and to [have] all the Spanish together is so great, and happy, it's beautiful, yeah," Alberto said.

Arrate and Alberto. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Arrate said they had created a WhatsApp group chat to celebrate with other Spanish fans in New Zealand.

"We are so, so happy," she said.

"During all the match, we were, like, over them, but we need the goal. We needed the goal.

"After they suspended the first one we were so, so depressed, but after that... finally Ferran [Torres] appears, and he makes us winners of the world."

However, Sophie Cotter never doubted Spain.

"I was always confident they'd win. I had a feeling from the beginning."

Sophie Cotter. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Nacho Fernandez planned to spend the rest of the day celebrating.

"It's very special to win the second World Cup, and more special to celebrate it here in New Zealand, in Auckland.

World.title: Spain's World Cup win a reminder collective spirit trumps solo stars
World.content:
You could see it in the Spanish players as they floated euphorically, each kissing the top of the trophy.

You could feel it from the fans in the stands as they straddled that blurry line between overwhelmed and overjoyed.

And you could hear it rumble through Spain, as a nation united through something which in reality should not mean this much but means more than almost anything else.

Nick Hornby summed it up best in his classic football-themed memoir Fever Pitch.

"I fell in love with football as I was later to fall in love with women: suddenly, inexplicably, uncritically, giving no thought to the pain or disruption it would bring with it."

Argentina felt its force too, the scenes of Lionel Messi in tears, fans distraught, Leandro Paredes losing control and lashing out.

Lionel Messi was crushed after the defeat. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

In that moment they thought may a love like this never find me.

World Cup football can twist and torment, ripping out your heart and stamping on it till you feel like it can never be repaired.

It can also make you fall head over heels and erase all the hurt you ever felt before.

La Roja ruthless in victory

Spain captain Rodri takes in the magnitude of the achievement. (Getty Images: Alex Pantling )

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente spoke about it in his own terms before the semi-final against France, drawing on inspiration from Julius Caesar, and the idea of having to suffer to achieve great things.

And this was a game that was a struggle for all, it lacked the overall quality and excitement you might expect from a final.

Argentina was stubborn and produced heroic defending in the box, but again questionable roughhousing tactics, eventually resulting in Enzo Fernández's send off.

The reigning champions showed little initiative to create much of anything until the final minutes of extra time as their dream dissipated in the warm New Jersey air.

Spain, having only conceded one goal all tournament, and with 20 shots to two in the decider, might not have produced its flashiest performance, but it was its most important.

This is what La Roja has done throughout the past six weeks, control the ball effortlessly, win it back almost immediately, build pressure through well-organised and committed structures, and wait till late to put it all to bed.

Ferran Torres celebrates the goal that proved to be the decider in the World Cup final between Argentina and Spain. (Getty Images)

The Spaniards were particularly effective in shutting out Messi, who saw little of the ball and was quickly dispossessed or forced into errors when he did have it.

Turns out he can be stopped; it just takes the most exceptional defensive team of this tournament to do it.

The European Champions are now World Champions for the second time, unbeaten for 38 straight matches, a magnificent footballing dynasty growing with every game, becoming the first country to simultaneously hold the men's and women's World Cups.

"I'm so proud of this generation of footballers who have grown up with this philosophy, remained true to it, made it even better and set an example as a team and a family," Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said.

"They're excellent, world-class footballers with exceptional talent. I'm very moved. Looking back and thinking about them, we've won everything, absolutely everything, with this generation of players."

Spain's collective triumph

Celebrations in Madrid will continue long after tonight. (Getty Images: Chris McGrath)

Argentina is a team built around one player, the likes of whom we have never seen before.

Spain is built around a collective approach, filled with exceptional players, but all who work in harmony, allowing each other to shine in different moments.

Like Mikel Merino with his repeated winners off the bench, or Rodri holding the side together as the linchpin in midfield, or Ferran Torres with his vital assists, and today's match-winning strike.

"I think in the end the goal came from 47 million people, not just those of us that are here," Torres said.

"Today destiny was written, it was made for us to win. We're far from our people today but we tried to be as close as possible to them.

"A huge relief [to score]. I've been criticised throughout the whole tournament but as I said before, destiny was written."

It says so much that Lamine Yamal, 19, seen by most as Messi's heir, did not play much of an influential role in this final, or at any stage during the tournament.

Lamine Yamal did not quite have the breakout tournament some predicted. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

He was not a passenger, but was certainly not a conductor, and that can only breed even further confidence, and strike further fear into other nations, as he goes from boy to man.

This World Cup started slowly for Spain, a scoreless draw with the tournament's best underdog story, Cabo Verde.

But as the superstars like Messi, Kylian Mbappé, Erling Haaland, Harry Kane, and Jude Bellingham took all the headlines and dominated social media algorithms, Spain was the quiet, conscientious achiever.

That all changed with the terrifyingly efficient dismantling of France in the semifinals, and now a completely deserved win in the final.

"This generation of players is an example for Spanish sport, for the Spanish youth," de la Fuente said.

"Together we are much stronger, and that is why we don't forget anyone."

A team forged through fire, built on discipline and togetherness, now enjoying its love story.

World.title: Tears streaming down his face, Messi leaves the World Cup stage a legend
World.content:
Lionel Messi had so desperately hoped his World Cup would end differently.

Tears running down his cheeks, a silver medal around his neck, his teammates in various states of depression, strewn around him like the detritus of some cataclysmic event as Spain roared amid garish golden confetti and an explosion of colour and joy.

Arguably the greatest player to ever grace a pitch was distraught.

It's impossible to know exactly what was going through his mind.

A decade earlier, on the same Metlife Stadium pitch where he was currently sobbing, Messi had tearfully decided to retire from international football after losing the Copa América final against enormous underdogs Chile.

The pain of that defeat was simply too much to bear for Messi, saddled with the expectation of a nation desperate to anoint him as Maradona's heir.

The world was the beneficiary as Messi reversed that decision.

Fans around the world have rejoiced at Messi's success. (Getty Images: Wang HE)

So too were Argentina, who claimed the 2021 Copa América title, the 2022 Finalissima and, most tellingly, the 2022 World Cup under Messi's leadership, cementing his legacy among his fellow countrymen for all time.

But once again in the New Jersey sunshine, Messi's tears were the defining feature for a generation of football fans.

Was this another tearful goodbye to the international stage?

Messi is 39 years old.

With 19-year-olds Lamine Yamal and Pau Cubarsí on the other side of the divide and winning for Spain, the next generation is not just arriving to force him out but has already arrived.

To play another World Cup in four years may be beyond even his mystic powers, even despite his impressive ability to adapt to the constraints his age has imposed on him.

The next generation, personified by Lamine Yamal, is snapping at Messi's aging heels. (Getty Images: PA Images/Bradley Collyer)

At this World Cup, Messi has walked for roughly half the time he was on the pitch, strolling and stalking for about 5 kilometres per game.

And yet, inarguably, no one player has had a greater role in his team's success than Messi has for Argentina.

His goals, eight of them, and his four assists dragged the defending champions through the group stage and the knockout rounds.

His ability to bend a game to his will, no matter the situation, made him seem nothing short of inevitable.

Despite all the walking, whenever Argentina threatened, the little magician was there in the heart of the action, conjuring and scheming and dragging his team home just when they needed him to.

His very presence seemed to inspire his teammates to feats beyond their capabilities, a totemic figure to rally around, his energy imbuing those around him with positivity and confidence and class.

Lionel Messi came close to lifting the World Cup for the second time. (Getty Images: FIFA/Tullio Puglia)

Against England in the semifinal, his two assists powered the Albiceleste to a famous victory in stoppage time.

Against Egypt, as his team faced elimination at 2-0 down, he provided the cross for the first and delivered the shot for its equaliser.

Against Spain in the final? It just didn't happen.

The fact that his tears only came after he had been given his silver medal was almost illustrative: No matter how late it got, Messi perhaps still had hope that he might somehow manage to influence the game in his favour.

He'd done it before, after all.

Only when Donald Trump laid the heavy silver slice of defeat around his neck did he realise there would be no more magic, that no amount of sorcery from his phenomenal feet could change history now.

Against Spain, the little master managed just 55 touches, none of which came in the Spain penalty area.

Lionel Messi was unable to stamp his authority on the contest. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maja Hitij)

He was stifled as effectively as if Spain wrapped him in a blanket.

And his Argentina teammates simply couldn't back up their superstar when it mattered most.

Messi could not deliver the magical moment that his nation demanded.

It was telling that Argentina offered so little other than niggly fouls and angry words as opposed to the free-flowing football Spain occasionally managed when the mood took them.

Let's not beat around the bush: Argentina were woeful in this final.

Argentina didn't have a single shot on goal in the first 90 minutes of the game, the first time any team has failed to do so in a World Cup final.

Their first attempt on goal did not come until the 26th minute of extra time.

Lionel Messi had Argentina's first shot of the game, in the second half of extra time. (Getty Images: FIFA/Maja Hitij)

Their 25 total fouls resulted in seven yellow cards, one of which was a second that saw Enzo Fernández up-end Pau Cubarsí, making him the sixth player ever to be dismissed in a World Cup final.

Argentina's nefarious skulduggery was finally, belatedly, penalised by a referee brave enough not to stand for it.

Coach Lionel Scaloni said afterwards that his team "showed that we know how to lose" in his post-match press conference, but nothing could be further from the truth.

The Argentines thoroughly disgraced themselves after the game's conclusion, Leandro Paredes lashing out and sparking a minor brawl that ended with him shown a red card after the final whistle.

Fractious barely covers it.

If this is to be his international swan song, the landscape post-Messi may as well be post-apocalyptic, so absent of joy and light does it appear to hold.

Claudio Tapia, the president of the Argentina Football Association, knows how important Messi is to the team. (Getty Images: Andrew Harnik)

It was not Messi's fault that he could not have the impact on the game he might have hoped for.

Spain were able to successfully nullify a far better team than Argentina in the semifinal with their Rodri-led midfield dominance suffocating their opponents' creativity.

Messi simply didn't have the space.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

He was closed down as ominously and relentlessly as the ticking of the clock that will one day herald the end of his stellar career.

Messi couldn't muster the magic to help Argentina become the third men's team to win back-to-back World Cups.

It is not the finale that Messi might have envisaged.

But if this is to be his tearful sign off, fans will still look back at having been blessed by one of football's greatest of all time.

World.title: The 13 photos that summed up the chaos of the 2026 World Cup final
World.content:
It was a tournament where the football was magical, the off-field antics were questionable, and ultimately, Spain left the United States as the champions of the world.

A day after the utter chaos of the third-placed playoff between France and England, where 10 goals were scored, Argentina and Spain played things a little more conservatively — right up until the game exploded into action.

Here are the 13 photos that tell the story of the 2026 FIFA World Cup final.

1. The Fresh Prince of Barcelona

Teenage superstar Lamine Yamal arrives at the stadium looking like the coolest dude on earth. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

While much of the tournament had been focused on the more established superstar names like Lionel Messi, Erling Haaland and Kylian Mbappé, teenager Lamine Yamal had floated under the radar for the World Cup passers-by.

Coming to the final having never lost a match where he had started for Spain, expectations were high on the 19-year-old as he came into the stadium. Would he be the hero that Spain needed to overcome the perceived might of Argentina?

Whatever the pressure, he arrived looking like the coolest dude on the planet, calm, collected and rocking a style straight out of The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air.

2. Smoke and mirrors

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney greets US President Donald Trump ahead of the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

All eyes turned to the skies before kick-off as US President Donald Trump made his usual subtle entrance into the area, coming in low and fast in the Marine One helicopter.

Once settled in prime position in a corporate box on the wings, Trump was afforded the questionable chance to give the trophy a little pat as FIFA boss Gianni Infantino brought the iconic gold statue to Trump's seat.

Before that, though, there was the potentially awkward meeting between Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, just a couple of days after Trump accused Canada of being "filthy" and "polluted" over its wildfire smoke that had blanketed New York in the lead-up to the tournament.

All-in-all things seemed reasonably diplomatic, given Mother Nature had done her job to send the smoke packing just in time for the game.

3. America makes a double Buff

American announcer Bruce Buffer turns the World Cup into a blood sport briefly with his iconic introduction. (Getty Images: Sebastian Widmann)

In the most American moment of this entire game, event organisers decided that what this little old soccer match needed was a double Buffer.

Bruce and Michael Buffer, to be exact, the legendary ring announcers from every blood sport imaginable.

Flipping from one brother to the next, the pair excitedly announced that the game was "ready to rumble", in scenes not far off that time that soccer came to Springfield in The Simpsons.

4. The GOAT meets the rising star

Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal share a laugh together early in the match. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Looking a little less cool than when he arrived, but still the picture of confidence, Yamal made a beeline for Lionel Messi before the match to wish arguably the greatest player in history some luck.

It was a full circle moment for the pair, who originally met on a photo shoot in 2007 when Yamal's parents won a Unicef raffle to have Yamal photographed for a calendar with the then rising star Messi.

This time around Messi's hair was a little shorter and his face a little more wearied, while Yamal was a little less nude.

5. The World Cup's Mariah Carey

Shakira performs during the halftime show, a spectacle one England footballing legend would go on to call "crap". (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

Shakira was rolled out for the halftime show, with the Colombian star fast becoming to the World Cup what Mariah Carey is to Christmas.

She's just always there.

While her performance was fantastic, the rest of it — from Justin Bieber to Madonna to BTS — left a little bit to be desired.

So much so that English footballing champion Wayne Rooney didn't hold back with what he thought.

"I thought it was crap," he said on the BBC coverage.

6. The spectacular red card

Enzo Fernandez fouls Spain's Pau Cubarsi, leading to the Argentinian's second yellow card and a send-off. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

As soon as we all saw it happen on the TV, we knew that the photos were going to be spectacular.

And veteran Getty photographer Al Bello didn't let us down.

Rising Spanish star Pau Cubarsi was sent flying by Argentina's Enzo Fernandez, but it was made all the more spectacular by Cubarsi really leaning into the flip.

Had Fernandez not already had a yellow, it's unlikely he would have been sent off at all, but the red card made it all the more dramatic as the scores stood at 0-0 heading into the death.

7. Hydration break goes to a new level

Spain's Dani Olmo takes the hydration break to the extreme as he utilises the sprinklers to cool down. (Getty Images: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu)

Two things have been major talking points during this tournament — it's been bloody hot and the hydration breaks have been bloody irritating.

So it was fun to see the two come together in the final regular time break of the tournament, as the Spanish players took advantage of the sprinklers to cool off.

Was it the trick that won them the World Cup? Who's to say. But almost certainly yes.

8. Free kick wipes a goal

Nico Williams reacts after his goal was marked off for a foul that was immediately obvious on the replays afterwards. (Getty Images: Carl Recine)

In a moment of brilliance, Nico Williams looked to have won it for Spain when he slotted a goal past the keeper to make it 1-0 late.

But the referee called it back. There was a free kick somewhere in the mess of bodies in the box.

In live action it wasn't immediately clear where the free kick was. On replay, it still wasn't totally clear.

But on the fifth or sixth watch — yeah, no idea.

Williams was furious, and rightfully so.

9. Deadlock ends in headlock

Nico Williams gives Ferran Torres a little chokehold celebration after Torres scored the winning goal. (Getty Images: Nick Potts)

Go back to the very first photo at the top of this story and you can experience the majesty of the Ferran Torres goal that broke the game open.

Hair blowing in the breeze, his teammates running in behind him, the fans screaming and cheering in ecstasy.

And then Williams decided to choke Torres for some reason.

Angry that he wasn't the hero after his goal was wiped? An in-joke that we don't know about?

Who knows. But it made for an odd scene in an incredible moment.

10. Tears of a legend

Lionel Messi slumps to the ground after the final whistle, in what will likely be the football legend's last World Cup game. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

Small in stature but grand in legacy, Messi cut a forlorn figure after the final whistle.

His tiny body huddled in the middle of the massive stadium was enough to make anyone feel sorry for the attacking superstar.

His place as the greatest player the game has ever seen would have been secured had he managed to drag his teammates to victory, but even Messi couldn't get his countrymen through the incredible defensive wall that Spain had built.

11. Infantino chases after Trump

Rodri prepares to lift trophy as Gianni Infantino attempts to move Donald Trump out of frame. (Getty Images: Dan Mullan)

Trump had made headlines this time last year when he joined Chelsea on stage for the celebrations in the Club World Cup final, despite the apparent confusion of the players.

This time there was surely no way that Trump would be caught right in the middle of the pack as the Spanish players lifted the most coveted trophy in world sport, right?

Well, kind of. This time Trump wandered right across stage as Infantino pivoted left, leaving the FIFA boss to scramble after the US president, with the pair awkwardly caught in the team celebration photos.

On the broadcast, you could hear someone say "they'll crop him out" in an unexpected, but funny, hot mic moment.

12. Utter heartache for Argentina

Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez shows his dejection as the ceremony for the winners gets into full swing. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

Goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez had been immense through the World Cup.

But as Spain lifted the trophy, the Aston Villa keeper let the emotions flow, caught by the camera as he sat on the sidelines thinking about what might have been.

It was a reminder of what this thing, this silly, epic, immense mess of a game, means to the people who play it.

13. The love of a mum

Lamine Yamal's mum races out onto the field to celebrate the victory with her son. (Getty Images: John Todd)

In the end, all we really want is the hug of a mum who's proud of you.

And that's what Yamal got as his mum, Sheila, ran onto the ground to give her son a big old cuddle.

Having given birth at just 16 years old as an immigrant from Equatorial Guinea, Sheila's story is the one that really captures the essence of the World Cup.

Not the championship rings or corporate boxes. Not the powerful men in powerful suits making powerful political moves.

A mum with a dream for her son to shine on the world stage.

This was the moment that really mattered.

World.title: Bombers star cleared for return despite abrupt mid-game hospital visit
World.content:
Essendon's star forward Nate Caddy has been cleared to return to action after being hospitalised with an elevated heart rate.

Caddy was sent to hospital during the Bombers' win against GWS on Sunday but was discharged that night.

The 21-year-old is expected to train with his teammates this week and play against Hawthorn on Saturday.

"There was some concern in the first quarter when Nate's heart rate became elevated," Essendon's football boss Dan McPherson said on Monday.

"He was removed from the game and our medical team assessed him at the ground before sending him to hospital for further assessment.

"He was discharged last night and is back at home."

McPherson said Caddy, who recently signed a contract extension until the end of 2031, was expected to "train and play without concern this week".

World.title: Reese accepts Brondello's apology over 'protected species' comment
World.content:
Angel Reese has accepted Australian coach Sandy Brondello's apology for an inappropriate comment about the Atlanta Dream star.

The WNBA suspended Brondello for one game after she was overheard calling Reese a "protected species" during the Dream's 111-92 win over Brondello's Toronto Tempo at the weekend.

"First, I appreciate Sandy's apology, but I also appreciate the love and support that I've had for the last 48 hours," Reese said before the Dream played the Chicago Sky on Monday (AEST).

"It has been very overwhelming with a lot of love and also other things. But I am grateful that the league did take action."

Brondello's comment about Reese was picked up by the broadcast after Toronto player Nyara Sabally went down with an injury and was called for a foul following contact with Reese.

Brondello apologised on social media and Reese posted "ARE WE SURPRISED?!" after the game, tagging Brondello's account, followed by a clown face emoji.

The "protected species" phrase is used in Australian sports to express frustration for a lack of calls against a player. However, in the US, the phrase suggests that someone isn't human and could be seen as derogatory toward Black people.

"There is no place for discrimination or hate in this league from anyone — from fans to coaches to players," Reese said.

"I'm just grateful that we are able to move on from the situation and just play winning basketball. The WNBA is supposed to be positive and we are going in a great light right now, so I just want to continue that and move forward."

AP

World.title: Quick hits: Trump crashes Spain's party, Argentina lose heads in defeat
World.content:
Argentina's players lash out in defeat, Ferran Torres becomes a Spanish icon forever, and Donald Trump attempts to crash the winners' party.

Here are today's quick hits.

1. Ferran Torres. Remember the name

The surest way to ensure your name lives forever in the annals of football history is to score the winner in a World Cup final. With a brilliantly struck half-volley in the 106th minute of the 2026 final, Spain's Ferran Torres joined that illustrious group.

Spain had dominated the game. It had ridden the many, many challenges of an Argentina side hell-bent on destroying the match's flow, but had still been taken deep into extra time without a breakthrough.

Ferran Torres celebrates scoring the winning goal in a World Cup final. (Getty Images: David Ramos)

Lamine Yamal nearly scored from a free kick in regulation. Nico Williams thought he had scored, before the referee's whistle intervened. Mikel Merino should have scored moments later, but his free header blazed wide.

But in the end, it was all just in service of Torres's magic moment. Williams did brilliantly to keep a cross alive with a clever header back into a dangerous spot. Without the requirement of a settling touch, Torres lifted the killer blow above Argentina's keeper, Emi Martinez.

An injury time winner settled Spain's first World Cup title, Andres Iniesta the provider in 2010. He now has company in Spanish folklore. Ferran Torres, a legend forever.

Loading...

2. Disgraceful Argentinian head-loss in defeat

There are ways to win, and there are ways to lose. Argentina had already tread the line of the former this World Cup, but blew any notion of sportsmanship out of the water in the final defeat.

As Spain's players ran onto the field in celebration at the final whistle, Argentina's Nahuel Molina threw a punch to the chest of Spanish midfielder Rodri.

Rodri turned, reacting with surprise and anger, and from there, a scrap broke out.

Leandro Paredes lashed out Gavi after full-time. (Getty Images: Marvin Ibo Guengoer)

Argentina's Leandro Paredes, who had already been yellow carded in the game for pushing a player over in an earlier stink, completely lost his head.

Paredes went after Spain's Gavi, grabbing him by the neck and throwing him to the ground.

Paredes was shown a red card after the match had finished for his outburst, while Argentina's manager Lionel Scaloni had to run onto the field to break up the melee.

A disappointing exit for Argentina on an overall disappointing day.

3. Wild challenge and red card cost Argentina

Paredes was not the first Argentinian to see red, and indeed the game's first dismissal had far more bearing on the result.

Enzo Fernández was shown a second yellow and then a red just before the end of regulation time, forcing Argentina to try to hold on with 10 men through the 30 minutes to come.

Pau Cubarsi goes flying after Enzo Fernandez's tackle.

Fernandez's first booking was seemingly for dissent, as he vociferously disagreed with a refereeing decision, but his second was an outrageously dumb and reckless challenge.

With a 50-50 there to be won, Spain's Pau Cubarsi got to the ball a split second before Fernandez, but the Argentine made no effort at all to avoid the contact he was about to create. He leapt into the challenge, sending Cubarsi flying head over heels through the air.

Fernández again tried to argue the point with the referee, but there was no chance at all of a reprieve. A moment of recklessness had taken Argentina's precarious position and made it somehow even worse.

4. Messi can't rescue a dismal performance

Lionel Messi could not hold back the tears at the full-time whistle, or indeed after he had received his runners-up medal. If this is to be his final World Cup bow, as must surely be the case, it was a desperate way to say goodbye.

Argentina was pitiful for almost the entirety of this final. It did not manage a single shot until the 116th minute of the game — not just a shot on target, a single shot at all. Not one!

Lionel Messi slumped to the turf after Argentina's defeat. (Getty Images: Michael Regan)

It had clearly come with a plan to try to frustrate Spain, disrupt its rhythm with fouls and time-wasting, and hope Messi could create some magic the other way.

It succeeded on the first two fronts, but even Messi, playing a lone hand against a disciplined and tactically supreme Spain side, could not find a way to threaten.

Spain, to its credit, remained patient with the ball and alert to any danger in defence. It continued to play its football, metronomic at times and very easy on the eye at others, and eventually got the result it deserved.

As did Argentina.

5. Trump crashes the Spanish party

It had long since been telegraphed that Donald Trump's first game day appearance at this World Cup would be at the final, and that he would join his mate Gianni Infantino on the pitch to present the medals and trophy after the game.

And yet it remained a curious sight as he stood in the middle of the Spanish celebrations, aimlessly wandering around and gesturing towards players, refusing to get out of the way so they could enjoy the fulfilment of their lifelong dream.

Donald Trump inserted himself in Spain's World Cup celebrations. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

This too was no surprise, as Trump did the same thing last year when Chelsea won the Club World Cup. That time, the players were surprised as Trump stood in the middle of the trophy celebration, grinning widely.

This time, Spain captain Rodri made a point of trying to usher him out of the way. Infantino chased him across the stage, trying in vain to get him out of the way. He remained on the periphery, but crucially still within camera shot, when Rodri lifted the World Cup.

Perhaps a perfect way to sum up this tournament. Brilliant at its heart, when the football was the focus, but rather unseemly in the background and on the fringes.

World.title: A quick breakdown of the offside rule
World.content:
Spain has just won the FIFA World Cup 1-0 in a match against Argentina that ran down to the wire.

During extra time, it looked as though Ferran Torres had scored a goal that would have brought Spain's lead to two and sealed a victory.

It was the second goal disallowed for Spain, this time for offside.

So what is the offside rule?

It's an infamous question asked by millions of football newbies every tournament.

If you've jumped on the World Cup bandwagon and found yourself trying to wrap your head around this section of the rule book, we're here to help.

Here's a quick breakdown of the rule.

Why does it exist?

The offside rule aims to prevent players from lingering next to the opponent's net to wait for a pass.

It forces teams to build up play carefully and use complex tactics to score goals.

Without the rule, teams would be incentivised to constantly launch long balls, making the game less dynamic.

So how does it work?

If a player is called for an offside offence, the referee will stop the play and award an indirect free kick to the opposing team.

The free kick is taken from the spot where the offside player had been located when their teammate passed them the ball.

What is a free kick? Read more A free kick is awarded when a player on one team does something wrong, with the referee giving the other team a chance to kick the ball while play has stopped. A penalty is essentially the same thing, except the kick is taken inside the penalty box, which is directly in front of the goal, and opposing players aren't allowed to interfere until after the shot is taken. Goals can be scored from either a free kick or a penalty kick, but they are more easily achieved from penalties.

When is a player offside?

A player is in an offside position if:

they're standing in their opponent's half; and

they're nearer to the goal than both the ball and the last line of defenders at the exact moment the ball is passed to them by a teammate.

However, an offside player is only penalised if they become involved in play.

And there's no offside offence if a player receives the ball directly from an opposition player, a goal kick, a throw-in or a corner kick.

World.title: Vingegaard forced out of Tour after fracture in 'devastating' crash
World.content:
Jonas Vingegaard will undergo surgery on a fractured collarbone after his Tour de France ended abruptly with a crash near the end of the 15th stage.

The 2022 and '23 Tour champion was among a few riders who fell close to a kerb some 20 kilometres from the end of the stage. After a few moments, Vingegaard's Tour was over as he limped into an ambulance with his right arm in a sling.

"Jonas sustained a fractured collarbone and multiple abrasions," his Visma–Lease a Bike team said in a statement posted on X. "Due to the severity of the collarbone fracture, surgical intervention has been recommended and will be performed in the coming days. Join us in wishing Jonas a smooth recovery."

Vingegaard had been in second place overall behind defending champion Tadej Pogačar heading into Stage 15, which finished with a big climb.

"It is devastating that Jonas has had to leave the Tour de France," the team's sporting director, Marc Reef, said. "It was quickly clear that Jonas could not continue. He was in a lot of pain."

The 29-year-old Danish rider became one of only eight male riders to have won all three Grand Tours this year.

"I'm really sad to see Jonas crash out," the four-time Tour champion Pogacar said.

" Without him, the Tour will not be the same. "

Vingegaard's teammate Sepp Kuss and Pogačar's UAE Emirates XRG teammate Isaac Del Toro also fell but were able to continue.

Pogačar's yellow jersey group slowed down after hearing news of the crash — perhaps unsure whether he would continue or not — but resumed racing normally after a few moments when it became clear Vingegaard was out.

Before crashing, Vingegaard looked poised to attack in the 11-kilometre final climb up Plateau de Solaison in the French Alps.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"We had two riders in the breakaway and controlled the peloton," Reef said. "Jonas felt extremely good, and we wanted to go for the victory today. Unfortunately, cycling can be very cruel at times."

Del Toro finished the stage in third place behind Pogačar and stage winner Remco Evenepoel.

Evenepoel climbed to second in the standings, five minutes behind Pogačar, with Del Toro 5:58 back in third place.

Pogačar said after the stage that he and Vingegaard were woken in the early hours of Sunday morning by officials conducting unannounced anti-doping tests.

Pogačar said his test was carried out at 5am and that Vingegaard's was at 2am.

AP

Also, shoutout to subscriber morgannels for bringing this one to my attention in last week’s what are you listening to thread. ʅ͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡(̸̢̛̼̞̭͋ͅ)̸͚̰͛̔̾̀̿͒͂:̴͓̞̑̌̂̆̊͋̀:̸͎̟̯̂̓̌ ҉ ͡ ͞ ͞ ͞ ҉● ࿀ ● ࿀ ● ҉⃝ ⃝͢ ͞ ͘ ͞⃝̕ ͢ ̛ ⃝ ̸ ̡ ͢⃝̧ ͡ ͡ ̀ ̧ ̢⃝͜ ҉ ͞ ͞ ⃝͞ ͞ ͡⃝ ⃝҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉ :̶̢͙͙͕̠̩͆(̷̮͍͚̫͚͂̍)̵̳̗̊( ̟̞̝̜̙̘̗̖҉̵̴̨̧̢̡̼̻̺̹̳̲̱̰̯̮̭̬̫̪̩̦̥ by ⣎⡇ꉺლ༽இ•̛)ྀ◞ ༎ຶ ༽ৣৢ؞ৢ؞ؖ ꉺლ For years, Hebden has kept this alias somewhat of a secret. But now that this collection of wingdings has racked up millions of listens on services like Spotify, it’s get a more formal release with wingdings. Some of the tracks here have been released previously, including track five, which Fred Again dropped during his incredible Boiler Room set as “Feelings,” under one of Hebdens’ other aliases, KH. Wingdings leans heavily towards Four Tet’s dancier outputs. And, despite what the project’s origins as some sort of secret b-side dumping ground might lead you to believe, these are not throwaways. They’re undeniable, infectious, and highly polished. Four Tet’s sense for sound design shines from crushed 8-bit drums to the hypnotic handpan grooves and sharp synth melodies. While the songs are definitely groovy and danceable, they’re not high-octane rave-ups, for the most part. Instead, tracks like number seven build to a more ecstatic and spiritual climax as layers pile up and textures demand you turn your eyes towards the sky. Not unlike last week’s recommendation, Shall We Go On Sinning So That Grace May Increase?, Wingdings is a celebration. No, I might not drop the triphop-esque track one at the club, but it’s perfect for finding your groove while trying to write, or cleaning, or any other activity where you want good vibes and grooves. Track two would feel more at home on a dance floor with its deep four-on-the-floor thump and plucked arpeggios that seem to be constantly climbing off into infinity as house hi-hats tick along. Track three blends metallic gamelan-inspired melodies and ultradeep EDM wubs, while track eight is beautiful comedown ambiance. Four Tet’s Wingdings is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Apple Music, Spotify, Deezer, and Qobuz.
